acanthoma-fissuratum: Spectacle-frame lesion: firm flesh-coloured papule, nodule or plaque with a central furrow ('coffee bean' appearance) on the lateral nasal bridge or behind the ear, often painful if ulcerated. Despite the name granuloma fissuratum, no granulomas on histology (acanthosis, hypergranulosis, fibrotic stroma). Can mimic BCC; resolves if the pressure is removed.
ace-inhibitor-induced-angioedema: Bradykinin-mediated (not histamine) swelling of lips, tongue or face without itch or urticaria, usually in the first weeks but can be delayed months to years; more common in African descent. No response to antihistamines, adrenaline or steroids; GI form can lead to unnecessary laparotomy. Stop the ACEi permanently; ARNi also contraindicated.
achenbach-syndrome: Paroxysmal painful blue-purple bruising of a finger or palm (usually 2nd or 3rd finger, palmar dominant hand) in middle-aged women, often after minor trauma; fingertip and nail bed are spared. Resolves in 3-6 days without the usual bruise colour changes. Pulses, perfusion, capillaroscopy and clotting tests are normal. Benign; avoid aspirin and NSAIDs.
achromic-naevus: Uncommon, stable, usually solitary well-defined hypopigmented (not completely white) patch, often with small satellite macules like a paint splash; present at birth or early childhood, mostly on the trunk, may follow Blaschko lines (mosaicism). Wood lamp: off-white, versus chalk-white in vitiligo. Multiple ash-leaf macules point to tuberous sclerosis.
acne-agminata: Red-brown papules on the eyelids, forehead, cheeks and chin; synonym lupus miliaris disseminatus faciei. Histology shows dermal epithelioid granulomas that may be caseating without tubercle bacilli. Comedones absent and eyelids involved (unlike acne vulgaris). Exclude sarcoidosis, TB; regresses with scarring in 2-3 years.
acne-due-to-medicine: Drug-induced acne: oral corticosteroids (steroid acne), anabolic steroids (danazol, stanozolol, nandrolone) causing acne conglobata or fulminans, testosterone, progestogen contraceptives. Others: halogens (iodides, bromides), antiepileptics, antituberculous drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin), lithium, B vitamins, EGFR inhibitors.
acne-excorie: Picked acne in which active lesions have been removed, leaving only excoriations, crusts, pigmentation and scars with few or no primary lesions. More common in females, particularly late-onset acne. Linked to body dysmorphic disorder or compulsive picking; may need psychological therapy.
acne-fulminans: Abrupt onset of painful, ulcerated nodular acne with bleeding crusts on the chest and back plus systemic features: fever, arthralgia (sacroiliac), malaise, weight loss. Mostly adolescent males; raised ESR/CRP and possible osteolytic bone lesions. Triggers: testosterone/anabolic steroids and oral isotretinoin. SAPHO is a complication; start with systemic steroids.
acne-scarring: Most acne scars are atrophic: ice-pick (most common, narrow, V-shaped, deeper than wide), boxcar (round or oval with sharp edges) and rolling (sloping edges). Keloid or hypertrophic scars favour the jawline, chest and upper back and are more common in skin of colour. Smoking worsens scarring; treat active acne before scar management.
acne-urticata: Intensely itchy papules, vesicles and pustules in the face, neck and upper trunk/arm 'cape' distribution, which are picked and leave crusts and small white scars. Typically middle-aged women under stress. Not true acne; may be compulsive picking or polymorphous light eruption when confined to sun-exposed sites.
acquired-blaschkoid-dermatitis: Rare, unilateral eczematous eruption along Blaschko lines, not present at birth (blaschkitis); may be the adult form of lichen striatus. Histology shows spongiotic dermatitis; biopsy helps exclude other Blaschko-linear dermatoses such as lichen planus or linear psoriasis. Relapses, especially with stress; topical steroids generally ineffective.
acquired-dermal-macular-hyperpigmentatio: Umbrella term for erythema dyschromicum perstans, lichen planus pigmentosus and idiopathic eruptive macular hyperpigmentation: blue-brown to slate-grey macules from persistent dermal melanophages. Histology shows dermal melanin and melanophages with interface change. Hair dye patch test positive in up to 36%. EDP is chronic and progressive; idiopathic eruptive form resolves spontaneously.
acquired-keratoderma: Non-inherited palmoplantar thickening in adults, with causes including drugs (lithium, hydroxyurea, imatinib, capecitabine), arsenic, dermatoses (psoriasis, lichen planus, PRP), crusted scabies, Trichophyton rubrum, and keratoderma climactericum. Think internal malignancy if progression is rapid with acanthosis nigricans (tripe palms) or if psoriasiform plaques and paronychia suggest acrokeratosis paraneoplastica.
acquired-lymphangiectasia: Frogspawn-like clear or haemorrhagic papules that ooze clear or milky fluid, arising after lymphatic injury or blockage (lymph node dissection, radiotherapy, cancer). Sites include axilla after mastectomy, thighs and vulva. Can predispose to cellulitis. Biopsy shows thin-walled lymphatic vessels.
acral-persistent-papular-mucinosis: Subtype of localised lichen myxoedematosus: 2-5 mm ivory or skin-coloured asymptomatic papules on the backs of hands, wrists and forearms that persist and increase; women 3:1. Histology: mucin in papillary and mid-dermis with a grenz zone, variable fibroblasts (Alcian blue, colloidal iron). Unlike scleromyxoedema, no gammopathy, thyroid or systemic disease. Treatments generally unsuccessful.
acrocyanosis: Painless, symmetrical, persistent blue discolouration of hands and feet from cold-induced vasospasm; pulses are normal with no ulceration or gangrene. Crocq sign: slow, irregular return of colour after blanching. Calcium channel blockers do not help, unlike in Raynaud. Asymmetry or pain suggests secondary acrocyanosis; nailfold capillaroscopy helps exclude connective tissue disease.
acrodermatitis-chronica-atrophicans: Late-stage Lyme disease from Borrelia afzelii (Europe): unilateral violaceous swelling of the extensor limbs that progresses to thin, tissue-paper atrophy with loss of adnexa. Mostly middle-aged to older women; may follow erythema migrans. Diagnosis: high Borrelia IgG; biopsy shows lymphocytes and plasma cells. Treated early the changes are reversible; atrophy persists if late.
acrokeratoelastoidosis: Autosomal dominant punctate palmoplantar keratoderma (type III) with 2-5 mm firm skin-coloured or yellowish papules along the sides of the hands and feet, starting around puberty. Histology: hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, hypergranulosis and elastorrhexis; focal acral keratosis is the variant without elastorrhexis. Stable and asymptomatic; no cure and treatment usually not needed.
acrokeratosis-neoplastica: Bazex syndrome (paraneoplastic acrokeratosis): psoriasis-like scaling of fingers and toes, far more common in males, with nail dystrophy and painful paronychia without infection, scaly ears/nose/cheeks and honeycomb palmoplantar keratoderma. Usually squamous cell carcinoma of the upper aerodigestive tract; resolves with tumour removal, recurrence suggests relapse. Distinct from the genetic Bazex syndrome with many BCCs.
acrokeratosis-verruciformis-of-hopf: Autosomal dominant ATP2A2 mutation (the Darier disease gene; SERCA2 calcium pump); flat-topped skin-coloured keratotic papules on the dorsal hands and feet from birth or early childhood. Nails may be dystrophic with longitudinal ridges and nicks; palmar pits can occur. Histology: hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis and 'church spires'. Asymptomatic; no treatment needed.
acromegaly: Excess GH/IGF-1 in adults, over 98% from a pituitary adenoma. Skin: thick doughy skin, enlarged hands and feet, deep forehead creases, large pores, hyperhidrosis, seborrhoea, skin tags, acanthosis nigricans, cutis verticis gyrata. Associated with Carney and McCune-Albright syndromes; pachydermoperiostosis mimics it without GH excess. Raised GH and IGF-I; risk of diabetes, cardiovascular disease and colon polyps.
acropustulosis-of-infancy: Itchy red macules becoming vesicles and pustules on the palms and soles of infants in the first 2-3 years, in recurrent crops that heal with temporary pigmented marks. Some cases follow scabies, possibly an allergic reaction to the mite. Treatment often not needed; dapsone for difficult cases.
actinic-prurigo: Intensely itchy papules, plaques and nodules on sun-exposed skin (also lips in 60–70%, conjunctiva in 45%); persists year-round and can involve covered sites. More common in Latin American and American Indian people; HLA DRB1*0407 increased. Looks like atopic dermatitis but worse on exposed sites. Also called Hutchinson prurigo; thalidomide has been used.
acute-haemorrhagic-oedema-of-infancy: Small-vessel vasculitis of infants aged 4 months-2 years: cockade (target-like) purpura on the face, ears and extremities with tender oedema and low-grade fever, yet the child is well; trunk and mucosa spared. Leukocytoclastic vasculitis like HSP, but IgA on DIF in only one-third. Resolves spontaneously in 1-3 weeks.
acute-hair-matting: Sudden stiff, impenetrable mass of matted scalp hair on the vertex (plica polonica, plica neuropathica, "bird's nest" hair), mostly in women with long curly, weathered hair. Contributors: poor hygiene, head lice, harsh shampoo or chemicals, impetigo, intense rubbing. Main complication is bacterial infection; trichoscopy shows tufted knots, twisting, nits.
acute-hepatic-porphyrias: AIP, variegate porphyria and hereditary coproporphyria are autosomal dominant with low penetrance (10% or less); recurrent neurovisceral abdominal pain. Skin lesions (photosensitivity, blisters, milia) occur in VP and HCP but not AIP. Test light-protected urinary porphobilinogen. Triggers: drugs, female hormones, fasting, alcohol.
acute-inflammatory-oedema: Pseudocellulitis of critically ill patients (ICU stay, fluid overload, organ dysfunction, hypoalbuminaemia): bilateral red, non-tender, pitting, blanchable plaques on dependent sites with generalised oedema; may show peau d'orange or oedema bullae. Unilateral disease points elsewhere. Biopsy: papillary dermal oedema with neutrophils and lymphocytes, no organisms. Treat fluid overload; stop unneeded antibiotics.
acute-localised-exanthematous-pustulosis: Localised form of AGEP: sudden clustered pustules on red oedematous skin, usually the face, days after starting a drug; tight rather than itchy. Amoxicillin-containing antibiotics most often. Pus culture usually sterile; subcorneal/intraepidermal pustules with neutrophils and eosinophils; patch test positive in about half.
acute-urticaria: Weals lasting under 24 hours, with or without angioedema, for under 6 weeks; mast cell and basophil mediators (histamine), bradykinin in angioedema. Triggers: viral infection, food allergy, antibiotics, aspirin and NSAIDs, opiates, radiocontrast (pseudoallergy). Vessel-wall damage on biopsy indicates urticarial vasculitis. ACE inhibitors can cause angioedema without urticaria.
adult-acne: Persistent (onset in teens) or late-onset (after age 25) acne, more often in women. Inflammatory lesions on the jawline and neck, premenstrual flares and macrocomedones are typical. Consider hormonal factors (polycystic ovarian disease, androgenic medicines); antiandrogens such as spironolactone are used; isotretinoin must not be taken in pregnancy.
adult-onset-still-disease: Triad of arthritis, high spiking fevers once or twice daily and a non-itchy salmon-pink rash on limbs and trunk that comes and goes with the fever; flagellate eruption may occur. Neutrophilia, raised ferritin, negative rheumatoid factor. Yamaguchi criteria (at least 2 major and 5 total) after excluding sepsis, mononucleosis and malignancy. Juvenile form is systemic-onset JIA.
aerobic-vaginitis: Vaginal inflammation and epithelial atrophy with increased aerobic bacteria (E. coli, S. aureus, enterococci) and decreased lactobacilli; sticky yellow-green rotten-smelling discharge, stinging, dyspareunia, raised pH. Diagnosed by wet-mount microscopy (aerobic vaginitis score). Often confused with bacterial vaginosis (fishy grey discharge, no inflammation); metronidazole and antifungals are ineffective.
aeromonas-skin-infection: Gram-negative aquatic bacterium (usually A. hydrophila) entering broken skin exposed to fresh or salt water; all leeches carry it, so leech bites and medical leech therapy are a source. Presents as folliculitis, abscess, impetigo-like rash leading to ecthyma gangrenosum, cellulitis, necrotising fasciitis or sepsis. Usually resistant to penicillin; worse in immunocompromised patients.
ageing-skin: Intrinsic ageing gives thin, dry, pale, finely wrinkled skin; extrinsic photoageing (UV, smoking) adds solar elastosis. Hypertrophic photoageing: deep furrows, leathery, Favre-Racouchot, few dysplastic lesions. Atrophic: smooth, telangiectasia, senile purpura, poikiloderma of Civatte, common AK/BCC/SCC (phototypes I-II). Dermatoporosis: fragility, stellate pseudoscars, dissecting haematomas.
airborne-contact-dermatitis: Symmetric dermatitis of exposed sites (face, dorsal hands, neck, upper chest, forearms); eyelids may be the only site. Non-airborne photodermatitis spares shadow areas (eyelids, retroauricular, submental). Causes: methylisothiazolinone in water-based paints, PPD, epoxy resin, Parthenium and Compositae. Patch and photopatch test; some progress to chronic actinic dermatitis.
alezzandrini-syndrome: Acquired unilateral melanocyte destruction of skin, hair, eye and ear: gradual visual loss, then ipsilateral facial vitiligo and poliosis years later, with hypoacusis. Related to Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada but unilateral, without VKH neurological features (CN VIII damage, sterile meningitis). Only a handful of cases; risk of retinal detachment, so regular eye review.
alkaptonuria-and-ochronosis: Autosomal recessive deficiency of homogentisic acid oxidase: urine darkens on standing, with blue-black pigmentation and thickening of ear cartilage, dark earwax, scleral pigment and arthropathy of the spine and large joints from the 40s. Exogenous ochronosis follows hydroquinone, quinine or phenol and spares cartilage.
allergic-contact-cheilitis: Type IV hypersensitivity eczema-like cheilitis of the vermilion/perioral skin, rarely the inner mucosa; patch testing is the key to diagnosis, including the patient's own products. Lip cosmetics are the top source in women, toothpaste in men; often atopic. Contact urticaria and oral allergy syndrome (more rapid onset and recovery) are mimics.
allergic-contact-dermatitis-in-children: Common because child skin is thinner, absorbs more and is often atopic; sensitisation mainly at age 0-3 years. Typical allergens: nickel (piercings, fasteners), Myroxylon pereirae, isothiazolinones in baby wipes, fragrance mix, colophonium (adhesive tapes). Confirm with patch testing. Systemic contact dermatitis is rare; Myroxylon pereirae in food flavourings is the likely culprit.
allergic-contact-dermatitis-to-essential: Type IV reaction (24-72 h) to oils such as tea tree, ylang-ylang, lemongrass, sandalwood, clove and jasmine absolute; aromatherapists and masseurs get hand and forearm dermatitis. Patients often react to many oils; most, but not all, are fragrance mix I positive, so extended patch testing (including own products) is needed. Neat oils on skin sensitise; diffusers cause airborne disease.
allergic-contact-dermatitis-to-glucose-m: Eczematous rash at the sensor site that can spread beyond the device margins (irritant dermatitis is usually confined to it). Acrylates are the commonest allergens (e.g. isobornyl acrylate), in the plastic housing or adhesive; also colophonium, epoxy resin, nickel, isocyanates. Patch test baseline plus acrylate series; manufacturers do not list constituents. Hydrocolloid barrier can be trialled.
allergic-contact-dermatitis-to-isocyanat: Isocyanates (MDI, TDI) in polyurethane foams, resins, coatings and adhesives are potent respiratory allergens and a leading cause of occupational asthma; skin exposure can induce respiratory sensitisation. Contact dermatitis is often mild and missed. Commercial patch tests are unreliable (false negatives), MDI reactions may appear late so read at day 7; MDA positivity may mark MDI sensitivity.
allergy-to-benzocaine: Ester local anaesthetic (PABA-derived) in many OTC products (haemorrhoid, sore throat, mouth ulcer, sunburn preparations); causes delayed allergic contact dermatitis 12-24 h after re-exposure. Cross-reacts with other ester anaesthetics, PPD, sulfonamides, sulfonylureas, thiazides and PABA sunscreens; amides are usually safe. Benzocaine sprays can cause methaemoglobinaemia.
allergy-to-cobalt: Affects about 2% (female 2:1), often with atopic dermatitis and nickel or chromate allergy; patch test 1% cobalt chloride. Purpuric patch-test reactions are peculiar to cobalt and do not indicate allergy. Sources: hard metal tools, jewellery, cosmetics, leather, cement, vitamin B12; blue tattoo pigment can cause sarcoidal reactions. Oral B12 can cause vesicular hand dermatitis.
allergy-to-imidazolidinyl-urea: Formaldehyde-releasing preservatives in cosmetics (imidazolidinyl urea and diazolidinyl urea, which cross-react). A relatively uncommon contact allergen, so often found in products labelled 'hypoallergenic'. Type IV; lesions develop 48-72 h after exposure. Patch test 2% in petrolatum; also avoid other formaldehyde releasers (quaternium-15, DMDM hydantoin, bronopol).
allergy-to-paraphenylenediamine: Permanent hair dye allergen (partially oxidised intermediate sensitises); darker shades contain more. Mild reactions: itchy eyelids and ear rims; severe: facial swelling and blistering. Black henna tattoos cause blistering in 1-2 days, then a lichenoid eruption at 1-2 weeks. Lifelong sensitisation; cross-reacts with azo dyes, PABA, benzocaine, procaine and sulfonamides. Patch test 1% (0.3% if clear history).
alopecia-areata-in-children: Round or oval, smooth bald patch with exclamation mark hairs and a positive hair tug at active edges; onset by 10 years. First-decade onset is strongly associated with atopic dermatitis (about one-third) and lupus; thyroid disease is not increased, unlike adults. Mimics: tinea capitis (scale, inflammation) and trichotillomania. Poor prognosis: young age, ophiasis, totalis/universalis, atopy, nail involvement.
alopecia-from-drugs: Usually reversible, diffuse nonscarring hair loss within days to weeks of a new drug. Anagen effluvium: chemotherapy (rarely gold, colchicine, arsenic, thallium); telogen effluvium: virtually all other drugs (anticoagulants, beta-blockers, valproate, lithium, retinoids), evident after 2-4 months. Confirm by stopping the drug for at least 3 months.
alopecia-mucinosa: Follicular mucinosis: mucin in the pilosebaceous follicle and sebaceous glands on biopsy; clinically grouped follicular papules in dry red plaques on face, neck, scalp with non-scarring hair loss. Primary acute (Pinkus) type in children usually resolves spontaneously. Secondary form in those over 40 is most often associated with cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (10-30%), so biopsy and careful follow-up are needed.
alpha-1-antitrypsin-deficiency-panniculi: Liquefying panniculitis: erythematous nodules/plaques on trunk and proximal limbs that ulcerate and leak oily material, often after trauma; does not improve with antibiotics or systemic steroids. Predominantly lobular with neutrophils, dermal collagen dissolution and skip areas of normal fat beside necrosis. Seen in ZZ homozygotes (~0.9%). Tetracyclines, dapsone, colchicine and A1AT replacement reported.
amalgam-tattoo: Blue, black or slate-grey oral macule, usually on the gingiva near an amalgam filling, from amalgam lodged in the mucosa during placement, polishing or removal (or after apicoectomy). Clinical diagnosis; X-ray shows only large particles; biopsy if doubtful. Harmless; needs no treatment.
american-trypanosomiasis: Chagas disease: Trypanosoma cruzi spread in faeces of triatomine (kissing) bugs. Acute skin signs: chagoma at the inoculation site, Romana sign (unilateral periorbital swelling), measles-like schizotrypanides. Chronic cardiac (dilated cardiomyopathy) and GI (megaoesophagus, megacolon) disease develop in 30-40% decades later; reactivation in HIV is AIDS-defining. Acute phase: benznidazole or nifurtimox.
amputation-stump-dermatoses: Affect 34-74% of amputees; pressure ulcers and skin breakdown (39%) and infection (25%) are commonest. Contributors: poorly fitting prosthesis, trapped sweat, vascular disease, scarring. Also verrucous hyperplasia from venous congestion, epidermoid cysts, Koebner phenomenon (psoriasis, lichen planus), and allergic contact dermatitis to prosthetic materials (confirm by patch test).
amyloidosis-cutis-dyschromica: Primary cutaneous amyloidosis with dotted or reticular hyperpigmentation mixed with lentil-sized hypopigmented macules, sparing palms, soles and mucosae; childhood onset, usually familial, mostly East/South-East Asian. Little or no itch separates it from macular/lichenoid amyloidosis. Subtle papillary dermal amyloid needs Congo red (apple-green birefringence). Mimics: dyschromatosis hereditaria, dyskeratosis congenita, xeroderma pigmentosum.
anagen-effluvium: Abrupt diffuse non-scarring shedding of damaged anagen hairs, up to 90% loss, usually from chemotherapy (doxorubicin, nitrosoureas, cyclophosphamide) within 2-4 weeks. Other causes: radiation, thallium or arsenic, alopecia areata, pemphigus vulgaris. Tapered or broken hair ends with pigmented long roots. Reversible; regrowth in 3-6 months, sometimes curly or a different colour.
anaphylaxis: Acute multisystem hypersensitivity, IgE-dependent in most; skin and mucosal signs in up to 90% (urticaria, angioedema) plus respiratory, cardiovascular or GI involvement. Drug or venom triggers more often cause shock; penicillins are the commonest medical cause. Biphasic relapse in 3-20%. Check tryptase within 2 hours (normal does not exclude). IM adrenaline; beta-blockers may blunt the response.
anetoderma: Loss of dermal elastic fibres giving round 1-2 cm lesions of wrinkled skin over a palpable depression ('button-hole sign'); routine stains look near-normal, so elastic stains must be requested. Primary or secondary to other skin disease. Associated with antiphospholipid antibodies, also Lyme, SLE, Graves disease, HIV. No treatment reverses established lesions.
angelman-syndrome: Loss of expression of the maternal UBE3A gene at 15q11.2-q13: deletion 65-75%, maternal gene mutation 5-11%, paternal uniparental disomy 3-7%, imprinting defect 3%. Prader-Willi is the distinct paternally derived defect on the same chromosome. Seizures, developmental delay, minimal speech, happy excitable personality with frequent smiling, hand flapping, microcephaly; hypopigmentation with light blue iris.
angina-bullosa-haemorrhagica: Tense blood-filled oral blister, usually solitary and most often on the soft palate, that ruptures spontaneously and heals uneventfully. Possible factors: trauma, long-term topical or inhaled steroids, diabetes. Biopsy shows a blister under the mucosa with red cells and sparse inflammation; investigate only to exclude mucous membrane pemphigoid, bullous pemphigoid, linear IgA disease and others.
angioedema: Deep dermal/subcutaneous swelling of eyelids, lips or genitals; non-pitting, burning rather than itchy, resolves in 24-48 h. ACE-inhibitor angioedema occurs without urticaria, can appear weeks to months after starting the drug, and is the subtype most likely to need admission. Hereditary (C1 inhibitor, SERPING1): bradykinin-mediated, no wheals, low C4 and C1-INH.
angiofibroma: Firm flesh-coloured dome-shaped papules under 5 mm; histology shows an 'onion skin' pattern around vessels and follicles. Facial clusters in the butterfly area from childhood suggest tuberous sclerosis (TSC1 hamartin, TSC2 tuberin; adenoma sebaceum, periungual Koenen tumour). Also seen in Birt-Hogg-Dube (FLCN) and MEN1 (menin). Acquired forms: fibrous papule of the nose (mistaken for BCC) and pearly penile papules.
angioimmunoblastic-t-cell-lymphoma: Nodal peripheral T-cell lymphoma of follicular helper T-cell origin in older adults: fevers, night sweats, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and a non-specific rash in 50% (papules, petechiae, rarely erythroderma). Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia, eosinophilia, Coombs-positive haemolytic anaemia; EBV-positive B cells common. CD10+, PD-1+, Bcl-6+, CXCL13+ with CD21+ follicular dendritic cells. Median survival under 3 years.
angiolymphoid-hyperplasia-with-eosinophi: Clustered brown or red translucent nodules around the ear or hairline of young adults; also called epithelioid or histiocytoid haemangioma. Histology: proliferating capillaries lined by plump epithelioid/histiocytoid endothelial cells with lymphocytes and many eosinophils. Kimura disease is probably distinct (deeper, no overlying skin lesion). Simple excision tends to recur.
angioma-serpiginosum: Tiny red puncta grouped in a serpiginous or gyrate array, mainly on the buttocks and legs, with no bleeding, inflammation or pigmentation; palms, soles and mucosa spared. Starts in early childhood, about 90% female. Harmless; vascular laser only for cosmesis.
angular-cheilitis: Bilateral, symmetrical fissuring, maceration and crusting at the oral commissures, most often from saliva exposure (irritant eczematous cheilitis). Risk factors: ill-fitting dentures, nutritional deficiencies (iron, B12, folate, zinc, riboflavin), IBD, Sjogren, atopy, Down syndrome, oral retinoids. Swabs may grow Candida, S. aureus or HSV; unilateral cases raise secondary syphilis.
annular-erythema: Pink-red spot expands 2-5 mm/day into rings of 6-8 cm with central clearing and sometimes an inner rim of scale, mostly thighs and legs; histology shows perivascular lymphocytes. Often no cause; linked to infections (TB, secondary syphilis, tinea), drugs (hydroxychloroquine, penicillin), blue cheese, tomatoes. Average duration 11 months.
annular-lichenoid-dermatitis-of-youth: Rare; asymptomatic annular red-brown macules and patches with central hypopigmentation on the trunk, groin and axillae, mean age 10 years. Histology: interface dermatitis confined to the tips of the rete ridges with keratinocyte loss giving squared-off ridges. Mimics: morphoea, hypopigmented mycosis fungoides, annular erythema. Responds transiently to steroids, tacrolimus or NB-UVB.
ant-bites-and-stings: Only female ants sting. Fire ant: immediate pain and red spot, then a tender itchy pustule hours later, often clustered under clothing. Jack jumper ant (Myrmecia pilosula) is the most common cause of fatal Hymenoptera anaphylaxis in Tasmania. Large local reaction is over 10 cm for at least 24 hours and needs no skin testing; allergy referral is for severe systemic reactions.
antiphospholipid-syndrome: Acquired autoimmune disorder: recurrent arterial or venous thrombosis and/or pregnancy loss with persistent anticardiolipin antibodies and/or lupus anticoagulant. Livedo reticularis in up to 80% of those with antibodies; also splinter haemorrhages, leg ulcers, blue toe. Secondary form usually with SLE or levamisole-adulterated cocaine; false-positive syphilis serology.
antisynthetase-syndrome: Antibodies to aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (anti-Jo-1 most common). Myositis, non-erosive polyarthritis, interstitial lung disease, mechanic's hands, Raynaud and fever. ILD develops in most with anti-Jo-1. Malignancy reported within 6-12 months of diagnosis, so age-appropriate screening as for dermatomyositis.
apocrine-chromhidrosis: Coloured sweat (blue, black, green, brown, yellow) in apocrine areas: axillae, cheeks, areolae, anogenital. Due to lipofuscin granules in apocrine glands; biopsy shows PAS-positive granules and Wood lamp may show yellow fluorescence. Differentiate from the more common pseudochromhidrosis (sweat discolours after secretion); treat with capsaicin or botulinum toxin.
aquagenic-pruritus: Severe prickling itch triggered by water of any temperature, with no visible skin change (unlike aquagenic urticaria, which has wheals); thighs and upper arms symmetrically. Severe cases can herald haematological disease: polycythaemia rubra vera (over 45%), essential thrombocytosis, myelodysplasia, lymphoma. Blood disorders may appear years later, so annual haematology testing is advised.
aquagenic-urticaria: Rare inducible urticaria: 1-3 mm folliculocentric wheals with flare within 20-30 min of water contact at any temperature (also sweat, tears), on the trunk and upper arms with palms and soles spared. Resembles cholinergic urticaria but is not provoked by raised core temperature. Confirm with a water provocation test (wet cloth on upper trunk for 30 min).
aquagenic-wrinkling-of-the-palms: White translucent palmar papules and plaques after brief water exposure (about 3 min, versus 11 min for normal wrinkling); 'hand in the bucket' test uses 7 min. Strongly associated with cystic fibrosis and carriers (CFTR), so the diagnosis should prompt early CF workup. Histology: eccrine acrosyringeal dilation. Aluminium chloride 20% at night is the page's first-line treatment.
arthropod-bites-and-stings: Insect bites are intensely itchy papules in crops on exposed sites, sometimes with a central blister; papular urticaria in young children (fleas, mosquitoes) reactivates old bites in symmetrical crops. Biopsy: central punctum, eosinophilic spongiosis, wedge-shaped mixed infiltrate. Latrodectus bites cause neurotoxicity, Loxosceles bites local cytotoxic effects. Scrape out bee stingers rather than squeezing with tweezers.
aspergillosis: Mould (A. fumigatus, flavus, niger) usually inhaled; patterns are acute invasive, allergic (asthma, cystic fibrosis), aspergilloma (fungus ball in a pre-existing lung cavity) and chronic necrotising pulmonary. In 5-10% of invasive cases red-violet plaques develop central blisters then black necrotic ulcers; primary cutaneous disease occurs at IV cannula sites, burns or under occlusive dressings and resembles cellulitis at first.
ataxia-telangiectasia: Autosomal recessive; inactivating ATM mutations (11q22-23) impair double-strand-break DNA repair. Progressive cerebellar ataxia once walking starts, telangiectases from age 3-5 (eye corners, then ears and cheeks), recurrent sinopulmonary infections and cancer predisposition. Raised serum alpha-fetoprotein; also called Louis-Bar syndrome.
atopic-hand-dermatitis: Occurs in at least 50-60% of active atopic dermatitis; favours the backs of the hands (90%), fingers and wrists, with palms less often involved. No specific morphology; clues are hyperlinear palms, keratosis pilaris and atopic changes elsewhere. Irritant contact dermatitis complicates it more than allergic. Mimics: palmar psoriasis, tinea manuum, other hand dermatitis.
atrophoderma-of-pasini-and-pierini: Asymptomatic slightly depressed patches, usually on the lower back, with a sharp 'cliff-drop' edge ('footprints-in-the-snow'), no preceding inflammation and no surface wrinkling or induration. Regarded as a morphoea variant; female predominance. Some have Borrelia burgdorferi antibodies and improve with doxycycline. Biopsy is subtle: dermal atrophy with normal collagen and elastic fibres. Mimics anetoderma.
atypical-melanocytic-naevus: Benign acquired naevus that marks melanoma risk, rising with count (1.5-2.4x for one or more, up to 32x for ten or more). Asymmetric, irregular border, variegated, over 5 mm, macular with central papule (fried-egg). 'Dysplastic' is a histologic term, not a precursor; most melanomas arise de novo. Look for the ugly duckling. FAMM: autosomal dominant, CDKN2A/CDK4, pancreatic cancer.
atypical-mycobacterial-infection: Skin pathogens: M. marinum (fish tank or swimming pool granuloma; nodules along lymphatics on hands, elbows, knees, feet), M. ulcerans (Buruli ulcer; painless nodule then spreading ulcer from mycolactone toxin), M. chelonae and M. fortuitum (after tattoos, trauma, surgery). MAC and M. kansasii mainly cause lung disease. Culture needs cool temperature, so alert the lab.
atypical-solar-lentigo: Large, irregular, variably coloured solitary macule on sun-damaged skin that may be hard to tell from melanoma in situ (lentigo maligna). Unstable solar lentigo shows melanocytic proliferation on histology and can be a precursor. Main risk is missing melanoma in situ; excise or follow with serial dermoscopy.
australian-box-jellyfish-stings: Chironex fleckeri: immediate exquisite pain with linear brownish-purple welts, blisters, later necrosis and whip-like pigment change. Total welt length over 700 mm means rapid collapse; death is from cardiovascular effects of pore-forming toxins. Apply vinegar for at least 30 seconds to deactivate nematocysts; do not use pressure immobilisation bandages (more toxin discharge). Antivenom is available.
autoimmune-polyglandular-syndrome-type-1: Triad of mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism and Addison disease (APECED), usually appearing at age 3–5 years. Autosomal recessive AIRE mutation (21q22); clusters in Iranian Jews, Sardinians and Finns. Vitiligo and alopecia areata are the skin associations.
autoimmune-polyglandular-syndrome-type-2: Schmidt syndrome: Addison disease plus autoimmune thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes; the most common immunoendocrinopathy syndrome. Autosomal dominant, 3–4 times more common in women, usually presenting at age 20–30. Pernicious anaemia and coeliac disease can also occur.
autoimmune-progesterone-dermatitis: Rare cyclical hypersensitivity to luteal-phase progesterone: rash appears 3-4 days before menses and resolves a few days after onset. Usually urticaria (+/- angioedema, anaphylaxis) or dermatitis; also erythema multiforme-like and fixed drug eruptions. Reproducible after intramuscular progesterone and prevented by suppressing ovulation; biopsy is non-diagnostic. Resolves at menopause; avoid progesterone-containing HRT.
autonomic-denervation-dermatitis: Eczematous rash confined to a surgical incision site, most often after total knee replacement (SKINTED); onset 3 weeks to 3 years later, often with hypoesthesia from injury to the infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve. Clinical diagnosis; patch tests usually negative. Mimics: ACD to implant metals/dressings, wound infection.
bacillary-angiomatosis: Bartonella henselae (cats, fleas) or B quintana (body louse) in immunocompromised hosts (HIV, transplant, CLL): red-purple papules/nodules that bleed easily, mimicking pyogenic granuloma and Kaposi sarcoma. Histology: lobular vessel proliferation with epithelioid endothelial cells and neutrophils; organisms on Warthin-Starry stain. Hepatic involvement is peliosis hepatis. Erythromycin or doxycycline for 3-6 months.
balamuthia-mandrillaris-infection: Free-living amoeba of water and soil that enters via nasal mucosa, lungs or broken skin. Classic skin sign is an asymptomatic, rubbery granulomatous plaque on the central face that precedes CNS spread; amoebic encephalitis follows weeks to years later and is fatal in 95%. Biopsy: granulomatous infiltrate; trophozoites and cysts rarely seen.
basal-cell-carcinoma-in-skin-of-colour: More than 50% of BCCs in skin of colour are pigmented ('pearly' brown or black), making diagnosis difficult; nodular is the predominant subtype, morphoeic is uncommon and adenoid BCC is more common than in Caucasians. Second most common skin cancer in African Americans and Asian Indians. Metastatic BCC is rare (0.03-0.55%) with median survival of 8 months.
bascule-syndrome: Triad of Bier anaemic spots, cyanosis and a red-orange urticaria-like eruption centred in the spots, on the lower limbs of children and adolescents. Paroxysmal (10–15 minutes), provoked by standing and relieved by lying down or walking. Associated with orthostatic intolerance/POTS; benign and self-limiting.
bazex-dupre-christol-syndrome: Triad of congenital hypotrichosis, follicular atrophoderma (ice-pick scars on dorsal hands, elbows, feet, face; easily missed) and multiple facial BCCs from early adult life. X-linked dominant, no male-to-male transmission; milia common. No internal malignancy; avoid radiotherapy. Unrelated to Bazex syndrome (acrokeratosis neoplastica).
bee-and-wasp-stings: Honeybee stinger is barbed and left behind (bee dies); wasps sting repeatedly. Melittin causes most pain; hyaluronidase is a potent allergen. Scrape the stinger out rather than using tweezers. Type I IgE reactions start about 10 minutes after the sting. Check baseline tryptase for an underlying mast cell disorder; venom immunotherapy for systemic reactions, not for toxic reactions (usually 500+ stings).
benign-lymphoplasmacytic-plaque: Pseudolymphoma of children (mostly girls aged 7-15): solitary or linear cluster of asymptomatic reddish-brown papules or scaly plaques, usually on the lower legs, resistant to topical and systemic treatment. Histology: dense infiltrate with many polyclonal plasma cells and no atypia. Exclude infection (atypical mycobacteria, leishmaniasis, borreliosis, syphilis).
benzalkonium-chloride-contact-dermatitis: Quaternary ammonium antiseptic/preservative (eye drops, wipes, cleaners) that is a well-known irritant; irritant dermatitis is more common than allergic. Patch test 0.1% aqueous; weak reactions may be irritant. Can cross-react with other quaternary ammonium compounds; can provoke granular parakeratosis in folds.
bindii-dermatitis: Irritant contact dermatitis from the spiny seed of the bindii weed (Soliva species; Onehunga weed in NZ). Discrete red papules with a central puncture site on hands, feet, elbows and knees in boys 5-18 years, late spring and early summer. Histology: spongiosis, foreign-body giant cells; may not respond to steroids; self-limited.
bird-mite-infestation: Suspect when a patient has scabies-like itch (worse at night or early morning, small red papules and vesicles) but does not respond to scabies treatment. Unlike scabies there are no burrows; mites cannot complete their life cycle on humans. Species include Ornithonyssus bursa and Dermanyssus gallinae. Exposure to poultry, pigeons or nests; collect mites with adhesive tape.
bjornstad-syndrome: Pili torti plus congenital sensorineural hearing loss, evident by age 2. Usually autosomal recessive BCS1L mutation (mitochondrial complex III assembly); other BCS1L mutations cause GRACILE syndrome. Pale hair, anhidrosis and hypogonadism can occur; mimics include Menkes disease and trichothiodystrophy.
black-henna-tattoo-reaction: Allergic contact dermatitis to para-phenylenediamine (PPD) added to henna; pure henna does not cause it. Eczematous or blistering reaction in the tattoo pattern 7–14 days after first exposure, within 48 hours if already sensitised. Cross-reacts with hair dye and azo dyes; can leave hypopigmentation or hyperpigmentation. Patch test with PPD.
blepharitis: Eyelid margin inflammation. Anterior (lash base): staphylococcal, seborrhoeic dermatitis, ocular rosacea, Demodex, contact allergy (rosin in mascara). Posterior: meibomian gland dysfunction. Complications are stye and chalazion; distinguish a persistent lesion from sebaceous carcinoma.
blue-toe-syndrome: Painful blue-violet toe(s) from small-vessel occlusion; foot pulses may be normal. Cholesterol emboli from ulcerated atherosclerotic plaques are the most common cause, classically after angiography or vascular surgery in an older man. Livedo reticularis/racemosa is the most frequent skin sign; biopsy shows intravascular cholesterol crystals.
blueberry-muffin-syndrome: Descriptive term for an infant with multiple blue-purple skin nodules due to dermal extramedullary erythropoiesis, purpura or metastases. Causes: congenital infection (TORCH), haemolytic disease of the newborn or hereditary spherocytosis, and tumours (leukaemia cutis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, neuroblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma).
bowel-bypass-syndrome: Bowel-associated dermatitis–arthritis syndrome: relapsing papules, pustules and blisters on the trunk and upper arms (Sweet-like) with fever, polyarthritis and tenosynovitis, 1–6 years after bowel bypass surgery. Blind-loop bacterial overgrowth; peptidoglycan immune complexes in skin and joints. Excision or revision of the blind loop cures.
brachioradial-pruritus: Neuropathic itch without primary rash on the proximal forearm (C6 distribution), typically in fair-skinned late-middle-aged women; burning/tingling and the ice pack sign (relief from cold). Proposed causes: UV damage to C fibres or cervical spine pathology, so consider cervical imaging. Mimics: dry skin, dermatitis artefacta.
bromhidrosis: Offensive body odour from bacterial breakdown of sweat, sebum and keratin; apocrine type (axillae, anogenital) is most common in adults. Look for erythrasma, pitted keratolysis, trichomycosis axillaris. Generalised odour with breath/urine involvement suggests metabolic causes such as trimethylaminuria or phenylketonuria. Differential includes olfactory refractory syndrome.
brown-spots-and-freckles: An ephelis fades in winter, whereas a lentigo persists. Ephelides: under 3 mm, mid face, red-haired children, MC1R; melanin rises in keratinocytes without more melanocytes. Solar lentigines: sharply defined, from UV, with keratinocyte proliferation and rete pegs; atypical lesions must be distinguished from lentigo maligna.
bullous-drug-eruptions: Mostly a clinical diagnosis; biopsy rarely proves a drug cause, and stopping the drug is the key step. Fixed drug eruption recurs at the same sites (lips, genitals, hands, feet) leaving pigmentation; sulphonamides and tetracyclines are common causes. Thiol drugs (D-penicillamine, captopril, gold) cause pemphigus; vancomycin is the most common cause of drug-induced linear IgA bullous dermatosis.
bullous-systemic-lupus-erythematosus: Subepidermal blisters in a patient with SLE, usually sun-exposed sites; little itch, heals without scarring or prominent milia. Type I (most common) has antibodies to type VII collagen. Histology resembles dermatitis herpetiformis; DIF shows linear or granular IgG/IgM/IgA at the DEJ. Dapsone gives rapid response.
buschke-ollendorff-syndrome: Autosomal dominant LEMD3 mutation; present at birth with yellowish papules, nodules or plaques (connective tissue naevi: elastomas or collagenomas) mainly on the torso and extremities. Osteopoikilosis (increased bone density in long bones) is the key extracutaneous finding. Generally benign.
calcaneal-petechiae: Talon noir: red-black heel patches from intracorneal haemorrhage after shearing or pounding in young athletes (basketball); asymptomatic. Mimics acral lentiginous melanoma, but paring with a scalpel removes the colour without bleeding (warts show pinpoint bleeding), so no biopsy is needed. Resolves in 4-6 weeks.
capillaritis: Pigmented purpura: cayenne-pepper petechiae with haemosiderin in the upper dermis; no true vasculitis on biopsy. Variants: Schamberg (most common, lower legs, asymptomatic), Doucas-Kapetanakis (itchy, eczematid), Gougerot-Blum (lichenoid), Majocchi (annular, telangiectatic), lichen aureus (solitary brown-yellow patch, often over a varicose vein). Drugs and food additives are reported triggers.
carcinoma-cuniculatum: Rare, slow-growing, low-grade SCC variant (verrucous carcinoma, Ackerman tumour): solitary warty papillomatous plaque, most often on the sole (53%), also oral cavity, nails, genitals; rarely ulcerates (unlike usual SCC) and rarely metastasises. Risk factors: HPV warts, tobacco, vulvar lichen sclerosus. Biopsy confirms; excise. Avoid radiotherapy, which can trigger an anaplastic SCC.
carcinoma-erysipeloides: Cutaneous metastasis via dermal lymphatics: red, thickened cellulitis-like patch with a raised edge, usually afebrile, most often on the chest near the primary (commonly breast adenocarcinoma) and sometimes the first sign of the tumour. Misdiagnosed as cellulitis/erysipelas or radiation dermatitis; punch biopsy shows malignant cells in cutaneous lymphatics. Poor prognosis.
carcinoma-in-situ-of-oral-cavity: Oral intraepithelial carcinoma: grey-white plaque (leukoplakia or erythroleukoplakia), most often on the buccal mucosa; linked to tobacco (six times more common in smokers), alcohol, betel quid and oral submucous fibrosis. Higher SCC risk: floor of mouth, lateral/ventral tongue, speckled non-homogeneous type especially proliferative verrucous leukoplakia, dysplasia. Biopsy is mandatory; lifelong follow-up.
carotenoderma: Yellow-orange skin from raised beta-carotene (diet such as carrot, pumpkin, sweet potato; diabetes, hypothyroidism, liver or kidney disease, anorexia nervosa), seen first on nose, nasolabial folds, palms and soles. Sclerae and mucous membranes are spared (no stratum corneum); yellow sclerae indicate jaundice. Canthaxanthin tanning pills can cause retinopathy.
carrion-disease: Bartonella bacilliformis spread by sandflies in Peru, Ecuador and Colombia. Systemic Oroya fever (red cell invasion, severe haemolytic anaemia, Salmonella superinfection; 40–85% untreated mortality) and/or verruga peruana (endothelial proliferation; red-purple nodules that bleed and ulcerate). Warthin–Starry or Giemsa stain shows bacteria.
catscratch-disease: Bartonella henselae from a kitten scratch or bite (cats spread it via fleas): papule or crusted vesicle 3-10 days later, then tender regional lymphadenopathy (head, neck, axilla) up to 10-12 cm. 80% of patients are under 21. Complications: Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome, bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised patients, neuroretinitis, encephalopathy. Usually self-limiting.
chancroid: Haemophilus ducreyi STI: painful deep genital ulcer with shaggy undermined borders and a purulent, easily bleeding base, plus painful inguinal buboes (about 50% if untreated). Gram stain may show 'school of fish' clumping (poor sensitivity). Diagnosis requires excluding syphilis and herpes simplex; ulcers increase HIV risk.
chediak-higashi-syndrome: Autosomal recessive LYST mutation: oculocutaneous albinism with light, metallic-sheen hair, plus recurrent infections, easy bruising, nystagmus and neuropathy. Diagnose by large granules in white cells and pigment clumping on hair microscopy. About 80% enter a viral-triggered accelerated phase (HLH), often fatal in childhood.
chemical-burn: Acids cause coagulation necrosis with eschar; alkalis cause deeper liquefaction necrosis (protein denaturing plus saponification of fats). Hydrofluoric acid: dilute forms do not burn or hurt on contact; treat with calcium gluconate gel. Elemental metals (lithium, sodium, potassium, magnesium) must not be irrigated with water; otherwise irrigate copiously for at least 20 minutes.
chikungunya-fever: Alphavirus spread by Aedes aegypti/albopictus; sudden high fever then severe symmetric polyarthralgia of small hand and foot joints, which can last months. Skin: early maculopapular rash, postinflammatory pigmentation characteristically on the nose, painful aphthous-like oral and groin ulcers; vesiculobullous in children. Confirm by PCR or serology; also test for dengue and zika.
childhood-bullous-pemphigoid: Rare; autoantibodies to BP180 (less often BP230) in the NC16A domain of collagen XVII. Unlike adults, mucous membranes are commonly involved; infants under 1 year often have palm and sole blisters, and vulvar disease occurs in later childhood. Subepidermal split with linear DIF at the basement membrane; good prognosis.
childhood-melanoma: Melanoma under 18; older children resemble adults (ABCDE+EFG), but age 10 or younger often amelanotic, red, nodular and thicker. Mimics: Spitz naevus and pyogenic granuloma. Melanoma arises in up to 15% of young children with a giant congenital naevus (over 40 cm), especially with neurocutaneous melanocytosis; prophylactic removal does not reduce risk. Also xeroderma pigmentosum, retinoblastoma history.
chloracne-madish: Caused by halogenated aromatic hydrocarbons (dioxins, PCBs); not true acne. Open and closed comedones with uninflamed nodules and cysts on cheeks, behind ears, axillae and groin; sebaceous glands are often smaller than normal (MADISH: dioxin-induced skin hamartomas). Seveso 1976 outbreak; Yushchenko poisoning. Porphyria cutanea tarda may occur.
cholesterol-emboli: Atheroembolism from ulcerated plaques, typically within hours to days of angiography, angioplasty or vascular surgery (anticoagulation also reported). Classic: livedo reticularis with leg/foot pain and good pedal pulses, or livedo with renal impairment and eosinophilia (up to 80%). Biopsy shows cholesterol clefts in vessels with thrombi. MI and stroke do not usually result.
cholinergic-urticaria: Small 1-4 mm punctate wheals with flare triggered by sweating (exercise most common; also hot baths, spicy food, emotional stress); starts on trunk and neck, resolves within 90 min; almost never palms, soles or axillae. Intradermal methacholine is positive in only one-third, so cannot exclude the diagnosis. Rapid skin cooling may abort an attack.
chondrodermatitis-nodularis: Painful, tender solitary 4-6 mm nodule with central crust on the helix (men) or antihelix (women) of the ear, on the sleeping side; also called Winkler disease. Linked to pressure, cold and poor blood supply. Mimics: SCC, keratoacanthoma, BCC, gouty tophus. Pressure relief; 10-30% recur after surgery.
chronic-arsenic-poisoning: Sources: contaminated well water, smelting and other occupational exposure, Fowler's tonic. Hyperpigmentation in non-sun-exposed areas with raindrop hypopigmentation, palmoplantar arsenical keratoses, Mee's lines, stocking-glove neuropathy. Skin cancers (especially Bowen disease); increased risk of lung, liver, bladder, kidney and colon cancer.
chronic-inducible-urticaria: Chronic urticaria with a reproducible trigger; wheals appear about 5 min after the stimulus and last minutes to 2 h. Diagnosed by provocation testing (stop antihistamines 3 days and systemic steroids 7 days before); delayed pressure urticaria may need hours. Local heat, aquagenic and vibratory forms rarely respond to antihistamines. Cholinergic urticaria can be confused with exercise-induced anaphylaxis.
chronic-pruritus-of-unknown-origin: Itch lasting more than 6 weeks with no identified cause; a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out dermatological, systemic, neurological and psychiatric causes (IFSI classification). Work-up includes CBC, liver, renal and thyroid tests; if under a year, look for Hodgkin lymphoma and liver tumour. Ciclosporin usually ineffective.
chronic-spontaneous-urticaria: Wheals with or without angioedema on most days for 6 weeks or more with no specific trigger; each wheal resolves within 24 h. Many cases are autoimmune (functional autoantibodies to the high-affinity IgE receptor); strong association with autoimmune thyroid disease. Activity scored by UAS7 (maximum 42). Omalizumab is used when symptoms persist despite antihistamines.
chronic-superficial-scaly-dermatitis: Parapsoriasis: round or oval pink scaly patches with finger-like (digitate) extensions, can resemble cigarette paper; small plaque (2-5 cm) is benign, large plaque (>5 cm) is potentially premalignant with about 7.5-14% progressing to mycosis fungoides. Clonal CD4+ T cells; biopsy and long-term skin checks.
circumscribed-palmar-hypokeratosis: Solitary persistent red patch of thin atrophic skin on the thenar or hypothenar eminence, usually in women aged 40-70, with an abrupt edge to normal skin. Histology: absent stratum corneum centrally with a sharp transition to compact orthohyperkeratosis at the edge. Mimics: porokeratosis and SCC in situ. No reported cancer; treatment not required.
clear-cell-acanthoma: Solitary shiny, most commonly blood-red dome-shaped plaque or nodule (3-20 mm) on the lower leg of middle-aged or older adults, with wafer-like crust at the edge. Dermoscopy: vessels lined up in strings. Histology: accumulation of clear, glycogen-containing cells in the epidermis. Also called Degos acanthoma; diagnosis is rarely made before biopsy.
cloves-syndrome: Congenital Lipomatous Overgrowth, Vascular malformations, Epidermal naevi, Spinal/skeletal anomalies. Sporadic somatic mosaic PIK3CA gain-of-function mutation (PROS). Large truncal lipoma with overlying vascular malformation at birth; often misdiagnosed as Proteus syndrome, which is normal at birth. Wilms tumour reported at increased incidence.
cobb-syndrome: Dermatomal capillary malformation (port-wine stain) on the trunk from birth, with spinal arteriovenous malformation causing neurological deficits (hyperreflexia, sensory/motor loss, paralysis) by about age 5. Also called spinal arteriovenous metameric syndrome. Not familial; spinal lesions are shown on MRI. Complications include Foix–Alajouanine syndrome.
cockayne-syndrome: Autosomal recessive ERCC6 (CSB, about 80%) or ERCC8 (CSA) mutation. Microcephaly, growth failure, photosensitivity, cold hands and feet, lipoatrophy, premature ageing, cataracts, sensorineural deafness and salt-and-pepper retinal pigmentation. Metronidazole is contraindicated (acute liver failure). Skin cancer occurs, other malignancies do not.
cold-urticaria: Itchy wheals and angioedema within 2-5 min of cold exposure, lasting 1-2 h; ice cube on the forearm for 1-5 min reproduces the weal. Mostly idiopathic; secondary causes include cryoglobulinaemia, CLL and infections. Swimming in cold water is the commonest cause of severe reactions. Distinct from familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome (CAPS). Avoid opiates and other histamine-releasing drugs under anaesthesia.
collodion-baby: Baby born in a tight, shiny yellow membrane that sheds over 2-3 weeks to reveal the underlying disorder, usually autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis (lamellar ichthyosis, non-bullous CIE); 10% have normal skin (self-healing). Complications: fissures, infection, dehydration, ectropion, constriction bands. Do not debride the membrane.
colloid-milium: Numerous yellow-brown, semi-translucent 1-4 mm papules on sun-exposed skin of fair-skinned outdoor-working men aged 30-60; gelatinous material can be expressed. Histology: amorphous eosinophilic deposits with clefts, solar elastosis and a Grenz zone; immunohistochemistry needed to separate from amyloid. Pigmented form follows hydroquinone (ochronosis); juvenile form can cause ligneous conjunctivitis.
comedo-naevus: Grouped dilated follicular openings with dark keratin plugs in a honeycomb pattern, often linear or Blaschkoid; about 50% present at birth. Mosaic somatic mutations (FGFR2, NEK9). Comedo naevus syndrome adds skeletal, CNS (seizures), cataract and dental anomalies. Cysts, abscesses and scarring complicate it in adolescence; oral antibiotics are not effective apart from secondary infection.
comedonal-acne: Acne pattern with mostly comedones, typically forehead and chin. Open comedones are blackheads (black from melanin, not dirt); closed are whiteheads; macrocomedones exceed 2-3 mm. Associated with smoking, oily pomades and occlusive cosmetics. Treat with comedolytics (retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, azelaic acid); long-term treatment is needed.
comedones: A comedo is a plugged follicular orifice: open (blackhead; grey to black papule) or closed (whitehead; skin-coloured papule that must be punctured). Seen beyond acne in hidradenitis suppurativa, solar comedones/Favre-Racouchot syndrome, discoid lupus, comedone naevus and seborrhoeic keratosis (dermatoscopy).
common-variable-immunodeficiency: Low IgG (sometimes IgA/IgM) with recurrent sinopulmonary infections, bronchiectasis, lymphoma risk and autoimmunity (25%). Skin: non-infectious granulomas, necrotising or not, that histologically resemble granuloma annulare or sarcoidosis, plus bacterial infections, vitiligo, alopecia areata and pyoderma gangrenosum. Confirm with B-cell counts and immunoglobulin levels; no vaccine antibody response.
compositae-allergy: Allergic contact dermatitis to Asteraceae plants (daisies, sunflowers, chrysanthemum, ragweed, parthenium); allergens are sesquiterpene lactones, patch test with sesquiterpene lactone mix and compositae mix. Airborne face/neck/hand pattern; linked to chronic actinic dermatitis. Cross-sensitisation with fragrances, balsam of Peru and colophony.
compulsive-skin-picking: Dermatillomania (neurotic excoriation); picking at normal skin, scabs or imagined defects, often on the face; acne excorie is a subtype. Often co-exists with OCD (52% in one study), depression or anxiety; more common in women, starting in adolescence. Exclude anaemia, uraemia, liver disease and methamphetamine or cocaine use. Habit reversal training; SSRIs.
computer-mouse-dermatitis: Unilateral palmar hand dermatitis from prolonged mouse use, mostly irritant (sweat, friction, pressure) and affecting the thenar/hypothenar eminences and MCP regions with the central palm spared. Allergens: phthalates, resorcinol monobenzoate, neoprene/dialkyl thiourea in mouse pads. Improves off the mouse, relapses on reuse; patch test.
congenital-cartilaginous-rests-of-the-ne: Congenital 'wattle': solitary firm, skin-coloured sessile or pedunculated papule/nodule (5-25 mm) on the lateral neck anterior to sternocleidomastoid, with no sinus or cyst. Histology shows tubular hyaline or elastic cartilage under normal skin. Associated with other congenital anomalies (Treacher-Collins, Goldenhar, Nager), so do a systems review and cardiac/abdominal ultrasound.
congenital-malalignment-of-the-great-toe: Lateral rotation of the nail matrix causing lateral deviation of the great toenail plate, usually bilateral, with transverse ridging ('oyster shell'), onychogryphosis, chronic paronychia and ingrown nails. Autosomal dominant inheritance has been observed; clinical diagnosis. Spontaneous resolution in about half of children under 10; earlier surgery is likely to give better results in severe cases.
connective-tissue-naevi: Developmental excess of dermal components: collagenoma (shagreen patch, orange-peel plaque on lower back/nape, in tuberous sclerosis; familial cutaneous collagenoma on upper back) or elastoma. Buschke-Ollendorf syndrome: hereditary yellowish wrinkled nodules with osteopoikilosis. Elastosis perforans serpiginosa: arcs/rings of scaly papules, linked to Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos, osteogenesis imperfecta, PXE, Down syndrome.
consort-allergic-contact-dermatitis: Allergic contact dermatitis from an allergen carried by another person (contact dermatitis by proxy, connubial); partners are the most common consorts, and the face is the main site (49%). Clues: unexpected distribution, a handprint-shaped rash, genital involvement, or an unexpectedly strong patch test. Treatment is allergen avoidance; consort need not be avoided.
contact-allergy-to-cocamidopropyl-betain: Coconut-derived surfactant in shampoos, soaps, wipes, contact lens solutions and cosmetics. Contact allergy is more common in women, found in 6% of an Australian patch-tested ACD population; presents on face and hands, with possible eye irritation. Patch test 1.0% aqueous, read at 48 and 96 hours.
contact-allergy-to-gold: Type IV allergy to gold jewellery, dental restorations or occupational exposure, with 90% of cases in women and frequent co-allergy to nickel and cobalt. Earlobe, finger, neck, eyelid and face dermatitis; persistent nodules in piercings may show pseudolymphomatous or sarcoidal histology. Patch test GST: delayed up to 3 weeks, low clinical relevance (10-15%).
contact-allergy-to-lauryl-glucoside: Alkyl glucoside surfactant from plant sources in cosmetics, hair dyes, shampoos, sunscreens and deodorants; allergy reported in 0.7-2.0% of patch-tested patients, more in women aged 40-50 and in hairdressers and cleaners. Patch test 3% in petrolatum (cosmetic series); can cross-react with other alkyl glucosides.
contact-allergy-to-propolis: Bee resin (poplar bud-derived caffeates) found in cosmetics, lip balms, natural remedies and violin varnish; seen in beekeepers, violinists and in chronic venous insufficiency or anogenital disease. Presents as hand, perioral or lip dermatitis, stomatitis, urticaria, fiddler's neck. Cross-reacts with balsam of Peru, colophony, fragrance mix I. Patch test 10% in petrolatum.
contact-dermatitis-to-nitrile: Mostly allergic contact dermatitis to rubber accelerators (thiurams, dithiocarbamates, mercaptobenzothiazole) in nitrile gloves, often in latex-allergic healthcare workers, hairdressers and food handlers who switched to nitrile. Patch test local baseline series plus rubber accelerators. Acrylonitrile allergy is extremely rare; accelerator-free nitrile gloves.
contact-reactions-to-lanolin: Wool-fat emulsifier in emollients, steroid creams, lip products and haemorrhoidal preparations; free alcohols are the main sensitisers. Higher risk with leg ulcers, venous or atopic eczema. Patch test 30% lanolin alcohols in petrolatum, plus the patient's own product. Irritant reactions are more common than allergic. 2023 ACDS Allergen of the Year.
contact-reactions-to-toothpaste-and-othe: Toothpaste is the second most common cause of contact cheilitis after lipsticks, and the most common in males; flavourings (mint derivatives such as spearmint, peppermint, menthol, carvone; cinnamal) are the major allergens. Patch test with an extended toothpaste series plus own products. SLS and tartar-control pyrophosphates are irritants; chlorhexidine mouthwash stains teeth.
contact-urticaria: Immediate, transient wheal and redness within minutes to an hour of contact, clearing within 24 h (contact dermatitis appears hours to days later). Non-immunological (nettle, sorbic acid, balsam of Peru) is mild; immunological occurs in atopics after prior exposure (latex, antibiotics, nickel) and can cause extracutaneous reactions up to anaphylaxis. Prick/scratch testing confirms but cannot separate allergic from non-allergic.
corn-callus: Localised hard thickened skin from friction and pressure (more keratinocytes, thicker stratum corneum). A corn (clavus, heloma) is inflamed and painful; a callus (tyloma) is painless; a soft corn (heloma molle) has a damp, peeling surface between squashed toes. Diffuse thickening of the whole palm or sole is keratoderma. Key point of management is relieving pressure.
cornelia-de-lange-syndrome: Mutations in NIPBL, SMC1A, HDAC8, RAD21 or SMC3 (none found in 30%); usually sporadic. Synophrys, upturned nose, thin lips, low-set ears, limb abnormalities with clinodactyly, intellectual disability, reflux and heart defects. Skin: cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita.
costello-syndrome: RASopathy from germline HRAS mutation (usually p.Gly12Ser), typically de novo. Coarse facies, curly hair, loose skin with deep palmar/plantar creases, periorificial papillomas, palmoplantar keratoderma, acanthosis nigricans. About 15% lifetime malignancy risk: rhabdomyosarcoma, neuroblastoma, bladder transitional cell carcinoma.
covid-19: SARS-CoV-2 (spike binds ACE2). Skin signs: morbilliform rash, chilblain-like 'COVID toes', livedo/retiform purpura, urticaria, vesicular and pityriasis rosea-like eruptions; ~20% report rash as the only sign. Telogen effluvium 2-3 months later; red half-moon nail sign; U-shaped lingual papillitis. PIMS: polymorphic eruption, hand/foot swelling, mucositis, conjunctivitis.
cowpox: Orthopoxvirus; human cases are rare, usually from the scratch or bite of domestic cats (catpox), with woodland rodents as natural hosts. One or few pustular lesions on hands/face ulcerate and form a black eschar, healing with a scar over 6-12 weeks. Not milker's nodules (parapox). Atopic dermatitis raises risk of generalised disease.
cracked-heel: Fissures over a dry thickened callus at the heel rim, as pressure makes the fat pad expand sideways and split the callus. Predisposed by dry skin, atopic dermatitis, juvenile plantar dermatosis, palmoplantar psoriasis or keratoderma, diabetes, hypothyroidism, obesity and open-back shoes. Can become infected (cellulitis); in neuropathic diabetic patients fissures may lead to ulcers.
cradle-cap: Infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis of the scalp: non-inflammatory greasy yellow scales on the vertex and frontal areas, usually non-pruritic in a well infant, peaking around 3 months. Mimics: atopic dermatitis, impetigo, tinea capitis, psoriasis. Benign and self-limiting; reconsider the diagnosis if it persists beyond 12 months.
crohn-skin-disease: Metastatic Crohn disease: granulomatous plaques on the trunk and limbs away from the gut, asymmetric, sometimes with panniculitis; perianal skin tags, fissures and abscesses are direct extension of gut disease. Reactive disorders include pyoderma gangrenosum, Sweet syndrome and erythema nodosum. Biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas; skin lesions may precede bowel disease.
cronkhite-canada-syndrome: Sporadic, age about 60, 75% of cases Japanese: diffuse GI polyposis sparing the oesophagus with nail dystrophy, alopecia, hyperpigmentation of palms/soles/face and hypogeusia. Protein-losing enteropathy; about 15% gastric/colorectal malignancy. Mimics familial polyposis and Peutz-Jeghers. Systemic corticosteroids are the mainstay.
crouzon-syndrome: Autosomal dominant FGFR2 mutation (FGFR3 can be involved); the most common craniosynostosis syndrome. Premature suture closure with exophthalmos, hypertelorism, hypoplastic maxilla, mandibular prognathism and beaked nose. Acanthosis nigricans is the main dermatological sign, usually by puberty. Half of cases are sporadic new mutations.
crusted-scabies: Hyperinfestation with Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis: hyperkeratotic plaques on hands, feet, elbows, knees with nail dystrophy; itch may be minimal or absent. Up to 4,000 mites per gram of skin versus 10-20 in typical scabies. Risks: immunosuppression, HIV, HTLV-1, Down syndrome, dementia, institutions. Sepsis and post-streptococcal complications; treat with oral ivermectin plus topical scabicide and keratolytics, and treat contacts.
cryoglobulinaemia: Cold-precipitating immunoglobulins. Type I (monoclonal; myeloma, Waldenstrom, CLL) causes acrocyanosis, severe Raynaud, ischaemic necrosis and blue toes; mixed types II and III (rheumatoid factor) cause palpable purpura, cutaneous vasculitis, glomerulonephritis and neuropathy. Type III is linked to hepatitis C, SLE, Sjogren and RA; antivirals are effective in hepatitis C-associated disease. Females affected 3:1.
cryopyrin-associated-periodic-syndromes: Autosomal dominant NLRP3 gain-of-function (excess IL-1) spanning FCAS (mildest), Muckle-Wells and NOMID/CINCA (most severe). Fever, migratory urticaria-like rash from infancy that burns or stings rather than itches, arthralgia, conjunctivitis. Biopsy: neutrophilic infiltrate without mast cells or vasculitis. Respond to IL-1 blockade.
cutaneous-abscess: Pus-filled cavity without a true capsule; hot, red, painful lump. S. aureus is the usual cause (boils, carbuncles); MRSA may cause recurrent abscesses. Sterile abscesses follow corticosteroid or bovine collagen injection, and occur in hidradenitis suppurativa, acne conglobata/fulminans, Crohn disease and panniculitis. Incise and drain; for recurrences consider iron or immune deficiency, diabetes.
cutaneous-adenoid-cystic-carcinoma: Rare, slow-growing sweat-duct-derived tumour: firm skin-coloured solitary nodule or plaque, most commonly on the scalp, age 50-70. Better prognosis than the salivary type; metastasis is very rare (usually lungs). Local recurrence is common (22-70%), more with perineural invasion or narrow margins, and can occur up to 35 years later; wide excision (e.g. 1 cm) is recommended.
cutaneous-adverse-reactions-to-antibioti: Morbilliform eruption is the most common antibiotic rash (7-14 days after starting, pruritic, no mucosal involvement); urticaria is second. Tetracyclines, especially doxycycline, are the most common antibiotic cause of photosensitivity. Amoxicillin/penicillins account for about 50% of SDRIFE (intergluteal and inguinal fold erythema). Vancomycin red man syndrome is histamine-mediated, not allergic.
cutaneous-b-cell-lymphoma: Primary cutaneous B-cell lymphomas are ~20% of cutaneous lymphomas. Follicle centre type is most common (scalp, forehead, trunk; bcl-2 negative, no t(14;18)); marginal zone is MALT-type (trunk, arms; Borrelia link); diffuse large B-cell leg type has the worst prognosis (older women, bcl-2 and MUM1+, 5-year survival about 50%). Intravascular type: tender nodules and telangiectases.
cutaneous-collagenous-vasculopathy: Rare acquired microangiopathy: bilateral blanching telangiectasias starting on the lower limbs and spreading cephalically; spares mucosae and nail beds. Mimics generalised essential telangiectasia (which can involve oral mucosa and conjunctiva), so biopsy is needed. Histology: thickened vessel walls, PAS-diastase positive perivascular material; EM shows veil cells and Luse bodies.
cutaneous-cysts-and-pseudocysts: Epidermoid cyst: central punctum, cheesy malodorous keratin, wall with a granular layer; multiple cysts may indicate Gardner syndrome ('sebaceous cyst' is a misnomer). Trichilemmal (pilar) cyst: 90% on scalp, no punctum, palisaded wall without a granular layer, autosomal dominant or sporadic. Steatocystoma multiplex: sebum-filled, K17 mutations, linked to pachyonychia congenita. Dermoid cyst: fully mature skin elements on face/scalp.
cutaneous-dysaesthesia: Localised variants map to a nerve or dermatome: brachioradial pruritus (dorsolateral forearm, worse with sun), notalgia paraesthetica (T2-T6 between scapula and spine; linked to MEN2A/RET), meralgia paraesthetica (lateral femoral cutaneous nerve), and trigeminal trophic syndrome (ala nasi ulceration with nasal tip spared).
cutaneous-endometriosis: Rare; usually 'scar endometriosis' in a caesarean, hysterectomy or laparoscopy incision, also umbilicus and vulva. Firm blue, black, brown or red subcutaneous mass that cramps and bleeds with menses ('menstruating tumour'). Histology/cytology: endometrial glands, stroma and haemosiderin. Excision; local recurrence; rarely malignant change.
cutaneous-horn: Hard conical projection of compact keratin; about half have a benign base (seborrhoeic keratosis, viral wart) and half a premalignant or malignant one (actinic keratosis, SCC). No clinical feature reliably excludes malignancy, so histology of the base is crucial. Suspicious features: pain, large size, induration or redness at the base, wide base/low height, lack of terracing, older men.
cutaneous-lupus-erythematosus: Lupus-specific lesions show vacuolar interface dermatitis. ACLE: malar rash sparing nasolabial folds. SCLE: annular or psoriasiform rash on trunk and upper limbs, no scarring; 20-40% drug-induced. DLE (80% of chronic CLE): scarring plaques with follicular prominence (carpet tack sign). Ro/La-positive mothers: neonatal LE with congenital heart block.
cutaneous-marginal-zone-lymphoma: Low-grade MALT-type B-cell lymphoma: red to violet papules, plaques or nodules on the trunk and arms, solitary or multifocal. Cells CD20+, CD79a+, BCL-2+, CD10-, BCL-6-. Some cases associated with Borrelia burgdorferi and hepatitis C. Excellent prognosis (5-year survival up to 99%) but about 40% cutaneous relapse; extracutaneous spread rare; may resolve spontaneously.
cutaneous-mucinoses: Group of uncommon disorders with excess dermal mucin (hyaluronic acid). Generalised: scleromyxoedema, reticular erythematous mucinosis, scleroedema, follicular mucinosis, cutaneous lupus mucinosis, pretibial myxoedema (thyroid disease). Localised: lichen myxoedematosus, acral persistent papular mucinosis, mucinous naevus, digital mucous cyst, focal cutaneous mucinosis. Multiple angiomyxomas may indicate Carney complex.
cutaneous-myeloid-sarcoma: Extramedullary tumour of myeloid blasts (chloroma, granulocytic sarcoma): greenish or skin-coloured papules and nodules, usually multiple, on the trunk; most often an AML relapse but may precede or occur without marrow disease. Spared epidermis with dermal/subcutaneous infiltrate; CD68 and CD43 most sensitive, CD34/CD117 more specific. Poor prognosis; radiotherapy preferred over surgery.
cutaneous-plasmacytosis: Rare benign proliferation of mature plasma cells; multiple red-brown macules, papules or plaques on trunk, neck, face and axilla, mostly in Asian populations. Systemic form (CSP) has lymphadenopathy, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia, anaemia and hepatosplenomegaly. Histology: perivascular and perineural plasma cells; test for polyclonality to exclude lymphoma.
cutaneous-squamous-cell-carcinoma-in-ski: Most common skin cancer in blacks and Asian Indians. In skin of colour it more often arises in non-sun-exposed sites (legs, feet, anogenital) and in chronically inflamed, ulcerated or scarred skin (burn scars, lupus, epidermolysis bullosa). Metastasis risk is 20-40% in such skin versus 1-4% in sun-damaged skin; perianal and scar-arising SCC are high risk.
cutis-marmorata: Physiologic pink-blue mottled or marbled skin on cooling that clears with rewarming; seen in about 50% of children, typically infancy. Due to superficial small vessels dilating and contracting together. Benign and improves with age; distinct from cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita.
cutis-marmorata-telangiectatica-congenit: Congenital capillary malformation: fixed net-like blue to purple (livedo) patches that do not fade with warming, unlike physiologic cutis marmorata; may be atrophic or ulcerate. Associated with ipsilateral limb hypotrophy, Adams-Oliver syndrome (CMTC, scalp aplasia cutis, distal limb reduction) and phakomatosis pigmentovascularis. Fades slowly over the first years.
cutis-verticis-gyrata: Soft, spongy convoluted folds of scalp skin resembling the brain surface that cannot be flattened by pressure; primary form is male-predominant (5:1). Primary essential has no associations; primary nonessential has neuropsychiatric disorders (cerebral palsy, epilepsy) or cataracts; secondary causes include acromegaly, cerebriform intradermal naevus and inflammatory scalp disease.
cytophagic-histiocytic-panniculitis: Painful multifocal subcutaneous nodules with fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly and progressive liver failure; death from bleeding. Biopsy shows histiocytes engulfing blood cells (cytophagocytosis). Infection (often herpesviruses) triggers about 50%; subcutaneous T-cell lymphoma can present this way.
dactylitis: Sausage digit. Causes: psoriatic arthritis (about one-third; marker of severity), reactive arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, gout, sarcoidosis, sickle-cell hand-foot syndrome (often first sign, within first 4 years), TB (spina ventosa), congenital syphilis (bilateral, symmetrical), blistering distal dactylitis (group A strep). Not typical of RA or osteoarthritis.
defects-of-the-hair-shaft: Bamboo hair (trichorrhexis invaginata, ball-and-socket) is classic for Netherton syndrome (SPINK5). Monilethrix: beaded hair, autosomal dominant, keratin genes (KRT31, 86, 81). Pili torti: flattened twisted shafts; Menkes disease (X-linked copper, "steel wool" hair), Bjornstad (deafness). Trichothiodystrophy: sulphur-deficient hair with dark bands on polarising microscopy. Trichorrhexis nodosa is the most common defect.
delusions-of-parasitosis: Fixed false belief of infestation with crawling sensations, excoriations and specimens brought as proof ("matchbox sign"); also called Ekbom syndrome. Primary form is thought to involve increased basal ganglia dopamine; secondary causes include dementia, B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, HIV, stimulants and drugs (amantadine, l-dopa, topiramate). Exclude true infestation; do not collude. Antipsychotics (pimozide, risperidone, olanzapine) are used.
demodex: Mites of hair follicles: D. folliculorum in small follicles and eyelashes, D. brevis in sebaceous glands. Demodicosis is diagnosed at a density above 5/cm2; dermoscopy shows spiky white structures occluding follicular openings. Associated with rosacea (papulopustular or granulomatous), perioral dermatitis, blepharitis and HIV; histology shows mites in follicular infundibula with follicular hyperkeratosis.
dengue: Flavivirus (DENV 1-4) spread by Aedes aegypti: fever, retro-ocular headache, 'break-bone' aches, rash, leukopenia, positive tourniquet test. Warning signs: mucosal bleeding, rising haematocrit, thrombocytopenia, effusions. Sequential infection with another serotype increases risk of severe dengue. Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs (bleeding).
dental-sinus: Chronic draining sinus from a necrotic tooth, intraoral or extraoral (chin, submental/jawline, cheek), often painless and far from the culprit tooth; misdiagnosed as skin cancer, boil or pyogenic granuloma. Recurrence despite antibiotics or surgery is the clue. Dental X-ray shows bone loss at the root tip; cure needs tooth extraction or root canal, not skin surgery.
dercum-disease: Adiposis dolorosa: chronic painful (at least 3 months) symmetric subcutaneous lipomas/angiolipomas in overweight or obese adults, mainly women aged 35–50. Clinical diagnosis; histology resembles ordinary lipoma. Distinguish from painless Madelung disease and familial multiple lipomatosis; fibromyalgia is a common comorbidity.
dermatitis-artefacta: Self-inflicted lesions that are bizarre, geometric or linear with sharp demarcation from normal skin, appearing overnight on sites the patient can reach; the patient denies self-infliction. More common in women, usually teens or early adulthood. Avoid direct confrontation; supportive follow-up, psychiatric referral often refused.
dermatitis-neglecta: Hyperpigmented patches or verrucous plaques with adherent flaking scale from inadequate frictional cleansing, often over surgical sites (pacemaker, cataract) or painful or disabled areas. Key mimic: terra firma-forme dermatosis. Clue: crust wipes off with isopropyl alcohol. Biopsy: orthokeratotic hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis, no inflammatory infiltrate.
dermatophytide-reactions: Id reaction: sterile allergic rash at a distant site from an inflammatory tinea; fungus cannot be cultured from the id. Follicular papules on the trunk follow a zoophilic kerion; pompholyx-like vesicles on palms and hands follow severe tinea pedis; erythema nodosum may also occur. Resolves once the primary infection is controlled; treat the id with topical steroids.
dermographism: Linear wheals with flare 1-3 min after firm stroking, resolving in 30-60 min; the commonest physical urticaria. Simple form is asymptomatic; symptomatic (factitious urticaria) itches, worse at night. Variants: red, delayed (wheal 3-6 h later, treatment-resistant), cholinergic, white (dermatitis), black (metal). Associated with scabies and some drugs; biopsy only to distinguish mastocytosis (Darier sign).
dermoid-cyst: Choristoma of normal skin tissues (keratinocytes, hair follicles, sweat glands) foreign to the site; solitary firm, dough-like lump on the outer eyebrow, eyelid, upper nose, neck or scalp, forming along fusion lines; about 40% present at birth. May have a nearby pit or sinus tract, so ultrasound/sinogram before excision. Histology shows mature skin elements including fat and hairs.
desmoplastic-melanoma: Firm, scar-like, often skin-coloured plaque or nodule on sun-damaged head and neck that lacks ABCD features; mimics scar, dermatofibroma, neurofibroma. Histology: paucicellular atypical spindle cells in fibrocollagenous stroma, overlying lentigo maligna in ~75%, neurotropism in about half. S100 and SOX10 positive; HMB-45 and Melan-A usually negative. Pure type (≥90% desmoplasia) has low reported nodal risk.
diabetic-foot-ulcer: Painless, circular punched-out ulcer within a callosity at a pressure site, often preceded by a haemorrhagic subepidermal blister; neuropathic and/or ischaemic. Pedal pulses may be absent with reduced sensation. Complicated by cellulitis and osteomyelitis; graded by the University of Texas system (depth, plus infection and ischaemia). Recurs in 40% within a year.
