diffuse-alopecia: Telogen effluvium is the most common cause of diffuse shedding, starting a few months after a trigger (high fever, childbirth, iron deficiency, thyroid disease, drugs); biopsy shows increased telogen follicles without inflammation. Anagen effluvium (chemotherapy, 1-2 weeks; thallium, colchicine) sheds 80-90%. Hair pull test is positive in both and diffuse alopecia areata, negative in pattern hair loss.
diffuse-dermal-angiomatosis-of-the-breas: Painful ulceration with dusky purple reticulate erythema over the lower breast quadrants, usually bilateral, in women with large pendulous breasts who are obese or smokers; also seen with peripheral vascular disease. Reactive angioendotheliosis variant from chronic skin hypoxia. Biopsy: dermal vessel proliferation, strongly CD31-positive. Smoking cessation, weight loss, breast reduction; isotretinoin is anti-angiogenic.
diffuse-hereditary-palmoplantar-keratode: Yellowish waxy palmoplantar thickening with a red, sharply demarcated edge, noticeable by age 3-4. Non-transgradient (Vorner, Unna-Thost; autosomal dominant) stays on palms and soles; transgradient types spread onto dorsal hands and feet (Mal de Meleda, Olmsted, Nagashima). Syndromic: Vohwinkel (starfish knuckles, pseudoainhum, deafness), Papillon-Lefevre (gingivitis, tooth loss), Huriez (SCC risk), Naxos (woolly hair, cardiomyopathy).
diffuse-melanosis-cutis: Rare complication (about 1–2%) of metastatic melanoma: progressive blue-grey discolouration of the entire skin and mucous membranes, often with melanuria (urine darkens on standing). Biopsy shows melanin in dermal histiocytes and free pigment with an unremarkable epidermis. Historically very poor prognosis, mean 4.4 months from onset to death.
digeorge-syndrome: 22q11.2 deletion in about 90% (FISH); also called velocardiofacial syndrome and CATCH22. Cleft palate, under-developed chin, low-set ears, heart defects (VSD, truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot), hypoparathyroidism and thymic dysfunction with frequent infections. Autoimmunity (ITP, haemolytic anaemia) and psychiatric disease are increased.
disseminate-and-recurrent-infundibulofol: Hitch and Lund disease: widespread mildly itchy follicular rash like 'goosebumps through a magnifying glass' on the torso, neck and arms. Mainly young, healthy people of African descent in hot, humid climates. Biopsy: infundibular oedema and lymphocytes; DIF negative. Poor response to steroids and antibiotics; resolves over years.
disseminated-intravascular-coagulation: Never a primary diagnosis; always secondary to another severe disease (sepsis, meningococcaemia, obstetric complications). Acute DIC: purpura, ecchymoses and mucosal bleeding with platelet and clotting factor depletion; purpura fulminans is the severe form, with symmetrical peripheral gangrene. Chronic DIC is thrombotic, linked to mucin-producing adenocarcinoma and Kasabach-Merritt syndrome.
disseminated-secondary-eczema: Id reaction (autoeczematisation): acute, symmetric, intensely itchy generalised eczema arising from a localised inflammatory focus such as venous eczema, inflammatory tinea pedis (dermatophytide), kerion, wound infection (bacterid), scabies or lice (pediculid). Find and treat the primary site; defer patch testing until it settles.
dowling-degos-disease: Adult-onset reticulate freckle-like pigmentation of the flexures, with comedone-like spots on the neck and pitted scars on the chin. Autosomal dominant; KRT5, POFUT1, POGLUT1; PSENEN variants linked to hidradenitis suppurativa. Histology: antler-like rete ridges with melanin at tips, no melanocyte increase; acantholysis defines Galli-Galli disease.
dracunculiasis: Guinea worm (Dracunculus medinensis): acquired by drinking water containing infected copepods. About 12 months later the female (up to 1 m) emerges, usually from the lower limb (about 90%): burning pain, papule, blister, rupture exposing the worm. No specific treatment; worm is slowly extracted by winding on a stick. No lasting immunity and no vaccine; dogs can be infected.
drug-induced-dermatomyositis: Hydroxyurea causes about 50% of reported cases, typically after 2-10 years, with skin changes on the backs of the fingers, hands and periorbital face; myositis rarely occurs. Calcinosis, Raynaud and adenocarcinoma are not reported. ANA, anti-Ro and anti-Jo-1 are usually negative; biopsy is identical to classic dermatomyositis; improves on stopping the drug.
drug-induced-lupus-erythematosus: Drug-induced SLE: procainamide and hydralazine are the high-risk drugs; arthralgia (90%) is characteristic while malar rash, kidney and CNS disease are rare. Anti-histone antibodies in 75-95%, anti-dsDNA rarely positive, complement normal. Drug-induced SCLE: suspect in an older patient, rash may involve the lower legs; triggers include calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors, terbinafine, TNF inhibitors.
drug-induced-nail-disease: Temporary matrix arrest gives Beau lines, onychomadesis and true leukonychia that move distally; blanchable white bands that do not move (Muehrcke lines) reflect nail bed damage with chemotherapy. Photo-onycholysis: doxycycline, psoralens, fluoroquinolones, NSAIDs. Minocycline: bluish grey nail bed. Retinoids and EGFR inhibitors: paronychia, pyogenic granuloma.
drug-induced-nummular-dermatitis: Bilateral, well-defined coin-shaped erythematous plaques, dry or exudative, on the limbs, trunk or feet with intense itch; yellowish crusting suggests Staphylococcus aureus colonisation or infection. Implicated drugs: diuretics, statins, interferon, ribavirin, IVIG, TNF inhibitors. May clear more quickly once the drug is stopped.
drug-induced-pemphigus: Thiol drugs (penicillamine, captopril) cause pemphigus foliaceus without oral involvement; non-thiol drugs (penicillins, cephalosporins, vancomycin, other ACE inhibitors, piroxicam) most commonly cause pemphigus vulgaris. Onset days to 6 months after starting. About 50% of thiol-induced cases resolve on stopping the drug; non-thiol cases with antibodies have a better prognosis.
drug-induced-pigmentation: Minocycline gives bluish pigmentation, especially in scars; amiodarone blue-grey on sun-exposed face and hands (reversible, up to a year); chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine blue-grey face, oral mucosa and nail beds. Silver causes argyria, gold golden-brown skin, bleomycin flagellate pigmentation, phenytoin/carbamazepine melasma-like facial patches. A resolved fixed drug eruption leaves a localised brown patch.
drug-induced-pruritus: Itch with no primary rash, just scratch marks. Most commonly reported causes: opioids (especially with spinal anaesthesia), chemotherapeutic agents and chloroquine (60-70% of black Africans prescribed it). Naloxone or naltrexone for mu-receptor itch (opioids, plasma volume expanders); ursodeoxycholic acid or cholestyramine for cholestatic injury. Itch may persist days to months after stopping.
drug-induced-psoriasis: Drug-induced psoriasis clears when the drug is stopped (no previous psoriasis); drug-aggravated psoriasis continues despite stopping, in those with a personal or family history. Triggers: beta-blockers, lithium, antimalarials, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, terbinafine, TNF-alpha inhibitors (paradoxical psoriasis). Onset can be months to years after starting; TNF inhibitors can cause palmoplantar pustulosis, nearly always in smokers.
drug-induced-urticaria: Second most common drug eruption after morbilliform. Strongly associated drugs: ACE inhibitors, penicillins, cephalosporins, tetracyclines, griseofulvin, NSAIDs, morphine, codeine, radiographic contrast, salicylates. Mechanisms: type I (IgE), type III, or non-immune direct mast cell release. ACE inhibitor angioedema can appear years after starting, without weals.
drug-induced-vitiligo: Resembles vitiligo but with rapid onset and extension, often confetti-like white macules, in older patients. Causes are immune-modulating or targeted drugs: PD-1 inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab; 15% in metastatic melanoma), BRAF inhibitors (vemurafenib, dabrafenib), TNF inhibitors, interferon, IL-2, imatinib, topical imiquimod. Usually resolves when the drug is stopped, over a variable time.
dry-gangrene: Localised tissue death from prolonged ischaemia, seen as grey or black necrotic tissue, often with claudication, rest pain, shiny thin cool skin and livedo reticularis. Causes include emboli, thrombosis, calciphylaxis, frostbite, DIC, atherosclerotic peripheral arterial disease and Buerger disease. A pale, paralysed, pulseless limb is a surgical emergency. Assess with Ankle Brachial Index and imaging.
dry-skin: Xerosis from a stratum corneum barrier defect with reduced lipids; shins are the most affected site and nearly everyone over 60 has it. Early-childhood onset suggests ichthyosis (ichthyosis vulgaris: FLG; X-linked: STS). Complications include eczema craquelé (asteatotic eczema) and winter itch. Drugs causing it include oral retinoids, diuretics and EGFR inhibitors.
dupilumab-associated-ocular-surface-dise: Eye adverse effects typically within 4 months of starting dupilumab; conjunctivitis and dry eye are most common, then blepharitis; keratitis is infrequent. Risk is higher in atopic dermatitis than other indications (26.1% conjunctivitis in a meta-analysis). Usually responds to medical treatment without stopping dupilumab; refer urgently for vision loss or purulent discharge.
dupuytren-contracture: Progressive palmar fascia fibrosis: nodule, then cord, then finger flexion contracture, classically 4th and 5th digits; diagnosed clinically. Associated with Caucasian men over 50, genetics, alcohol, smoking, diabetes, epilepsy and manual labour. Diabetic cheiroarthropathy affects all fingers sparing the thumb without nodules or cords. Recurrence after surgery is high.
dystrophic-epidermolysis-bullosa: Type VII collagen (COL7A1) mutation, dominant or recessive; blisters heal with scarring and milia. Severe recessive form: mitten hands from fused digits and rapidly growing SCC in chronic wounds at covered sites, often metastatic at diagnosis. Dominant form has normal life expectancy; Bart syndrome = aplasia cutis, oral lesions, nail abnormalities.
eccrine-porocarcinoma: Rare sweat gland cancer of the elderly, unrelated to sun exposure: ulcerated, red, shiny dome-shaped nodule or wart-like plaque, most often on the lower legs or feet, uncommon on palms and soles. Mimics seborrhoeic keratosis, pyogenic granuloma, wart and SCC; biopsy needed. Spreads via lymphatics, so examine regional nodes; about 20% local recurrence or metastasis.
ecthyma: Deep (dermal) form of impetigo: hard-crusted sore overlying an indurated ulcer that heals with scarring, usually on the buttocks, thighs, legs and feet. Caused by Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus; risk with poor hygiene, tropical humidity, insect bites, scabies and immunocompromise. Rare complication: post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
ectodermal-dysplasia: Group of about 150 inherited disorders with defects of hair, teeth, nails and/or sweat glands; present from birth and non-progressive. Hypohidrotic (anhidrotic) and hydrotic forms are the most common; hyperpyrexia can be fatal in hypohidrotic disease. Hay-Wells (AEC) and ectrodactyly-ED-clefting are recognised syndromes.
eczematous-cheilitis: Lip dermatitis with redness, dryness, scaling and fissuring of the vermilion and perioral skin, often with angular cheilitis. Endogenous cause is atopic dermatitis; exogenous causes are irritant (lip-licking is the major cause) and allergic contact (at least one-quarter of cases). Patch test (standard plus lipstick/toothpaste series and own products); prick test if contact urticaria suspected.
elastolytic-giant-cell-granuloma: Annular plaques with an elevated scaly erythematous border and central hypopigmentation on sun-exposed sites (face, dorsal hands, neck), age 40-70. Histology: elastolysis, elastophagocytosis, multinucleated giant cells. Most common comorbidity is diabetes; mimics granuloma annulare (may be a variant). Also called actinic or O'Brien granuloma.
elastosis: Dermal degeneration with increased elastin deposition; subtypes are separated by clinical and biopsy features. Solar elastosis: yellow, thickened, furrowed sun-damaged skin. Favre-Racouchot (nodular elastosis): cysts and comedones around the eyes or back of the neck. Buschke-Ollendorf: multiple elastomas with osteosclerosis.
elastosis-perforans-serpiginosa: Transepithelial elimination of abnormal elastic fibre; grouped 2-5 mm red papules in linear, circular or serpiginous arrays with a central keratotic plug, mostly on the back of the neck. Reactive form with Down, Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan; drug-induced with D-penicillamine. Males more than females (4:1); usually resolves spontaneously.
elephantiasis-nostras-verrucosa: Severe chronic non-filarial lymphoedema of the lower legs: non-pitting oedema (Kaposi-Stemmer sign), cobblestone papillomatous and mossy hyperkeratotic skin. Associated with obesity, recurrent infection, heart failure and venous insufficiency; exclude filariasis. Complications include squamous cell carcinoma and angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves).
eosinophilic-dermatosis-of-haematologica: Recurrent itchy papules, nodules, urticarial weals and vesicles/bullae resembling exaggerated arthropod bites in haematological malignancy, especially CLL; may precede, coincide with or follow the cancer. Biopsy: eosinophil-rich lymphohistiocytic infiltrate, with or without flame figures. Exclude drug reaction, insect bites, eosinophilic folliculitis, Wells syndrome. Treatments largely disappointing.
eosinophilic-granulomatosis-with-polyang: Formerly Churg-Strauss: asthma, blood and tissue eosinophilia, and small-vessel vasculitis with granulomas on biopsy. Phases: prodromal (asthma, rhinitis), eosinophilic, vasculitic. Skin involved in about half: purpura and nodules with central necrosis on elbows and knees. Heart involvement is most frequent and causes at least half of deaths. Leukotriene modifiers are a reported drug association.
eosinophilic-pustular-folliculitis: Ofuji disease: itchy follicular papules and pustules on the face, scalp, neck and trunk, with eosinophils around follicles and sebaceous glands on biopsy. Variants: classic (Japan), HIV-associated (CD4 below 300), infantile, cancer- and drug-associated. Peripheral eosinophilia and raised IgE; indomethacin is reported effective.
eosinophilic-pustular-folliculitis-of-in: Recurrent pruritic sterile papulopustules, usually on the scalp, in infants under 36 months (male predominance 4:1) who are otherwise well. Peripheral eosinophilia during flares; Tzanck smear shows eosinophils. Biopsy often lacks true folliculitis. Self-limited by about age 3; mild to moderate topical steroids work, antibiotics do not.
eosinophilic-ulcer-of-the-oral-mucosa: Solitary, rapidly growing, usually painful oral ulcer (tongue most common) in adults aged 50-80, with a raised firm edge and wipeable white-yellow base; self-heals within about a month, often quickly after biopsy. Histology: infiltrate deep into muscle with many eosinophils and scattered atypical CD30+ T-cells. Biopsy to exclude oral cancer; also called traumatic ulcerative granuloma with stromal eosinophilia.
epidermal-naevus-syndromes: Epidermal naevi plus brain, eye or skeletal anomalies, usually sporadic from postzygotic mosaic mutations. CHILD syndrome: X-linked dominant (NSDHL), females, unilateral ichthyosiform naevus with sharp midline cut-off and limb defects; foamy histiocytes in dermal papillae. Schimmelpenning syndrome: sebaceous naevus with HRAS/KRAS mutations.
epidermolysis-bullosa-pruriginosa: Rare dystrophic EB variant (COL7A1) with intensely itchy hypertrophic papules, nodules and lichenified plaques on the shins; scarring and milia, nail dystrophy common; face, neck and flexures spared. Mimics nodular prurigo and hypertrophic lichen planus. DIF negative; EM shows diminished anchoring fibrils. Lifelong, often refractory.
epulis: Non-specific term for gingival masses. Epulis fissuratum: fibrous overgrowth with a deep groove where an ill-fitting denture flange sits. Giant cell epulis: peripheral giant cell granuloma from the periodontal ligament, mainly women, may erode bone, recurrence 10% or more. Congenital epulis: newborn anterior alveolar ridge mass, female:male 8:1, regresses spontaneously.
erosive-lichen-planus: Chronic painful mucosal ulceration healing with scarring, mainly oral and genital; at least twice as common in women. Vulvovaginal-gingival syndrome (women) and peno-gingival syndrome (men) are severe variants. Larger, more irregular and longer-lasting than aphthae. About 1-3% develop SCC; suspect it with an enlarging lump or ulcer with thickened edges. Lichenoid histology may be lost because the epidermis is eroded.
erosive-pustular-dermatosis: Pustules, lakes of pus and crusts over erosions on the sun-damaged bald scalp of the elderly (often over 80, with actinic keratoses and prior SCC); triggered by minor injury or surgery (pathergy); reported with EGFR inhibitors such as gefitinib. Does not clear with antibiotics alone. Biopsy repeatedly to exclude SCC; mimics include Brunsting-Perry pemphigoid.
eruptive-vellus-hair-cysts: Small 2-3 mm red or brown dome-shaped papules, sometimes umbilicated, on the central chest/sternum; familial forms (autosomal dominant, K17 mutations in some) in early childhood, sporadic in teens. Histology: cyst lined by stratified squamous epithelium with a granular layer, laminated keratin and vellus hairs. Associated with steatocystoma multiplex, pachyonychia congenita, ectodermal dysplasia.
erysipeloid: Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae infection through a cut after handling meat, poultry, fish or shellfish (fishermen, butchers, abattoir workers, cooks, vets). Sharply defined bright red to purple, smooth, shiny lesions on the hands and finger webs, expanding slowly, sometimes with tiny blisters; self-limiting in 2-4 weeks. Rare systemic form can involve heart, brain, joints, lungs.
erythema-annulare-centrifugum: Annular or arciform erythema with a trailing scale on the inner edge behind the advancing margin; thighs, buttocks, upper arms. Biopsy: superficial or deep perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate ('coat-sleeve'). Associated with tinea pedis, internal malignancy, drugs, pregnancy, haematological and endocrine disease. Mimics: erythema gyratum repens, necrolytic migratory erythema, erythema marginatum.
erythema-dyschromicum-perstans: Ashy dermatosis (of Ramirez): well-circumscribed grey macular patches on the face, neck and trunk in an otherwise well patient; early lesions may be red with a raised border. Darker skin, notably Latin Americans and Indians. Histology: basal vacuolar change early, then pigmentary incontinence with dermal melanophages; often classed as a variant of lichen planus pigmentosus. Treatment-resistant.
erythema-elevatum-diutinum: Rare necrotising small vessel vasculitis: red, purple, brown or yellow papules, plaques and nodules, symmetric on extensor surfaces over joints (backs of hands) and buttocks. Biopsy: leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Associated with granuloma faciale, streptococcal infections, hepatitis B, HIV, haematological and rheumatological disease. Dapsone is considered the drug of choice; relapses on withdrawal; oral steroids generally ineffective.
erythema-gyratum-repens: Paraneoplastic, intensely itchy concentric erythematous rings with a 'wood-grain' look, the edge migrating about 1 cm/day with a trailing collarette scale. Underlying malignancy in 80%, lung cancer in 33-47%; mostly Caucasian men in their 60s. DIF: granular IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. Resolves after tumour removal; pemphigus foliaceus can mimic it.
erythema-palmare-hereditarium: Lane disease: inherited persistent redness of the palms and fingertips present from birth or early infancy, sparing the central palm and most prominent on the hypothenar and thenar eminences and fingertips. Benign; inheritance variable and no gene identified. Diagnosis: family history, early onset, and excluding other palmar erythema (pregnancy, liver disease, drugs). Biopsy: dilated dermal vessels, no inflammation.
erythrodermic-psoriasis: Generalised red dry skin; about a third of erythroderma is due to psoriasis. Triggers: infection, low calcium, withdrawal of oral or strong topical corticosteroids, strong tar, lithium and antimalarials. Complications include dehydration, heart failure, hypothermia and protein loss. Avoid oral steroids if possible (withdrawal can cause erythroderma or generalised pustular psoriasis), and avoid tar and phototherapy early.
erythrokeratoderma: Rare, mostly autosomal dominant keratinisation disorders with well-demarcated red scaly plaques, often from connexin gene mutations; biopsy is non-distinctive. Erythrokeratoderma variabilis is the commonest, with fixed plaques on the outer limbs plus migratory plaques lasting hours to days, triggered by stress, temperature change or friction; hair, teeth and nails are spared. Oral retinoids thin the plaques but the redness persists.
erythromelalgia: Triad of recurrent burning pain, erythema and warmth of feet and hands, brought on by warmth or dependency and relieved by cooling and elevation. Primary: SCN9A (Nav1.7) mutations; familial form is Weir-Mitchell disease. Secondary: myeloproliferative disorders (polycythaemia vera, essential thrombocythaemia), preceding them in 85%; aspirin relieves thrombocytosis-related symptoms. Repeated cold-water immersion risks ulcers and gangrene.
exanthems: Widespread rash with fever, malaise and headache, usually infectious. Childhood causes: varicella, measles, rubella, roseola (HHV-6B), erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19). Also EBV/aminopenicillin rash, pityriasis rosea (HHV-6/7), staphylococcal and streptococcal toxin disease (TSS, SSSS, scarlet fever), drugs, SLE, adult-onset Still disease; Kawasaki disease is of unknown cause.
exercise-induced-anaphylaxis: Mast cell degranulation during exercise: pruritus, urticaria, angioedema, flushing, dyspnoea, hypotension, usually within 30 minutes of starting; stopping exercise improves symptoms. Food-dependent form (one-third to half of cases): exercise 1-3 hours after eating wheat, shellfish, tomatoes, peanuts or corn; neither food nor exercise alone triggers it. Women twice as likely; onset 10-30 years.
exercise-induced-vasculitis: Golfer's vasculitis: benign neutrophilic small vessel vasculitis after prolonged exercise (running, hiking, golf), especially in warm humid weather. Lower legs and thighs with purpura, weals and oedema, sparing skin covered by socks; patient otherwise well; resolves in 3-4 weeks. Often women over 50. Biopsy: leukocytoclastic vasculitis; DIF shows complement and immunoglobulin in vessel walls.
exfoliative-cheilitis: Rare continuous peeling of the vermilion, usually lower lip, in young adults under 30; often factitial (lip picking, licking, biting) with psychiatric comorbidity. A diagnosis of exclusion: swab for Candida and S. aureus, biopsy is nonspecific. Some cases are localised psoriasis or HIV-associated; typically treatment resistant.
fabry-disease: X-linked lysosomal storage disease (GLA, alpha-galactosidase A deficiency) with Gb3 deposition. Clusters of non-blanching angiokeratomas in the bathing-suit area, hypohidrosis, acroparesthesia and corneal cloudiness; kidney, cardiac and cerebrovascular disease are the major complications. Females need genetic analysis as enzyme activity can be normal.
facial-discoid-dermatosis: Rare; discrete annular, well-demarcated pink-orange papulosquamous plaques limited to the face and neck, reported more in women of Asian background. Biopsy is non-specific but excludes fungal infection and atypical psoriasis. Mimics include seborrhoeic dermatitis, tinea faciei and cutaneous lupus; often unresponsive to topical steroids.
facial-psoriasis: Three subtypes: hairline psoriasis (scalp extension with bright red plaques), sebo-psoriasis (salmon-pink thin plaques with bran-like scale on eyelids, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, beard) and true facial psoriasis (sharply demarcated symmetrical plaques). Rarely solely facial. Facial steroid side effects include periorificial dermatitis, thin skin and telangiectasia; calcineurin inhibitors are useful on eyelids.
favus: Severe tinea capitis from Trichophyton schoenleinii: yellow cup-shaped crusts (scutula) pierced centrally by a hair, grouping like a honeycomb, with a mousy odour. Progresses to hair loss, atrophy and scarring; chronic, lasting 10-20 years if untreated. Confirm with microscopy and culture of scrapings and hairs pulled by the roots; needs an oral antifungal.
female-pattern-hair-loss: Diffuse thinning with hair miniaturisation rather than the male pattern of frontal recession; polygenic, and most women have normal androgen levels, so FPHL is preferred over "female androgenetic alopecia". Chronic telogen effluvium is the key mimic. Check androgens if acne, irregular menses or excess facial/body hair (PCOS; less often congenital adrenal hyperplasia). Treatment aims to slow progression; no cure.
fibreglass-dermatitis: Mechanical irritant contact dermatitis from fibreglass spicules penetrating the stratum corneum; exposed face, neck, forearms, hands and flexures, often follicular, with paronychia. Skin-stripping with KOH shows fibres under polarised light (birefringent on biopsy). Mimics: scabies and insect bites; family can be affected via work clothing. Barrier creams are not useful and may worsen it.
fibromatosis: Fibrous overgrowth of dermal and subcutaneous connective tissue, usually benign. Superficial forms (Dupuytren, Ledderhose, Peyronie, knuckle pads) are small and slow growing; deep desmoid tumours do not metastasise but can be locally aggressive and obstruct vessels, nerves and organs. Palmar, plantar and penile forms linked to diabetes, liver disease, hypertension.
fibrous-papule-of-the-nose: Firm dome-shaped 1-6 mm papule on or around the nose in late adolescence or early adulthood; considered a variant of angiofibroma. Histology: fibroblast proliferation (stellate, spindle, multinucleated cells), fibrotic stroma, dilated vessels. Multiple widespread papules suggest tuberous sclerosis, Birt-Hogg-Dube or MEN1. Mimics: BCC, naevus, dermatofibroma.
fingertip-dermatitis: Hand dermatitis confined to the fingertips; the digits involved point to the cause, e.g. thumb, index and middle finger of the non-dominant hand when chopping garlic (diallyl disulphide). Other causes: acrylates (artificial nails), tulips/Peruvian lily (Tulipalin A), protein contact dermatitis (fish, meat), wet work. Patch test for ACD, prick test for protein contact dermatitis; consider psoriasis and tinea manuum.
fissured-tongue: Benign grooves on the dorsal tongue (scrotal tongue, lingua plicata), more prominent with age. Associated with geographic tongue, psoriasis (especially pustular), Down syndrome and orofacial granulomatosis; may be the first sign of Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome (fissured tongue, orofacial swelling, facial palsy). Clinical diagnosis, no treatment needed.
fistulas-and-sinuses-of-the-neck-and-fac: Thyroglossal duct cyst: midline, below hyoid, moves up with tongue protrusion or swallowing. Branchial cleft cyst: lateral neck, anterior to sternocleidomastoid. Preauricular pits (1%, 25% bilateral) near the helix root. Medial nasal dermal fistula: midline dorsal nasal dimple with hairs, may reach the dura; image before excision.
flagellate-erythema: Itchy red linear streaks on the back and flanks, first described with bleomycin (onset one day to several months), leaving brown flagellate pigmentation. Also reported with peplomycin, docetaxel, dermatomyositis (more inflammatory, persisting erythema), adult-onset Still disease and shiitake mushroom dermatitis. Histology: basal band of melanin. Heat can cause recall; usually resolves spontaneously.
flea-bite: Intense itching from bites on the lower legs or waistband; allergy to flea saliva causes papular urticaria, and anaphylaxis has not been reported. Flea dirt looks like black pepper grains and turns red on a damp towel. Rat fleas transmit plague and rickettsial typhus; cat fleas may transmit Bartonella henselae; sand flea Tunga penetrans causes tungiasis on the feet.
flexural-psoriasis: Inverse psoriasis of the axillae, groin, inframammary, umbilicus, natal cleft and genitals; lacks silvery scale, appearing shiny and smooth with deep red well-defined borders, often with a fissure in the fold. Hard to tell from seborrhoeic dermatitis (thin, salmon-pink, less defined); overlap is called sebopsoriasis. Complicated by Candida and lichenification. Overuse of strong topical steroids in folds causes striae and skin thinning.
focal-dermal-hypoplasia: Goltz syndrome: X-linked dominant (PORCN), mostly females as most affected male embryos do not survive. Linear atrophic streaks along Blaschko lines with fat herniation, telangiectasia and verrucoid papillomas; also nail, eye (coloboma), dental and limb anomalies (ectrodactyly, syndactyly) and striated bones on X-ray.
follicular-eruptions-due-to-drugs: Monomorphic erythematous follicular papules and pustules on the trunk, shoulders, upper arms and face; unlike acne vulgaris, comedones are absent and bacterial culture is negative. Causes: corticosteroids/ACTH/androgens, halogens, lithium, anticonvulsants, EGFR inhibitors, sirolimus, isoniazid, rifampicin. Malassezia may be seen in steroid acne; acute eruptions within 2 weeks, lithium and anticonvulsants after months to years.
follicular-occlusion-syndrome: Follicular occlusion triad: hidradenitis suppurativa, acne conglobata and dissecting cellulitis of the scalp; pilonidal sinus completes the tetrad. Follicles plug with keratin then rupture. Smoking and obesity are risk factors; rare associations include Dowling-Degos disease, pyoderma gangrenosum, Crohn disease and KID syndrome.
folliculitis: Inflamed hair follicle from any cause: Staph aureus (commonest), Pseudomonas in spa pools, Malassezia (itchy, upper trunk), shaving, occlusion, topical steroids. Drug causes include corticosteroids, lithium, EGFR inhibitors, vemurafenib and dabrafenib. Deep sterile folliculitis causes scarring alopecia (LP, DLE, folliculitis decalvans).
folliculitis-barbae: Itchy, tender papulopustules in shaved areas such as the beard line, usually from Staphylococcus aureus colonisation of the follicle. Deep form is sycosis barbae with sinus tracts, abscesses and scarring hair loss. Differs from pseudofolliculitis barbae (ingrown curved hairs, curly hair). Recurrence suggests nasal carriage or contaminated razors.
fordyce-spots: Ectopic sebaceous glands without hair follicles: 1-5 mm yellowish-white papules on the buccal mucosa, vermilion lip, glans/shaft (Tyson glands) or vulva; Montgomery glands on the areola. Present in 80% of adults and a normal variant, though Muir-Torre variant of Lynch syndrome has been reported. Some STIs can mimic them.
foreign-body-granuloma: Reaction to exogenous material (tattoo pigment, fillers, silica, talc, zinc, aluminium, sutures) giving red-brown papules, nodules or plaques that may ulcerate. Silica crystals seen under polarised light; ultrasound helps with fillers. Natural gut sutures 'spit' more than nylon; cactus spines give papules with a central black dot.
fournier-gangrene: Polymicrobial necrotising fasciitis of the genitalia, perineum and perianal region; surgical emergency. Male predominance (10:1), diabetes in 60%, alcoholism; SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin) may raise risk. Severe pain, crepitus, wet gangrene; early skin signs may understate severity; testes usually spared. Fascial arteriole thrombosis is histologically pathognomonic; CT shows gas. Excision plus broad-spectrum IV antibiotics; mortality 20-40%.
fox-fordyce-disease: Apocrine miliaria: keratotic plug traps apocrine sweat, the duct ruptures, giving intensely itchy folliculocentric dome-shaped papules of axillae, pubic region and areolae in post-pubertal women. Flares with heat, humidity, friction, stress; laser hair removal reported. Histology: keratotic plug above the apocrine duct entry, follicular spongiosis. May clear in pregnancy.
fracture-blister: Tense blisters over an acute fracture where skin overlies bone (ankle, wrist, elbow, foot, distal tibia), from shearing forces; resemble second-degree burns but not due to heat. Biopsy: subepidermal blister with little inflammation. Leave intact; may delay surgical fixation. Early repair (within 24 h) lowers risk.
fragrance-allergy: Type IV allergic contact dermatitis, second only to nickel as a cause of ACD; often streaky, with transfer to unexpected sites (hands to face) and common axillary involvement. Screen with balsam of Peru, Fragrance Mix I (isoeugenol most common) and Mix II (Lyral); a weak positive may be irritant. Consort allergy occurs; the repeat open application test is a practical screen.
frictional-lichenoid-dermatitis: Benign, self-limiting eruption of 1-2 mm flat-topped flesh-coloured papules on extensors (elbows, knees, dorsal hands) in school-aged children, mainly boys, recurring in spring and summer. Synonyms: juvenile papular dermatitis, Sutton summer prurigo. Associated with friction from rough surfaces; histology nonspecific. Mimics: lichen nitidus, lichen planus, keratosis pilaris.
gardner-syndrome: Variant of familial adenomatous polyposis (APC, 5q22; autosomal dominant) with extra-colonic features. Multiple epidermoid cysts at puberty in atypical sites (scalp, trunk, limbs), sometimes with pilomatricoma-like histology; osteomas (mandible; essential for diagnosis, often precede polyposis), desmoid tumours, CHRPE. Near-100% colorectal cancer risk.
generalised-eruptive-keratoacanthomas: Grzybowski syndrome: hundreds to thousands of 1-5 mm pruritic, umbilicated papules with a central keratotic plug on sun-exposed and intertriginous skin and mucosa (tongue, buccal mucosa, larynx). Confluent periorbital lesions give a mask-like 'sign of Zorro'; ectropion can occur. No familial tendency; associated with BRAF and hedgehog inhibitors; malignant change not reported.
generalised-essential-telangiectasia: Primary telangiectasia of unknown cause with no preceding or coexisting skin or internal disease; lacework or branching dilated capillaries under 0.2 mm, mostly on the feet, ankles and lower legs, spreading gradually and persisting. Onset around 40-50 years, women more often. Usually unresponsive to sclerotherapy. Cutaneous collagenous vasculopathy is often misdiagnosed as this.
genital-crohn-disease-images: Granulomatous genital involvement in Crohn disease (metastatic Crohn if separate from bowel disease): 'knife-cut' fissures in groin, perianal and vulval folds, fistulas, and granulomatous lymphoedema from lymphatic blockage. More common in females; 20-35% have no GI disease. Biopsy shows noncaseating granulomas but may miss them. Mimics: HS, pyoderma gangrenosum, sarcoidosis.
genital-herpes-images: About 60-70% of primary genital infections are HSV-2, the rest HSV-1; HSV-2 recurs more often. Penile ulceration from herpes is the most frequent cause of genital ulcer in sexual health clinics. Recurrences: itch or burning then small grouped vesicles on a red base, 5-10 days. Highest neonatal risk with a first episode early or late in pregnancy.
germline-bap1-mutation: Autosomal dominant BAP1 tumour-suppressor mutation predisposing to uveal melanoma, mesothelioma, cutaneous melanoma and renal cell carcinoma. Skin clue: 5-50 pink to skin-coloured dome-shaped or pedunculated papules (scalp, trunk) of large epithelioid melanocytes with loss of BAP1 on IHC and no Kamino bodies. Formerly called atypical Spitz tumours; also BAP-oma or Wiesner naevus.
gingival-enlargement: Gum overgrowth that is red, soft and bleeding if inflamed; darker red/purple and soft or fibrous if non-inflamed. Drug causes: ciclosporin, phenytoin and other anticonvulsants, calcium channel blockers. Also pregnancy/puberty, scurvy, leukaemia, GPA, sarcoidosis, Crohn disease; stop the offending drug, gingivectomy for severe cases.
gingivitis-and-periodontitis: Gingivitis: puffy, dusky red, tender gums that bleed easily, from plaque and tartar. Untreated, it progresses to periodontitis with gum pockets, receding gums, pus, loose teeth and alveolar bone loss. Predisposing: smoking, diabetes, leukaemia, Down syndrome, Papillon-Lefevre syndrome, Crohn disease, scurvy, erosive oral lichen planus.
glandular-cheilitis: Rare chronic inflammation of the lower lip in older males: swelling and pouting with numerous pin-sized orifices from which saliva can be expressed. Linked to sun exposure, trauma and smoking; complications are secondary infection and squamous cell carcinoma. Biopsy is nonspecific (enlarged salivary glands and ducts); advise smoking cessation and lip sun protection.
graham-little-syndrome: Rare variant of lichen planopilaris, mostly in middle-aged and post-menopausal women. Triad: patchy scarring scalp alopecia, nonscarring loss of axillary and pubic hair, and spiky follicular papules on trunk or limbs. Anagen hairs pull out easily from active edges. Scarring loss does not recover; treatment aims to stop progression.
gram-negative-folliculitis: Acne-like pustular rash around the upper lip, nose, chin and cheeks, arising in acne patients after long-term tetracycline or topical antibiotics; suspect when pustules respond poorly to usual anti-acne antibiotics. About 80% superficial pustules (Klebsiella, Escherichia, Serratia); about 20% deep nodulocystic (Proteus). Diagnosed by Gram stain and culture.
granular-parakeratosis: Red or brown scaly rash of body folds, most often the axillae, usually reported in middle-aged women. Healing may show peeling resembling pellagra. Histology: parakeratosis, hypergranulosis (the name), acanthosis, papillomatosis and prominent vessels. Provoked by friction, occlusion and sweating; benzalkonium chloride in cosmetics or laundry products may be implicated. May resolve spontaneously.
granuloma-faciale: Soft red-brown, violaceous or skin-coloured papules, plaques or nodules with prominent follicular openings on the face, typically in middle-aged white men; sun exposure implicated. Histology: eosinophil-rich dermal infiltrate, grenz zone, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, haemosiderin. Mimics erythema elevatum diutinum; recurs after treatment.
granuloma-gluteale-infantum: Asymptomatic firm red-violaceous nodules in the napkin area of infants aged 1-9 months (inguinal folds, buttock convexities), long axis parallel to skin folds. Histology shows no granulomas (misnomer). Linked to occlusion, prior topical steroids or benzocaine, Candida; resistant to treatment, regresses in 1-2 months leaving atrophic scars.
granuloma-inguinale: Donovanosis: Klebsiella granulomatis STI diagnosed by Donovan bodies in a Giemsa-stained crushed smear or biopsy; culture is very difficult. Commonest ulcerovegetative type: painless, easily bleeding beefy-red ulcers with rolled borders ('knife cut' in folds). Other types: nodular, hypertrophic ('walnut'), necrotic, cicatricial. Mimics chancroid, LGV, genital cancer.
granulomatous-cheilitis: Miescher cheilitis: sudden upper-lip swelling that recurs and becomes permanent and rubbery, with granulomas on biopsy. Part of orofacial granulomatosis; Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome is cheilitis, facial palsy and fissured tongue. Causes include allergic contact dermatitis, Crohn disease and sarcoidosis. Facial palsy occurs in about 30%.
granulomatous-dermatitis: Histologic umbrella: interstitial GD ("rope sign" cords on lateral trunk; middle-aged women; arthritis/autoimmune disease), palisading neutrophilic GD (crusted elbow papules in RA or Churg-Strauss; flame figures) and interstitial granulomatous drug reaction (TNF inhibitors, statins, CCBs; clears when drug stopped). Versus granuloma annulare: GA has upper dermal histiocytes and abundant mucin.
granulomatous-mastitis: Rare benign breast disease that mimics breast cancer: unilateral firm tender lump with erythema, ulceration, abscess, sinuses, nipple retraction; usually spares the central breast, fever typically absent. Histology: non-necrotising, non-vasculitic granulomas centred on lobules. Corynebacterium kroppenstedtii often cultured; rare erythema nodosum or polyarthritis.
habit-tic-deformity: Nail picking or pushing of the proximal nail fold (usually thumb) causing 'washboard nail': median depression with parallel transverse ridges, bolstered nail fold, cuticle loss, macrolunulae. Associated with OCD and insensitivity to pain (Lesch-Nyhan, Smith-Magenis). Mimics include median canaliform nail dystrophy; treat with habit reversal.
hair-shedding: Normal shedding is 50-100 hairs/day; about 85-90% of scalp follicles are in anagen, 1-3% catagen, 5-10% telogen (club hairs lacking a root sheath). Telogen effluvium: shedding about 3 months after a shock (childbirth, surgery, illness, poor diet), up to 50% of hair enters rest. Anagen effluvium: sudden loss of up to 90% of structurally abnormal hairs, most commonly from chemotherapy.
hairy-tongue: Harmless 'hairy' elongation of filiform papillae with brown/black discolouration of the dorsal tongue, due to defective shedding of keratin; bacteria and yeast make porphyrins. Linked to smoking, poor hygiene, coffee and drugs such as penicillin, erythromycin, tetracyclines, linezolid, erlotinib, olanzapine, bismuth. Usually self-limiting; stop triggers and debride the tongue.
hamartoma: Benign disorganised overgrowth of mature cell types native to the site, congenital (birthmark) or acquired; rarely neoplastic evolution. Skin examples: congenital melanocytic naevus, sebaceous naevus, basaloid follicular hamartoma (Gorlin), chondroid syringoma. More common in tuberous sclerosis and Cowden syndrome; Lisch nodules are iris hamartomas of NF1.
hand-dermatitis: Common, especially in young women, atopics and wet-work occupations. Subtypes: atopic (dorsal hands/wrists), discoid, pompholyx (vesicles on palms and sides of fingers), hyperkeratotic, fingertip. Irritant type hits finger webs first and spares palms; ACD clues are asymmetry and sharp borders (glove cuff). Mimics: psoriasis (symmetrical), tinea manuum (asymmetrical, peripheral scale), contact urticaria. Patch test chronic cases.
heat-urticaria: Rare inducible urticaria: weals confined to skin in contact with a warm stimulus, appearing within about 10 minutes and resolving in 1-3 hours. Confirm by provocation test (warm test tube >44 degrees or heated cylinder on the inner forearm). Unlike cholinergic urticaria, it does not involve sweating or core temperature. A delayed subtype appears 0.5-2 hours later, lasts up to 24 hours, without angioedema.
heberden-bouchard-nodes: Heberden node: bony swelling of the DIP joint; Bouchard node: PIP joint, less common and linked to more severe arthritis. Signs of osteoarthritis (osteophytes), strongly familial; may accompany a digital myxoid pseudocyst. Mimics include rheumatoid PIP swelling, gouty tophus, knuckle pads and pachydermodactyly.
heparin-induced-thrombocytopenia: Type II HIT: antibody to heparin-platelet factor 4 complexes activates platelets, causing a fall in platelets (>=50%) 5-10 days after starting heparin (within hours if previously sensitised) and paradoxical thrombosis (about 30%). Skin: tender purpura with black centres, retiform purpura, necrosis at injection or distant sites; biopsy shows occluded vessels without inflammation. Warfarin alone is not recommended (warfarin skin necrosis).
hereditary-angioedema: Autosomal dominant; C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency (type I, low level, 80-85%) or dysfunction (type II) leads to excess bradykinin. Recurrent angioedema without urticaria that does not respond to antihistamines; low C4 with normal C1 and C3; C1q is normal (low in acquired angioedema). Abdominal attacks mimic an acute abdomen; laryngeal oedema can be fatal. Avoid ACE inhibitors and oestrogen.
hereditary-benign-telangiectasia: Autosomal dominant; numerous telangiectases appear in childhood (2-12 years) on the face, neck, upper trunk and hands, with mucosa spared except the lip vermilion. No systemic involvement or bleeding, unlike hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (the key diagnosis to exclude). Histology: dilated subpapillary venous plexus with upper dermal atrophy. Punctate lesions may have pale halos (steal phenomenon).
hereditary-coproporphyria: Autosomal dominant with low penetrance; deficiency of coproporphyrinogen oxidase (CPOX), the sixth enzyme of haem synthesis. Acute neurovisceral attacks (abdominal pain most common) with or without PCT/VP-like blisters, scarring, milia and hypertrichosis on sun-exposed skin. Triggers: drugs, alcohol, smoking, illness, pregnancy. Risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.
hereditary-focal-palmoplantar-keratoderm: Thickening over pressure points of palms and soles; check for syndromic types. Howel-Evans (tylosis; AD): oesophageal cancer in middle age, oral leukokeratosis. Richner-Hanhart (AR, tyrosinaemia): eye ulcers, photophobia, intellectual disability. Pachyonychia congenita: wedge-shaped thick nails. Striate PPK with woolly hair: cardiomyopathy (Naxos).
hereditary-leiomyomatosis-and-renal-cell: Autosomal dominant fumarate hydratase (Krebs cycle) mutation. Multiple cutaneous piloleiomyomas (arrector pili; tender when knocked), early large uterine fibroids with leiomyosarcoma risk, and aggressive early-onset papillary type 2 renal cell cancer, usually unilateral and solitary. Also called Reed syndrome; kidney surveillance usually needs MRI.
herpangina: Enterovirus (usually coxsackie A16) in young children: fever and sore throat, then tiny vesicles becoming yellowish ulcers with a red rim on the palate, tonsils, uvula and back of throat. Skin is normal, unlike hand, foot and mouth disease; primary HSV stomatitis is more extensive, includes the gums and lasts longer. Dehydration is the commonest complication.
herpetic-whitlow: HSV-1/2 infection of the distal finger or thumb: painful swollen digit with clustered 1-3 mm vesicles on erythema, often at the nail fold. Children: autoinoculation from oral herpes (thumb sucking); adults: genital herpes or healthcare/dental exposure. Tzanck: ballooning multinucleated giant cells. Avoid surgical drainage; mimics include bacterial paronychia and felon.
hirsutism: Male-pattern terminal hair growth in women, graded by the Ferriman-Gallwey score (9 areas; 8-14 mild, 15 or more moderate to severe). Late-onset suggests hyperandrogenism: polycystic ovaries, Cushing, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, androgen-secreting tumour. Virilisation is a red flag; elevated DHEAS suggests adrenal source, androstenedione ovarian.
hodgkin-lymphoma: B-cell lymphoma with Reed-Sternberg cells (large multinucleated) on lymph node biopsy; painless superficial lymphadenopathy, B symptoms, generalised pruritus; classical type 95%, nodular sclerosis favouring young adults and females. Skin signs are usually non-specific (acquired ichthyosis, eczematised plaques along node drainage); true cutaneous infiltration is very rare, on the chest, and implies advanced disease.
homocystinuria: Autosomal recessive (CBS deficiency among genes implicated) with elevated homocysteine. Marfanoid habitus, ectopia lentis, myopia, intellectual disability, osteoporosis, thromboembolism (DVT, arterial events). Skin: hypopigmentation, fair thin hair, thin skin, malar flush, livedo reticularis. Cyanide-nitroprusside test; about half respond to pyridoxine.
house-dust-mite: Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus and farinae; main allergens come from faecal pellets (Der p1 cysteine protease, Der p2); Der p11 is a major allergen in atopic dermatitis. Proteases activate PAR-2 causing non-histamine itch and barrier disruption. Consider in treatment-refractory atopic dermatitis, with flares on skin contacting bedsheets; atopy patch test, prick test, specific IgE. Benefit of eradication measures is uncertain.
hydroa-vacciniforme: Rare photosensitivity of children (3–15 years) with tense vesicles on sun-exposed skin that become necrotic, pit-like papules with black crusts and heal with pale, depressed vacciniform scars. UVA implicated; some cases linked to EBV, and severe EBV-associated disease can progress to NK-cell lymphoma. Usually remits by adolescence.
hydroxyurea-induced-cutaneous-ulcer: Painful, well-demarcated round ulcer around the malleoli in an older patient on long-term hydroxyurea (median 60 months) for a myeloproliferative disorder, most commonly essential thrombocythaemia; surrounded by erythema, fibrosis and atrophy, atrophie blanche may be present. Histology is non-specific. Heals only after stopping hydroxyurea, not with wound care alone; recurs if restarted.
hypereosinophilic-syndrome: Eosinophils >1500/uL for at least 6 months, multi-organ involvement, and no parasitic, allergic or other cause. About 90% male, middle-aged; the rash (over 50%) is nonspecific, with itchy nodules or urticaria-like lesions. Some have underlying leukaemia, diagnosed even years later. Death is usually from heart failure.
hyperhidrosis: Primary: symmetric axillae, palms and soles; starts in childhood or adolescence, family history, stops during sleep. Secondary: asymmetric or generalised, may occur at night, due to endocrine, neurological or drug causes (e.g. phaeochromocytoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, SSRIs). Minor iodine-starch test maps sites; topical antiperspirants (aluminium salts) are among the treatments.
hyperkeratosis-lenticularis-perstans: Flegel disease: asymptomatic 1-5 mm red-brown scaly papules on dorsal feet and lower legs; removing scale leaves a bright red base with pinpoint bleeding. AD with SPTLC1 variants (sphingolipid synthesis), though often sporadic. Histology: compact hyperkeratosis, thin epidermis, band-like lichenoid infiltrate. Ddx Kyrle disease (larger papules, perforating keratin plug).
hyperkeratosis-of-the-nipple-and-areola: Warty pigmented verrucous plaques of the nipple and areola, usually bilateral, typically in adolescent females; may follow oestrogen therapy or pregnancy. Histology: orthokeratotic hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis, acanthosis, keratotic plugging. Unilateral lesion with pain, bleeding, ulceration, discharge or retraction needs breast cancer work-up (Paget disease in ddx).
hyperkeratotic-palmar-dermatitis: Endogenous eczema with sharply demarcated, hyperkeratotic, fissured plaques in the centre of both palms, starting in one palm; no vesicles or pustules, nails spared; middle-aged men. No increased personal/family psoriasis history or psoriasis HLA, and histology cannot reliably separate it from palmar psoriasis. Exclude tinea manuum and ACD; chronic, with topicals less effective; acitretin reported effective.
hyperthyroidism: Graves disease (antibodies activating the TSH receptor) causes 80%. Warm, smooth, moist skin, flushing, fine hair, onycholysis and thyroid acropachy. Pretibial myxoedema (mucinosis; 0.5-4.3% of Graves, 1-2 years after diagnosis) gives orange-peel shin nodules and plaques. Low TSH with high T4/T3; amiodarone and lithium can induce it.
hypertrichosis: Excess hair beyond the norm for age, sex and race, unlike hirsutism (male-pattern hair in women). Acquired hypertrichosis lanuginosa ("malignant down") on the face may herald cancer; other causes include porphyria cutanea tarda, anorexia nervosa, ciclosporin, phenytoin, minoxidil. Faun-tail on the lower back may indicate spina bifida; congenital terminalis type is almost always associated with gingival hyperplasia.
hypomelanosis-of-ito: Streaky, whorled or linear hypopigmented macules along Blaschko lines, present from birth, covering more than two dermatomes, sparing palms, soles and scalp. Associated abnormalities in 30–50% (seizures, intellectual disability, hearing, eye, dental and orthopaedic problems). Due to chromosomal mosaicism; also called incontinentia pigmenti achromians.
hypothyroidism: Pale dry coarse skin, eczema craquelé, carotenoderma, sparse brittle hair with loss of the outer third of the eyebrows, ridged brittle nails, and myxoedema (puffy face and eyelids; a mucinosis). High TSH with low T4. Autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto when goitre present) is the most common adult cause; amiodarone, lithium and interferon-alpha can induce it.
ichthyosis: Ichthyosis vulgaris (95% of cases; FLG, AD) spares flexures, with keratosis pilaris, hyperlinear palms and atopy; absent granular layer. X-linked recessive (STS): males, grey/brown rhomboid scale, normal palms, corneal opacities, cryptorchidism. Adult-onset acquired ichthyosis suggests Hodgkin lymphoma or other malignancy, sarcoidosis, HIV or drugs (nicotinic acid, kava, vemurafenib, hydroxyurea).
ichthyosis-prematurity-syndrome: Rare AR (SLC27A4, FATP4) disorder: premature birth after maternal polyhydramnios, thick clay-like vernix, and neonatal respiratory failure from aspirated keratinocyte debris. Peripheral eosinophilia is usual. Skin improves rapidly to mild ichthyosis and follicular hyperkeratosis; higher rate of atopy later. Ddx collodion baby, harlequin ichthyosis.
idiopathic-facial-aseptic-granuloma: Solitary painless red-violaceous nodule on the cheek or eyelid of a young child (mean age 4), resembling an acne nodule; cultures negative, resolves within a year without scarring. Thought to be childhood granulomatous rosacea; raises later risk of rosacea, especially ocular. Ultrasound shows a hypoechoic lesion without calcification, unlike pilomatricoma.
idiopathic-plantar-hidradenitis: Painful red nodules and plaques on the soles and insteps (less often palms), usually in children and young adults, linked to heat, wet conditions and sweaty feet. Biopsy: neutrophils around sweat glands. Resolves spontaneously within about 4 weeks but may recur. Distinguish from chemotherapy-related hand-foot syndrome; colchicine reported effective.
iga-pemphigus: Very rare; flaccid vesicles and pustules in an annular pattern on trunk, axillae and groin, mucosa infrequently involved. Intraepidermal neutrophils with little or no acantholysis; DIF shows IgA on keratinocyte surfaces. SPD type targets desmocollin-1. Associated with monoclonal IgA gammopathy and multiple myeloma; dapsone plus steroids used.
igg-subclass-deficiency: Normal total IgG but low levels of at least one IgG subclass, presenting with recurrent sinopulmonary infections (Streptococcus, Haemophilus, Branhamella), sepsis or meningitis, and infected eczema or atopic dermatitis. IgG2 makes antibodies to pneumococcal polysaccharides. Repeat levels in several months; consider vaccine response.
igg4-related-disease: Inflammatory pseudotumours with lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, many IgG4-positive plasma cells and storiform fibrosis; serum IgG4 is raised in only 60-70%. Middle-aged or older men with multi-organ disease (autoimmune pancreatitis, Mikulicz disease, retroperitoneal fibrosis, Riedel thyroiditis). Skin: itchy plaques, papules, nodules on face or forearm. Systemic steroids are used.
incontinence-associated-dermatitis: Irritant contact dermatitis from urine and/or faeces (raised pH and friction weaken the barrier): circumscribed redness and swelling over convexities of genital and anal skin, with erosions or bullae; folds are less severely affected. Risk of Candida and S. aureus infection and pressure ulceration. Clinical diagnosis; mimics: pressure ulcer, tinea cruris, flexural psoriasis.
infantile-acne: Acne on the cheeks of infants aged 6 weeks to 1 year, more common in boys; comedones, papules, pustules and nodules, usually not due to excess androgens. Acne at ages 2 to 6 is rare and suggests hormone abnormality (congenital adrenal hyperplasia, tumour, precocious puberty); work up for virilisation. Avoid tetracyclines in children (tooth staining).
infantile-digital-fibroma: Single or multiple firm or gelatinous pink nodules on the fingers or toes of infants; one-third are present at birth. Histology: interlaced spindle cells and collagen with inclusion bodies, thought to be myofibroblasts. May be confused with exostosis (X-ray helps). Many resolve in 2-3 years; frequently recur after surgery.
infectious-mononucleosis: EBV (HHV-4) in 15-25 year olds: sore throat, cervical lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly in weeks 2-3, atypical lymphocytes and positive heterophile (Monospot) test. Itchy morbilliform rash classically follows ampicillin/amoxicillin (rate likely lower than once reported); palatal petechiae. Avoid sport for the first three weeks (splenic rupture).
infective-panniculitis: No specific clinical features; more likely with immunodeficiency. Biopsy usually lobular; bacterial forms give a neutrophil-rich suppurative panniculitis. Mycobacterial cases (mostly atypical, e.g. M. chelonae, fortuitum, abscessus, marinum) need acid-fast stains and culture. Classic subcutaneous mycosis: single lower-leg nodule in a healthy host after soil or plant inoculation.
inflammatory-lesions-in-acne: Papules, pustules, nodules and pseudocysts (fluctuant nodules), often painful. Typically follow rupture of a closed comedo, with free fatty acids, Cutibacterium acnes products and IL-1/TNF driving inflammation. Debris can provoke granulomatous reaction; hypersensitivity to C. acnes is the presumed cause of acne fulminans.
inflammatory-linear-verrucous-epidermal-: Unilateral pruritic, erythematous, hyperkeratotic papules and plaques along Blaschko lines, often one leg; onset in first 5 years, female predominance. Eczema- or psoriasis-like surface distinguishes it from other keratinocytic naevi. Histology: epidermal hyperplasia, papillomatosis, hyperkeratosis with parakeratosis. Mimics: psoriasis, lichen striatus.
ingrown-toenail: Onychocryptosis, mostly the lateral big toe; commonest causes are ill-fitting shoes and improper trimming (cut straight across). Oral retinoids (isotretinoin, acitretin), fungal nail infection and pincer nails also contribute. Stage 3 has granulation tissue and nail-fold hypertrophy; lateral nail avulsion plus matricectomy is highly successful.
intraepidermal-squamous-cell-carcinoma: Bowen disease: irregular scaly orange-red or brown plaque on sun-exposed ears, face, hands and lower legs; multiple plaques are asymmetric (unlike psoriasis). Dermoscopy shows crops of rounded and coiled vessels; histology shows full-thickness epidermal dysplasia. Causes: UV, arsenic, ionising radiation, HPV (fingers/nails). Invasive SCC arises in about 5%.
intralymphatic-histiocytosis: Rare; red to purple macules or plaques on one limb overlying a diseased joint or scar, usually asymptomatic, in older women. Associated with rheumatoid arthritis (over one-third), orthopaedic metal implants (25%) and cancer surgery such as mastectomy (10%). Histology: dilated dermal lymphatics containing CD68-positive histiocytes. Resistant to steroids; infliximab cleared two RA patients.
intravascular-lymphoma: Rare large B-cell lymphoma with neoplastic (usually CD20+) cells filling the lumen of capillaries and post-capillary venules; no tumour mass or circulating cells. CNS signs plus B symptoms, with nodules/plaques or telangiectasia on thighs and trunk. Diagnose by deep or random normal-skin biopsy, ideally of a cherry angioma. Skin-limited variant has the better outcome.
iron-deficiency: Skin and mucosal signs: pallor, angular cheilitis, atrophic glossitis, koilonychia, pruritus, telogen effluvium. Pagophagia (pica for ice) is quite specific; beeturia also occurs. Ferritin below 15 is diagnostic but is an acute-phase reactant, so normal or high levels do not exclude deficiency. IM iron injections cause long-lasting brown staining.
itchy-anus: Pruritus ani is idiopathic when examination is normal apart from excoriation/lichenification; secondary causes include pinworm (sticky tape test), perianal streptococcal dermatitis, erythrasma, candida, lichen sclerosus, flexural psoriasis, contact dermatitis, and rarely extramammary Paget disease or anal SCC. Men 4:1; unrelated to haemorrhoids. Avoid talc and fragranced or preserved wipes (e.g. methylisothiazolinone).
jessner-lymphocytic-infiltrate: Uncommon; non-scaly, asymptomatic red annular or arciform plaques on face, neck and upper back that resolve without scarring. Benign T-cell lymphoproliferative disorder; mimics are tumid lupus, lymphocytoma cutis and polymorphous light eruption. Reported with Borrelia and drugs (duloxetine, ramipril, leflunomide, glatiramer, ustekinumab).
job-syndrome: Hyper-IgE syndrome: atopic dermatitis-like rash present at birth or within weeks (atopic dermatitis appears after 3 months), with Staphylococcus aureus abscesses and folliculitis, recurrent pneumonia and mucocutaneous candidiasis. Very high IgE and eosinophilia; pitted facial scarring, fractures, scoliosis and double rows of teeth.
juvenile-dermatomyositis: Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, nailfold capillary changes and proximal weakness (Gowers sign); unlike adult disease, malignancy is not associated. Calcinosis up to 40%, lipodystrophy 10%, skin ulceration 20%. Anti-p155/140: ulceration, lipodystrophy; anti-MDA5: aggressive lung disease, ulceration; anti-Jo-1: lung disease, mechanic's hands.
juvenile-idiopathic-arthritis: Systemic JIA (juvenile-onset Still disease): quotidian high spiking fevers with transient salmon-pink macules or papules on trunk, axillae and proximal limbs that coincide with fever and show Koebner phenomenon; palms, soles and face spared. Neutrophil-dominant infiltrate on biopsy. Complications: uveitis, macrophage activation syndrome. ANA often negative.
juvenile-plantar-dermatosis: Chronic shiny, glazed red forefoot dermatitis in children aged 3-14 with loss of the epidermal ridge pattern and painful fissures; ball of the great toe usually first. Toe webs and instep are spared, distinguishing it from tinea pedis. Friction, occlusive synthetic footwear and sweating implicated. Usually clears in adolescence.
juvenile-spring-eruption: Sun-induced eruption of the ears in boys and young men in early spring: itchy red papules evolving to blisters and crusts, appearing 8-24 hours after sun exposure and healing in about 2 weeks with minimal scarring. Probably a localised form of polymorphic light eruption; cold weather may contribute; prominent ears more susceptible.
kava-dermopathy: Acquired ichthyosiform eruption in heavy kava drinkers (kanikani in Fiji, 'crocodile skin' in Australia): dry rough polygonal scales without erythema, starting on head, face and neck, often with palmoplantar keratoderma. May have peripheral neuropathy. Clears when kava is stopped; progresses if consumption continues.
keratoelastoidosis-marginalis: Acquired marginal keratoderma of sun-exposed older outdoor workers: crateriform keratotic papules on the lateral index fingers and medial thumbs, with yellowish surrounding skin. A form of solar elastosis; histology shows elastorrhexis with hyperkeratosis and acanthosis. More common than the inherited acrokeratoelastoidosis; lacks family history.
keratolysis-exfoliativa: Common focal peeling of the palms (less often soles) in young adults, worse in summer and with irritants; air-filled blisters burst to leave collarettes of scale and tender red peeled areas, not itchy. Cleavage within the stratum corneum (corneodesmosomes). Fungal scrapings and patch tests negative; does not respond to topical steroids, unlike hand dermatitis.
keratolytic-winter-erythema: Oudtshoorn disease: autosomal dominant (8p23.1-p22) recurrent palmoplantar erythema with centrifugal peeling, worse in winter and better in summer and pregnancy; erythema retains the fingerprint ridge pattern and can be transgradient. Described in South African Afrikaans families; proposed enhancer duplication near CTSB. Topical keratolytics, retinoids and steroids may aggravate it.
keratosis-circumscripta: Rare, harmless childhood eruption of circular patches of skin-coloured papules, each with a rough keratin plug, on the elbows and knees. Ddx circumscribed juvenile pityriasis rubra pilaris (type IV), psoriasis and lichen spinulosus. Typically refractory to treatment and may slowly enlarge and persist; some authorities do not accept it as a separate entity.
keratosis-pilaris-atrophicans-faciei: Ulerythema ophryogenes: keratotic follicular papules and erythema on the lateral eyebrows from infancy, progressing to atrophy and permanent eyebrow hair loss. Sporadic or inherited (autosomal dominant or recessive; DSG4 mutation reported). Associated with Noonan, Rubinstein-Taybi, Cornelia de Lange and cardiofaciocutaneous syndromes.
kerion: Boggy, pus-filled lump with loose hairs and localised alopecia from a dramatic immune response to dermatophytes; often misdiagnosed as bacterial infection. Causes: M. canis, T. tonsurans, T. verrucosum, T. mentagrophytes. Wood lamp gives yellow-green fluorescence with M. canis but is often negative. Topical antifungals are ineffective; oral antifungal for at least 6-8 weeks. May be followed by a dermatophytide.
klippel-trenaunay-syndrome: Triad of capillary malformation (port-wine stain), venous malformation (varicose veins) and limb hypertrophy, usually one lower limb; clinical diagnosis with 2 of 3. Slow-flow lesions; fast-flow arteriovenous malformations indicate Parkes Weber syndrome. PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum. Complications: DVT, pulmonary embolism, cellulitis, lymphoedema.
knuckle-pads: Well-defined smooth firm thickenings over finger joints, most often the PIP joint; a fibromatosis (with Dupuytren, Ledderhose, Peyronie, pachydermodactyly). Syndromic associations: epidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma (keratin 9), Bart-Pumphrey, acrokeratoelastoidosis. Mimics: granuloma annulare, rheumatoid nodules, synovitis; surgery may produce keloids.
laterothoracic-exanthem: Asymmetric periflexural exanthem of childhood: starts in the axilla or groin and spreads outward, predominantly unilateral on the side of the trunk, in children around 2 years (girls 2:1); often mistaken for eczema or ringworm. Itchy papules with a pale halo become scaly with dusky centres; axillary/inguinal nodes may enlarge. Self-resolves within 3 months; biopsy is a non-specific perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate.
latex-allergy: Latex proteins cause type I IgE-mediated reactions (contact urticaria within 5-15 minutes, asthma, anaphylaxis; a leading cause of operating-room anaphylaxis); rubber accelerators/antioxidants (thiuram, carbamates, mercaptobenzothiazole) cause delayed type IV dermatitis. Risks: healthcare workers, spina bifida, atopy; fruit cross-reactions (banana, avocado, kiwi). Prick test for urticaria, patch test for dermatitis; powdered gloves drive asthma.
laugier-hunziker-syndrome: Benign acquired pigmentation: smooth brown to black macules of the lips (usually lower) and buccal mucosa, often with longitudinal melanonychia. No systemic associations or treatment needed. Must be distinguished from Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11, GI polyps), which has similar cutaneous features.
leeches: Hirudotherapy salvages flaps and grafts threatened by venous congestion. Saliva contains hirudin (anticoagulant, effect up to 6 hours), a local anaesthetic and a vasodilator, so bites are painless with a Y-shaped incision and hard-to-stop bleeding. Gut Aeromonas hydrophila can cause infection; forcible removal may leave jaws in the wound.
leg-ulcer: Chronic leg ulcers are most often due to venous insufficiency (45-80%), arterial insufficiency (5-20%) or diabetes (15-25%); biopsy the edge if skin cancer is suspected. Venous: below the knee, medial ankle, relatively painless, with red-brown staining and lipodermatosclerosis. Arterial: toes and heels, painful at night, punched-out borders, ABPI <0.9. Compression must not be used in significant arterial disease.
legius-syndrome: NF1-like syndrome: multiple café-au-lait macules and axillary/inguinal freckling from SPRED1 mutation (autosomal dominant, 15q14). Unlike NF1, no neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, bone abnormalities or optic gliomas. May have macrocephaly, Noonan-like face, lipomas, learning difficulties. Confirm by SPRED1 genetic testing.
lentiginous-melanoma: Slowly progressive melanoma of sun-damaged trunk and limbs, usually diagnosed in situ; starts like a freckle or lentigo and grows to several centimetres over years. Histology: epidermal hyperplasia, focal junctional nests of atypical melanocytes, pagetoid spread. Dermoscopy is hard to separate from lentiginous naevus of the elderly; excise rather than partially biopsy.
lentigo: Pigmented macule with a clearly defined edge that, unlike an ephelis, does not fade in winter. Histology shows increased basal melanocytes without nests (unlike junctional naevus) and more melanin in keratinocytes. Causes: UV, PUVA, tanning beds, radiation. Widespread lentigines suggest a syndrome (Peutz-Jeghers, LEOPARD, Carney, Cowden). Solar lentigo is regarded as a precursor to seborrhoeic keratosis.
lentigo-simplex: Most common lentigo; round or oval, evenly light brown to black macule, 3–15 mm, from birth or childhood, not induced by sun and not darkened by it (unlike freckles). Multiple lesions alone are lentigines profusa; with other findings consider Peutz-Jeghers, LEOPARD, LAMB, Carney complex or xeroderma pigmentosum.
lepra-reactions: Type 1: delayed hypersensitivity in borderline leprosy, often after treatment starts; inflamed existing plaques and nerve pain or palsy, no systemic symptoms. Type 2 (erythema nodosum leprosum): immune complex vasculitis in lepromatous or borderline lepromatous disease; fever, tender red nodules, iridocyclitis, orchitis, renal involvement. Lucio phenomenon: necrotic punched-out ulcers.
leukaemia-cutis: Skin infiltration by leukaemic cells: asymptomatic firm papules, nodules or plaques (skin-coloured, red, brown or purple), mostly head, neck and trunk; gingival hyperplasia in acute leukaemia. Skin is the first sign in 7% (aleukaemic). Chloroma (granulocytic sarcoma) looks blue-green on cut section from myeloperoxidase. A cause of blueberry muffin baby; prognosis poor.
leukoderma: Clinical sign of a localised patch of white skin from total loss of epidermal melanin; not a diagnosis. Causes include vitiligo, lichen sclerosus, scarring, chemical or contact leukoderma (confetti-like spots), piebaldism and melanoma-associated leukoderma. Guttate leukoderma can be an early sign of Darier disease. Wood lamp accentuates.
lichen-simplex-of-the-scrotum: Itch-scratch cycle producing well-demarcated, lichenified, erythematous or hyperpigmented plaques of the scrotum ("wash leather scrotum"), uni- or bilateral, in men aged 35-50. Look for a driver: atopic or contact dermatitis, tinea/candida, psoriasis, lichen planus, neuropathy, psychiatric disorder, SCC. Biopsy if atypical; prolonged potent steroid on thin scrotal skin causes atrophy.
lichen-spinulosus: Variant of keratosis pilaris in children and adolescents: sudden onset of symmetric patches of 1-3 mm follicular papules, each with a horn-like spine, likened to a nutmeg grater. Neck, buttocks, thighs, abdomen, knees, extensor arms. Clinical diagnosis; histology resembles keratosis pilaris. Usually resolves in 1-2 years; cause unknown.
lichenoid-drug-eruption: Mimics lichen planus but favours a symmetric, photodistributed truncal and limb rash that may be scaly; Wickham striae usually absent, nail and mucosal involvement uncommon, and marked pigmentation lingers. Latency usually 2-3 months but can exceed a year. Reported triggers: ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, hydrochlorothiazide, antimalarials, gold, allopurinol, TNF antagonists.
lichenoid-keratosis: Solitary inflamed pink-brown macule or plaque, usually on the upper trunk of fair-skinned adults, arising in a regressing solar lentigo or seborrhoeic keratosis. Dermoscopy: clusters of grey dots (annular granular pattern). Histology like lichen planus but with parakeratosis. Often misdiagnosed as BCC; benign, resolves spontaneously.
linea-nigra: Midline vertical hyperpigmented band from symphysis pubis to umbilicus (sometimes to xiphoid), about 1 cm wide, in over 90% of pregnant women; oestrogen augmented by progesterone drives melanin production. Darkens with sun; also seen in men and children. Ligamentum teres sign: umbilicus deviates to the right. Clinical diagnosis.
linear-focal-elastosis: Yellow, palpable horizontal lines on the lower back that resemble striae; striae are red or white and depressed. Histology: increased elastic fibres in the mid dermis separating collagen (elastic stain); early lesions may show elastolysis. Adolescent onset, more reports in males; can coexist with striae distensae.
linear-porokeratosis: Porokeratosis in a linear, dermatomal/Blaschkoid distribution: grouped lesions with a ridge-like border (cornoid lamella) and central furrow, often unilateral on one limb; thought to reflect mosaicism. Biopsy must include the raised edge. Complication: BCC or SCC arising within lesions, so monitor and advise sun protection. Ddx linear epidermal naevus, lichen striatus.
lip-lickers-dermatitis: Irritant contact cheilitis from the wet-dry cycle of saliva: chronic redness, dryness and scaling matching the reach of the tongue, crossing the vermilion border onto perioral skin; common in school-aged children, worse in winter. Perioral dermatitis spares the vermilion and adjacent skin and is papular. Behaviour modification is essential.
lipodystrophy: Loss of subcutaneous fat without malnutrition. Congenital generalised (autosomal recessive): prominent muscles and veins, hyperphagia from low leptin, acanthosis nigricans, diabetes, hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis. Familial partial: buffalo hump mimicking Cushing. Barraquer-Simons: upper-body fat loss, low C3, C3 nephritic factor, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.
lipoid-proteinosis: Autosomal recessive ECM1 loss-of-function (Urbach-Wiethe). Weak cry or hoarseness in infancy; moniliform blepharosis (beaded yellow eyelid papules, pathognomonic) in 50%; pock-like scars, thickened frenulum. Bilateral bean-shaped amygdala calcifications on CT/MRI are pathognomonic; epilepsy in about 30%. Founder Q276X mutation in Namaqualand.
listeriosis: Listeria monocytogenes, a food-borne Gram-positive bacillus (unpasteurised dairy, soft cheese, pate, smoked seafood); risk in pregnancy, neonates, elderly, immunocompromised. Primary cutaneous listeriosis in vets and farmers handling birthing animals: painless purpuric, papulopustular or vesiculopustular eruption on hands and forearms. Resistant to cephalosporins; granulomatosis infantisepticum in neonates.
livedo-reticularis: Net-like cyanotic mottling around pale centres, mostly on the legs. Persistent livedo racemosa (broken irregular rings, also trunk and buttocks) is secondary to systemic disease: antiphospholipid syndrome (25% of patients), Sneddon syndrome (livedo racemosa with stroke in young women), vasculitis. Order a lupus anticoagulant panel for acquired livedo not induced by cold; take multiple deep biopsies. Amantadine is a drug cause.
lobomycosis: Keloid-like nodules or plaques with a smooth, shiny surface from Lacazia loboi, an uncultivable fungus implanted by trauma in rural Central and South America; no human-to-human spread. Histology: granulomatous inflammation with giant cells and asteroid bodies; oval yeast-like bodies on silver or PAS stain. Mimics chromoblastomycosis, blastomycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis; SCC reported in chronic lesions.
lymphatic-malformation: Vascular birthmark of dilated malformed lymphatics, always present at birth. Three types: cystic hygroma (macrocytic; neck, axilla, groin; seen with Turner, Down syndrome, hydrops fetalis, so consider chromosomal analysis), cavernous lymphangioma, and lymphangioma circumscriptum (microcytic; clusters of lymph-filled vesicles resembling frogspawn, may become warty, recur after treatment).
lymphocytic-thrombophilic-arteritis: Primary lymphocytic vasculitis presenting with persistent, usually asymptomatic livedo racemosa or macular hyperpigmentation of the lower limbs; female predominance. Histology: lymphocytic infiltrate of small to medium arteries at the deep dermis/subcutis with a concentric hyalinised fibrin ring around the lumen; neutrophils scant. Distinguish from cutaneous PAN (painful nodules, ulceration). Indolent; steroids not helpful.
lymphoedema: Swelling from damaged or blocked lymphatics; pits early, then becomes non-pitting with thick skin and warty change (elephantiasis nostras verruciformis). Secondary causes include venous insufficiency, nodal surgery, radiotherapy, cellulitis and filariasis. Prone to cellulitis; complicated by angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves), BCC and SCC. Distinguish from lipoedema (fat accumulation in thighs and lower legs).
lymphomatoid-granulomatosis: Rare angiocentric, angiodestructive EBV-positive B-cell lymphoproliferative disease with reactive T cells; lungs involved, skin and CNS commonly. Skin shows papules, nodules or ulcers. Histology triad: mixed lymphoid infiltrate, lymphocytes infiltrating vessel walls, focal necrosis. Occurs with immunodeficiency (transplant, HIV, Wiskott-Aldrich). Worse prognosis with grade 2-3 or neurological disease.
macroglossia: Tongue protrudes beyond the teeth or alveolar ridge at rest; true vs relative (pseudo) macroglossia, the latter commonly from Down syndrome. Smooth generalised enlargement in Beckwith-Wiedemann, hypothyroidism, acromegaly; multinodular surface in amyloidosis, NF1, MEN2B; lymphatic malformation gives a pebbly surface with vesicle-like blebs.
maculopapular-cutaneous-mastocytosis: Urticaria pigmentosa: the most common cutaneous mastocytosis; brown macules/papules that urticate and may blister on rubbing (Darier sign), usually from infancy and fading by the teens, but persistent in adult-onset disease. Avoid aspirin/NSAIDs, codeine, morphine, alcohol, anticholinergics; adults with systemic symptoms need work-up (serum tryptase) for systemic mastocytosis.
madarosis: Loss of eyelashes or eyebrows (milphosis if eyelashes alone), non-scarring or scarring. Hypothyroidism classically causes bilateral loss of the outer one-third of the eyebrow. Common causes: staphylococcal infection, herpes simplex, rosacea, alopecia areata, atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, chemotherapy. Uncommon: DLE, lichen planopilaris/frontal fibrosing alopecia, leprosy, HIV, trichotillomania.
madelung-disease: Multiple symmetrical lipomatosis: painless, non-encapsulated fat masses on the neck ('Madelung collar'), upper back, shoulders and arms, mostly in men aged 30-60 with chronic alcohol use (60-90%). Can compress trachea, oesophagus or SVC; autonomic neuropathy. Rare MFN2 or LIPE mutations. Abstinence does not reverse deposits; surgery is the mainstay.
majocchi-granuloma: Deep suppurative, granulomatous folliculitis from dermatophyte (most often T. rubrum) after follicle disruption; risks include shaving or trauma, topical steroids (tinea incognito) and immunosuppression. Red scaly plaque with follicular papules, pustules and nodules, usually on one lower leg; look for tinea pedis or unguium. Deep nodular form in the immunosuppressed. Topicals may fail; oral antifungal for 4-6 weeks.
malaria-and-its-skin-signs: Female Anopheles-borne Plasmodium infection (P. falciparum, vivax, malariae, ovale); skin signs are rare and non-specific: urticaria, angioedema, petechiae, purpura, reticulate erythema of the limbs sparing palms and soles. Diagnose on blood film (thick for sensitivity, thin for speciation), repeating every 6-12 h for 36-48 h if negative. Doxycycline prophylaxis causes photosensitivity.
malignant-atrophic-papulosis: Degos disease: occlusive small-vessel vasculopathy of skin, gut and CNS. Crops of 2-5 mm red papules on trunk and arms develop a depressed central white spot and heal as porcelain-white scars. Bowel infarction/perforation (50% of systemic disease) and strokes (20%) are the dangers; systemic form often fatal in 2-3 years, skin-limited form may be benign.
