marfan-syndrome: Fibrillin defect (chromosome 15), autosomal dominant. Tall thin stature with long extremities, lens dislocation, and aortic dilation or aneurysm. Skin: striae at shoulders, hips, buttocks and lower back without weight change or pregnancy, plus hernias; skin features are minor criteria only.
marjolin-ulcer: SCC arising in a scar or chronic ulcer, most commonly an old burn scar, on average about 30 years after the injury. Suspect when an ulcer persists over 3 months at a scar: non-healing, indurated, raised margins. Diagnose by incisional biopsy (can be misdiagnosed as pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia). Wide local excision; radiotherapy and chemotherapy not effective; recurrence 20-30% within 3 years.
martorell-ulcer: Excruciatingly painful lower leg ulcer in longstanding, poorly controlled hypertension (and diabetes), on the outer lower leg above the ankle or over the Achilles tendon; may be symmetrical. No significant arterial or venous disease and no kidney disease (calciphylaxis excluded). Deep elliptical biopsy: arteriolar wall thickening, calcium, no vasculitis. Think of it when PG is considered; immunosuppression gives a poor outcome.
mccune-albright-syndrome: Triad: large segmental café-au-lait macules with jagged borders that rarely cross the midline (unlike smooth-bordered NF macules), polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (ground-glass, lytic lesions), and endocrine overactivity, most commonly precocious puberty. Postzygotic GNAS1 mosaicism, not inherited; 2 of 3 features needed.
median-canaliform-nail-dystrophy: Midline longitudinal furrow or split with backward-angled transverse ridges in a fir-tree pattern, usually both thumbnails; macrolunulae are frequent. Believed due to matrix microtrauma; mostly sporadic, rare isotretinoin reports. Habit-tic deformity differs: its ridges are transverse, not fir-tree. Often grows out spontaneously.
melanocytic-naevus: Benign melanocyte proliferation classified by depth: junctional (flat), compound, dermal. Variants: halo (Sutton) naevus fades over years; Meyerson naevus has a surrounding eczema; Reed naevus is a darkly pigmented Spitz naevus with a starburst dermoscopic pattern. RAS mutations in congenital naevi; eruptive new naevi with BRAF inhibitors (vemurafenib, dabrafenib). Over 100 naevi raise melanoma risk.
melanoma-in-situ: Malignant melanocytes confined to the epidermis (and adnexa); AJCC stage 0, Clark level 1, no Breslow thickness reported, no metastatic potential. Subtypes: lentigo maligna, lentiginous, superficial spreading. About 8% are thickened and scaly. Patients have eight times the risk of another primary melanoma, so total body skin checks matter. Excision; Mohs or staged excision for large lesions.
melanoma-in-skin-of-colour: Less common in darker skin but diagnosed thicker with higher mortality; favours low-sun sites: acral (palms, soles), subungual, mucosal and ocular. Surrounding skin can mask pigment. Mimics to consider: naevi of special sites, postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, and keloid (can resemble desmoplastic melanoma).
melanoma-of-the-nail-unit: Usually acral lentiginous melanoma; a single narrow brown-black longitudinal band (melanonychia) on thumb or great toe, not sun-related. Concerning: width >3 mm, irregular pigment, blurred borders, Hutchinson sign (not always reliable; pseudo-Hutchinson, Bowen disease). Hypomelanotic or amelanotic in up to 50%. Needs nail matrix biopsy.
melanotic-macule: Well-defined brown to black flat patch, 1–8 mm, usually on the central lower lip (labial lentigo); also oral, vulval and penile. Histology: increased basal melanin, melanophages in the papillary dermis, no nuclear atypia and a normal melanocyte count. Multiple lesions: think Peutz-Jeghers, Addison disease, Laugier-Hunziker or multiple lentiginosis.
melioidosis: Burkholderia pseudomallei from soil or surface water (rice paddy workers; South-East Asia, northern Australia). Pulmonary disease is the commonest form and can mimic TB; skin inoculation gives nodule, ulcer or abscess. Latent for years (Vietnamese time bomb); septicaemic form mortality can exceed 80%. Culture is diagnostic; the lab must be warned (Hazard Group 3).
meningococcal-disease: Neisseria meningitidis (Gram-negative diplococci): petechiae in 50-75% of meningococcaemia, most commonly acral purpura, which can progress to necrosis. Risk: complement deficiency, asplenia, children 6 months-4 years. Complications include adrenal haemorrhage and DIC. Medical emergency; close contacts receive rifampicin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone prophylaxis.
meralgia-paraesthetica: Burning, tingling or numbness (rarely intense itch) on the lateral thigh from compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (L2-3), usually under the inguinal ligament; no rash unless rubbing causes lichen simplex. Precipitants: tight belts or clothing, obesity, pregnancy, diabetes. Worse with standing and walking, relieved by sitting.
metastatic-melanoma: Spread patterns: local recurrence (within 2 cm of scar), in-transit metastases (lymphatics, over 2 cm from primary), nodal, and haematogenous (lung, skin, liver, brain). Cutaneous metastases are firm, often black or red, dermal more than subcutaneous. Melanoma-associated leukoderma resembles vitiligo; checkpoint and BRAF inhibitors can also trigger it. LDH is often normal even in late disease.
metastatic-melanoma-with-unknown-primary: Metastatic melanoma with no detectable primary (regression, prior destruction or misread naevus are proposed); nodal disease most common (axilla 50%, neck, groin). Melanin plus S100, Melan-A, HMB-45 and SOX10 positive; BRAF V600E and NRAS mutations resemble cutaneous melanoma. Nodal presentation is staged III, visceral IV; survival similar to or better than known primary.
methylisothiazolinone-allergy: Preservative in wet wipes, shampoos, cosmetics, paints and glues; widespread household use since 2005 made it a strong allergen and drove a contact allergy "epidemic" (Allergen of the Year 2013). Patterns: hand, perianal/perivulval, napkin, facial and eyelid dermatitis; volatile, so airborne dermatitis after painting. Patch test MI 0.2% aq; MCI/MI mix alone missed 27% of MI-positive cases in one study.
meyerson-naevus: Benign melanocytic naevus surrounded by an itchy, dry or blistered eczematous halo; about three times commoner in males. Unlike a halo (Sutton) naevus, the central naevus never fades, even after the eczema resolves. Eczema settles on its own or with a short course of topical corticosteroid; excising the naevus clears the eczema. Reported triggers: sunburn, interferon-alfa-2b.
microgeodic-disease: Winter-onset swelling of one or more fingers or toes in children, often chilblain-like; thought due to cold-induced vasospasm with avascular necrosis (transient phalangeal osteolysis). X-ray shows small lucent 'microgeodes' with a sclerotic lining, usually the middle phalanx of the index or middle finger. Mostly resolves spontaneously.
mid-dermal-elastolysis: Acquired selective loss of elastic fibres in the mid dermis, mostly Caucasian women, on the trunk and upper arms. Type I (commonest): well-demarcated fine wrinkling; type II: perifollicular papules; type III: reticular erythema. H&E may be normal; elastic stain shows band-like or focal loss. Possible associations: UV, pregnancy, oral contraceptives.
mixed-connective-tissue-disease: High-titre anti-U1RNP antibodies with overlapping SLE, systemic sclerosis and polymyositis features that evolve in sequence. Early Raynaud and sausage-shaped digits; most common with HLA-DR4. Pulmonary hypertension is the main cause of death. Babies can get neonatal lupus and chondrodysplasia punctata.
morbihan-disease: Persistent firm, non-pitting erythematous oedema of the upper face (periorbital, glabella, forehead, cheeks, nose), painless and non-itchy; considered a refractory form of rosacea. Histology is nonspecific (dilated lymphatics, mast cells, mucin, non-caseating granulomas); biopsy excludes mimics such as sarcoidosis and orofacial granulomatosis.
morgellons-disease: Subtype of delusional infestation: fixed belief of fibres or filaments emerging from the skin, with the 'matchbox' (specimen) sign and excoriations sparing hard-to-reach areas. Middle-aged white women; associated with psychiatric illness or stimulant use. CDC study found no infectious cause. Low-dose second-generation antipsychotics (amisulpride, risperidone) are used.
morphoea-en-coup-de-sabre: Linear morphoea of the frontoparietal forehead/scalp: ivory streak with violaceous margin that indents skin and sometimes bone, with linear scarring alopecia. Mostly children. Associated with Parry-Romberg syndrome, seizures and ipsilateral eye problems; MRI may show brain abnormalities. Phases: active, regression, burnt-out.
mouth-ulcer: Most common presentation is recurrent aphthous stomatitis: round or ovoid ulcers with an erythematous halo and punched-out yellow-grey centre. Minor <10 mm heals in 10-14 days; major >10 mm may scar; herpetiform = crops of 1-3 mm ulcers on or under the tongue. Check iron, B12, folate, coeliac and IBD if frequent. Biopsy a non-healing ulcer for SCC. Behcet adds genital aphthae, ocular inflammation and pathergy.
mucocoele-of-the-lip: Mucous cyst from trauma to minor salivary ducts (lip biting or sucking); smooth, translucent to bluish dome on the inner lower lip (75% of cases), 1-15 mm. Ranula when on the floor of the mouth. Often ruptures and recurs; may look like a haemangioma if bleeding into it. Complete excision including adjacent minor salivary glands should prevent recurrence.
multicentric-reticulohistiocytosis: Rare non-Langerhans histiocytosis, women 3:1: red-brown papules and nodules on face, ears, hands and mucosa, 'coral-beading' around the nails, and destructive symmetric arthritis (arthritis mutilans in 50%). Histology: multinucleated giant cells and ground-glass eosinophilic histiocytes. About 1 in 4 have internal malignancy, so screen.
multiple-endocrine-neoplasia-type-2b: Early-life mucosal neuromas (glistening bumps on lips, tongue, thickened eyelids), medullated corneal nerves, gut neuromas (megacolon) and Marfanoid habitus. RET mutation at codon 918 (exon 16) in 95%; autosomal dominant but about 50% de novo. High risk of aggressive medullary thyroid carcinoma and phaeochromocytoma; thyroidectomy around age 1. Formerly MEN type 3.
multiple-self-healing-squamous-epithelio: Autosomal dominant (TGFBR1, 9q22) crops of SCC/KA-like lesions on the nose, ears and perioral face that regress to pitted scars; never on palms and soles. Histology resembles aggressive SCC but lacks the marked shouldering and leucocyte abscesses of usual KA; no distant metastases reported. Avoid radiotherapy (new lesions in the field).
mycoplasma-pneumoniae-infection: Most commonly identified infectious cause of SJS, especially in children and adolescents. MIRM (now under RIME): prominent oral, ocular and urogenital mucositis with sparse or absent skin lesions, vesiculobullous or target-like and acral; sparse skin involvement favours Mycoplasma over drug SJS/TEN or HSV. Also EM, erythema nodosum; cold agglutinins.
mycosis-fungoides-palmaris-et-plantaris: Very rare localised mycosis fungoides confined to palms and soles, mimicking chronic hand and foot eczema with thickened scaly red plaques that relapse despite treatment. Suspect with frequent relapses and treatment resistance; early histology can resemble eczema so repeat biopsies may be needed. Check blood count for Sezary syndrome. Slow-growing, rarely spreads.
myxoma-syndrome: Atrial myxomas plus lentigines; spectrum includes LAMB (lentigines, atrial and mucocutaneous myxomas, blue naevi), NAME and Carney syndrome (also mammary myxomas, testicular tumours, pituitary adenoma/Cushing). Some cases autosomal dominant with PRKAR1A mutations. Cardiology, endocrine and derm review needed; tumour fragments can embolise at surgery.
naevus-anaemicus: Congenital pale patch from localised vasoconstriction (increased sensitivity to catecholamines) that does not redden on rubbing; pressing the surrounding skin with a glass slide (diascopy) makes it disappear. Biopsy is normal skin. Mimics: achromic naevus, vitiligo, ash-leaf spots. Reported with NF1 and phakomatosis pigmentovascularis.
naevus-lipomatosus-superficialis: Hamartoma with mature adipose cells in the dermis, not connected to subcutaneous fat. Classical (Hoffmann-Zurhelle) type: clusters of soft yellow skin-coloured nodules on lower back, buttock and upper thigh in a zosteriform pattern; solitary type is a single subcutaneous swelling in adults. Mimics: neurofibromatosis, lipoma, sebaceous naevus, skin tag.
naevus-simplex: Salmon patch: midline pink patch present at birth on nape (stork bite), glabella or eyelids (angel's kiss); blanches and reddens with crying; seen in about 40% of Caucasian infants. Fades by 1-2 years except the nape, where 50% persist. Port-wine stain is unilateral and darkens with age. Lumbosacral lesion plus hypertrichosis, sinus, lipoma or deviated cleft prompts imaging for spinal dysraphism.
nail-cosmetics-allergy: Tosylamide formaldehyde resin is the chemical most responsible for nail enamel allergy; most reactors are not formaldehyde allergic. Dermatitis often appears at sites touched by the fingers (eyelids, mouth/chin, neck) more than on the fingers. Methacrylates in artificial nails are strong sensitisers; acrylates can cause paraesthesias and nail loss. Confirm by patch testing.
naxos-disease: Autosomal recessive triad of woolly hair (from birth), diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma and arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. Homozygous JUP (plakoglobin) deletion; ARVC appears by adolescence with syncope or ventricular tachycardia, fibro-fatty myocardial replacement, and risk of sudden death. Carvajal syndrome (desmoplakin) has predominant left ventricular involvement.
necrolytic-acral-erythema: Symmetric, painful scaly to psoriasiform plaques on the tops of the toes and feet, with palms, soles and nails almost always spared. Seen predominantly with hepatitis C (can be the first sign); zinc deficiency is the next most common association. Histology matches necrolytic migratory erythema. Oral zinc is listed; topical steroids and calcineurin inhibitors do not seem helpful.
neonatal-cephalic-pustulosis: Pustules on the face and scalp of newborns, often in the third week, with no comedones (unlike true neonatal acne). Related to Malassezia colonisation; resolves without treatment, topical ketoconazole can be used if needed.
neurocutaneous-melanosis: Congenital melanocytic naevi plus melanocytic proliferation in the CNS (leptomeninges); risk factors are giant (over 40 cm) or multiple CMN, many satellite lesions, bathing-trunk or posterior axis site. Linked to NRAS codon 61 mosaicism. Symptoms in first 2 years (seizures, hydrocephalus). MRI brain and spine with T1 hyperintensity, ideally within 4–6 months. Dandy-Walker in about 10%.
neutrophilic-sebaceous-adenitis: Rare; recurrent annular or arcuate oedematous plaques on the face and trunk of young men, sometimes worse in summer light, occasional pustules. Biopsy: necrotic sebocytes surrounded by neutrophils with a mononuclear infiltrate around vessels and follicles. Similar histology reported in painful vulval papules. Treatments unreliable; cases resolved in 3-4 years.
nickel-allergy: One of the most common causes of ACD: earlobes (earrings), wrists (watch strap), lower abdomen (jeans stud). More common in women (piercings); persists for years, often lifelong, with no desensitisation. Baseline series tests nickel sulphate. Dimethylglyoxime spot test turns the cotton bud pink if free nickel. May relate to pompholyx; 9-carat and white gold contain nickel, silver-coloured coins are cupro-nickel.
nicotine-stomatitis: Smoker's palate: redness then a white, cracked 'dried mud' hard palate with numerous red dots (inflamed minor salivary gland duct openings), caused by heat from pipe or reverse smoking. Dentures protect the covered palate. Not premalignant except with reverse smoking; improves within 1-2 weeks of stopping; biopsy suspicious areas to exclude dysplasia or cancer.
nipple-eczema: Erythema and scale of the areola, with the nipple itself and base of the areola usually spared; mostly teenage girls, often atopic; also irritant or allergic (lanolin, fragrance, preservatives, nickel from piercing). In an older adult, a unilateral chronic lesion lasting over 3 months not improving with topical steroid needs biopsy to exclude mammary Paget disease. Also consider tinea/candida (KOH) and S. aureus.
nipple-papillomatosis: Benign papillomas of lactiferous duct epithelium (florid papillomatosis, nipple adenoma, erosive adenomatosis); women aged 35-55 with nipple mass, erosion, serous or bloody discharge. Histology: proliferating ducts with double epithelial layer, keratin-filled cysts, apical snouts. Mimics: Paget disease, nipple eczema. Syringomatous adenoma variant is infiltrative.
nocardiosis: Rare soil bacterium. Primary cutaneous form (usually N. brasiliensis) in healthy people after a skin wound such as a cat scratch or thorn: pyoderma or abscess, lymphocutaneous nodules along lymphatics, or mycetoma. Pulmonary/disseminated disease (usually N. asteroides) occurs in immunodeficiency, spreading to brain and skin (10-30%). Slow growth (2-3 weeks); modified acid-fast stain.
nodular-panniculitis: Recurrent painful 1-2 cm subcutaneous nodules on thighs, lower legs and buttocks with fever and malaise; may ulcerate and discharge oily yellow fluid. Formerly Weber-Christian disease. Diagnosis of exclusion: lobular pattern with or without vasculitis after other febrile lobular panniculitis excluded. Visceral involvement carries a high mortality.
nodulocystic-acne: Severe acne with firm, tender nodules and pseudocysts on the face, neck and trunk that heal with scarring; male predominance. Acne conglobata variant (interconnecting abscesses, sinuses) is the 'A' in SAPHO, PASH, PASS and PAPA. Triggers: anabolic steroids, etanercept, imatinib, whey. Topicals fail; start oral isotretinoin early.
non-dermatophyte-mould-onychomycosis: Opportunistic mould nail infection (~10% of onychomycosis), usually one nail, toenails 25 times more than fingernails; paronychia often present. Most moulds are non-keratolytic (except Neoscytalidium) and need prior nail damage; Aspergillus niger gives a black nail. Diagnosis needs 3 or more criteria incl. repeat culture without dermatophyte. Harder to clear, higher relapse.
non-sexually-acquired-human-papillomavir: HPV 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 10 cause common, flat and plantar warts; HPV 7 causes 'butcher warts' in meat, poultry and fish handlers. Plantar wart: lost dermatoglyphics, pinpoint bleeding or black dots on paring, tender to lateral pressure (corns lack capillaries). Epidermodysplasia verruciformis: autosomal recessive, HPV 5 and 8, SCC risk.
noonan-syndrome: Autosomal dominant RASopathy (PTPN11 in over 50%): short stature, hypertelorism, low-set ears, webbed neck, pectus deformity, lymphoedema; Turner-like phenotype with normal karyotype. Most common heart defect is pulmonary valve stenosis. Eight-fold increased risk of haematological malignancy. Noonan with multiple lentigines (LEOPARD) adds café-au-lait macules and lentigines.
noonan-syndrome-with-multiple-lentigines: Formerly LEOPARD: lentigines, ECG conduction defects, ocular hypertelorism, pulmonary stenosis, abnormal genitalia, retarded growth, deafness. A RASopathy, autosomal dominant, PTPN11 in about 75%, RAF1 in 10%. Lentigines occur in over 90% and are not sun-dependent; also café au lait macules.
notalgia-paraesthetica: Intense itch on the medial border of one or both scapulae without a primary rash (thoracic cutaneous nerve entrapment; T2-T6 nerves vulnerable to compression); often follows intense exercise or inactivity. Scratching leaves hyperpigmentation or lichen simplex; biopsy is normal unless superimposed dermatitis. Botulinum toxin was ineffective in a double-blind trial.
obesity-associated-lymphoedematous-mucin: Rare pretibial dermal mucinosis in obese patients with normal thyroid function; mimics pretibial myxoedema (Graves). Asymptomatic papules, nodules and plaques on the shins with pitting oedema, later bilateral leg lymphoedema sparing the feet and ankles. Histology: dermal mucin (Alcian blue pH 2.5) and dermal angioplasia with vertically oriented vessels. Weight loss is the primary approach.
ocular-blistering: Progressive cicatrising conjunctivitis: dry eye from goblet cell loss, shortened fornices, symblepharon, trichiasis, corneal scarring and blindness. Most often in mucous membrane pemphigoid, EBA, linear IgA disease, pemphigus vulgaris and paraneoplastic pemphigus. May be asymptomatic despite advanced signs; surgery on inflamed eyes can exacerbate disease.
ocular-melanoma: Most common primary malignant eye tumour in adults; uveal (over 90% choroid) outnumbers conjunctival. GNAQ/GNA11 mutations in 80-85% of uveal melanomas; BAP1 loss and monosomy 3 mark poor prognosis, SF3B1 a more favourable one. Spreads by blood (no uveal lymphatics), liver in over 80%. Tebentafusp is listed for unresectable or metastatic uveal melanoma.
ocular-rosacea: Rosacea involving the lids and eye: blepharitis, conjunctival hyperaemia, chalazia/styes and keratitis; may precede skin disease. Demodex and meibomian gland obstruction implicated. Keratitis is rare but sight-threatening (corneal thinning, vascularisation, perforation). Mimics: seborrhoeic dermatitis and periorificial dermatitis; antibiotics help.
oil-folliculitis: Follicular pustules with a red halo (follicles may be plugged with oil) on forearms and thighs after occupational contact with oils: crude petroleum, diesel, wool fats, coal tar distillates. Coal tar creams used for eczema or psoriasis can also cause it. Pustules are sterile or grow Staphylococcus epidermidis; avoid the offending material.
onchocerciasis: Onchocerca volvulus filarial worm spread by day-biting blackflies (Simulium); adult worms sit in subcutaneous nodules over bony prominences. Skin patterns: chronic papular onchodermatitis (most common), 'leopard skin' depigmentation on the shins, 'lizard skin', 'hanging groin'; eye disease causes river blindness. Diagnose by microfilariae in skin snips; ivermectin kills microfilariae but not adult worms.
onychogryphosis: Ram's horn nail: opaque yellow-brown thickened nail plate with elongation and increased curvature, from slow nail growth; usually a great toenail. Older people, poor personal care, dementia; linked to ichthyosis, psoriasis, poor circulation, trauma, ill-fitting shoes. Mimic pachyonychia congenita (fingernails more affected). Recurs after conservative treatment.
onycholysis: Nail plate separated from the nailbed with a sharply defined white opaque area, usually distal; oil spot sign is an island of onycholysis. Causes: trauma, psoriasis, lichen planus, thyroid disease, photosensitising drugs (tetracyclines, NSAIDs, psoralens, retinoids), taxanes. Leukonychia stays attached. Complicated by Candida and Pseudomonas; persistent cases consider subungual SCC or melanoma.
onychomatricoma: Rare benign fibroepithelial tumour of the nail matrix, typically Caucasian women in the fifth decade. Yellow thickened nail plate, proximal splinter haemorrhage and longitudinal overcurvature; finger-like projections create 'woodworm' cavities seen from the free margin. Clippings show cavities with serous material. Treated by complete surgical excision.
onychopapilloma: Benign nail matrix neoplasm presenting as a longitudinal red streak (erythronychia) from lunula to tip, with distal splitting or onycholysis, subungual keratosis and splinter haemorrhage. Usually one nail; multiple digits suggest BAP1 tumour predisposition syndrome. Mimics SCC and melanoma, so biopsy if enlarging; Darier disease affects multiple nails.
onychophagia: Nail biting, a form of onychotillomania; associated with other habit disorders (trichotillomania, skin picking) and with OCD, ADHD, oppositional defiant disorder, separation anxiety and Tourette syndrome. Complications: paronychia, onychomycosis, tooth root resorption, malocclusion. Behaviour modification can be effective; bitter-tasting compounds are controversial.
oral-cancer: Over 90% are squamous cell carcinomas; most common sites are lower lip, tongue and floor of mouth. Early lesion is painless: a leukoplakia/erythroplakia or an indurated ulcer resembling an aphthous ulcer that fails to heal. Risks: tobacco plus alcohol (synergistic), HPV 16/18, erosive oral lichen planus. 30-80% have cervical node metastases at presentation.
oral-irritated-fibroma: Benign scar-like reaction to chronic irritation (cheek/lip biting, rough tooth, dentures); firm smooth dome-shaped or pedunculated papule, most often on the inner cheek where the teeth meet. Histology: dense fibrous tissue with few cells. Multiple lesions should prompt consideration of tuberous sclerosis or Cowden syndrome. Does not become oral cancer; recurs if irritation persists.
orofaciodigital-syndrome-type-1: X-linked dominant (OFD1 ciliopathy), lethal in males. Lingual hamartomas, bifid tongue, unusual palatal clefting and digit anomalies. Distinguished from other orofaciodigital syndromes by inheritance and polycystic kidneys (50%), which may progress to kidney failure; milia on ears or face and hair loss reported only in OFD1.
osler-nodes-and-janeway-lesions: Skin signs of bacterial endocarditis. Osler nodes: tender red-purple raised nodules, often with pale centre, on fingers and toes, lasting hours to days; neutrophilic vasculitis or microabscess. Janeway lesions: non-tender, haemorrhagic, on palms and soles (thenar/hypothenar), more in acute endocarditis (S. aureus); septic microemboli. Splinter haemorrhages also occur.
osteoma-cutis: Bone formation in the skin by osteoblastic metaplasia of dermal fibroblasts; stone-hard nodules, visible on X-ray. At least 80% are secondary: scars, acne, haematoma, scleroderma/CREST, dermatomyositis, morphoea, tumours (BCC, pilomatricoma). Check calcium/PTH for Albright hereditary osteodystrophy. Calcinosis cutis is calcium salt, not bone.
pachydermodactyly: Benign digital fibromatosis: asymptomatic symmetrical thickening at the sides of the PIP joints of fingers 2-4 in adolescents and young men (4:1); thumbs rarely, toes never, with no pain, stiffness or synovitis. Linked to repetitive finger habits (cracking, rubbing). Biopsy: abnormal dermal collagen and mucin without inflammation; mimics knuckle pads and arthritis.
pachyonychia-congenita: Autosomal dominant keratin disorder (K6a, K16, K17, K6b, K6c): thickened brownish nails from early life, painful plantar keratoderma (95%), oral leukokeratosis and steatocystoma/pilosebaceous cysts. K17: almost all have steatocystoma multiplex, natal teeth possible; K6a: first bite syndrome. Oral retinoids thin calluses but increase pain.
paederus-dermatitis: Linear or streaky erythema 24-48 hours after brushing or crushing a rove beetle (Nairobi fly), then vesicles and pustules at 2-4 days; toxin is paederin. Clues: "kissing lesions" on apposed flexures, burning, "Nairobi eye" (periocular dermatitis/keratoconjunctivitis), balanitis by hand transfer. Beetles are attracted to UV light; clustered cases in the rainy/warm season. Early histology: neutrophilic spongiosis, reticular necrosis.
paediatric-psoriasis: Guttate, facial and flexural psoriasis are particularly common in children; guttate often follows streptococcal infection and may clear within months. Early-onset large chronic plaque psoriasis tends to persist. Complications include psoriatic arthritis and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Clinical diagnosis; not contagious.
palmar-erythema: Symmetric, painless, non-itchy, slightly warm redness of the heel of the palm from dilated surface capillaries. Primary: hereditary, pregnancy (30-70%) or idiopathic. Secondary: cirrhosis, Wilson disease, haemochromatosis, thyrotoxicosis, rheumatoid arthritis (over 60%), drugs such as topiramate or amiodarone. Work-up looks for liver, thyroid, glucose and hepatitis causes.
palmoplantar-keratoderma: Thickened palms and soles: diffuse, focal (pressure areas) or punctate; transgradient if extending onto the dorsal hands and feet. Acquired forms are more common than hereditary and occur with eczema or psoriasis, infection, drugs, internal cancer, systemic inflammatory disease. Rare syndromic hereditary forms can mark internal organ abnormality.
palmoplantar-keratoderma-nagashima-type: AR, SERPINB7 loss-of-function; the most common PPK in Asian populations. Mild diffuse transgradient keratoderma with erythema extending onto the dorsal hands and feet and Achilles area; skin turns white and spongy after 10 minutes of water immersion. Nails, hair and mucosa spared; non-progressive. Biopsy shows non-epidermolytic thickening.
pancreatic-panniculitis: Tender nodules on the shins and ankles that ulcerate and drain brown sterile viscous fluid from fat liquefaction. Hallmark: 'ghost cells' (necrotic adipocytes) in neutrophilic lobular panniculitis. Schmid triad: eosinophilia, panniculitis, arthritis. Skin lesions are the presenting feature in up to 40%; seen with pancreatic cancer and pancreatitis.
panniculitis: Inflammation of subcutaneous fat; most forms look alike (firm, tender nodules and plaques), so biopsy decides: septal vs lobular, with or without vasculitis. Erythema nodosum is the most common form. If fever, malaise and arthralgia are prominent, consider vasculitis, infection, Sweet syndrome, pancreatic, alpha-1-antitrypsin or cytophagic histiocytic panniculitis.
panton-valentine-leukocidin-staphylococc: Phage-encoded exotoxin (LukS-PV, LukF-PV) of some S. aureus that lyses neutrophils. Suspect with recurrent boils or necrotising skin infections in healthy people, pain out of proportion, rapid spread, affected household contacts; ask the lab to test for PVL. Found in MSSA and MRSA. Necrotising pneumonia mortality up to 75%; decolonisation of contacts.
papular-purpuric-gloves-and-socks-syndro: Painful symmetric erythema and oedema of hands and feet progressing to petechiae and purpura, sharply demarcated at the wrists and ankles. Usually parvovirus B19; also EBV, CMV, HBV, HHV-6, measles, coxsackie B. Clinical diagnosis; confirm with serology or PCR. Resolves in 1-3 weeks without scarring.
papular-urticaria: Persistent insect bite reaction, mainly in children in summer and autumn; fleas and mites from cats and dogs are common culprits. Clusters of itchy papules, each with a central punctum, on legs and exposed sites; new lesions appear as old ones clear. Mimics: scabies, atopic dermatitis, prurigo simplex. Histology: dermal oedema, extravasated red cells, interstitial eosinophils. Self-limiting as desensitisation develops.
papuloerythroderma-of-ofuji: Rare, mostly elderly men; widespread pruritic flat-topped papules coalescing in a cobblestone pattern with sparing of skin folds ("deck-chair sign", called pathognomonic). Associated with CTCL, other malignancy, atopy, drugs, HIV and hepatitis C; eosinophilia and raised IgE. Histology nonspecific; CTCL must be excluded (flow cytometry, TCR clonality). Primary disease is a diagnosis of exclusion.
paradoxical-psoriasis: Psoriasiform plaques or pustules arising during TNF-alpha inhibitor therapy for IBD, RA or psoriasis; about 2-5% of patients, mean onset 11 months, more in women and smokers. Infliximab more likely to cause it than adalimumab or etanercept. Scalp, palmoplantar and pustular patterns are common; may involve alopecia. Management includes switching to another biologic.
parakeratosis-pustulosa: Young children (girls three times more often) with a deformed thumb or index fingernail surrounded by red scaly skin: subungual hyperkeratosis, onycholysis, pitting, lost cuticle. Not itchy; clinical diagnosis, often misdiagnosed as psoriasis or atopic dermatitis. Usually improves with time, but some children later develop psoriasis.
paraneoplastic-pruritus: Generalised itch without an obvious rash, which may precede the cancer by years; severity does not track tumour extent. Excoriations spare unreachable sites such as the mid-upper back. Associated especially with lymphoma (Hodgkin) and leukaemia, less often with lung, gastric or laryngeal tumours and insulinoma. May resolve when the cancer is treated.
parry-romberg-syndrome: Progressive unilateral facial atrophy of skin, fat, muscle and bone, mainly the lower face with forehead sparing; skin is soft, not sclerotic. Considered a variant of linear morphoea (en coup de sabre may coexist). Neurologic (epilepsy, about 15%) and ophthalmic (up to 35%) involvement. Progresses over 2-20 years then stabilises.
pearly-penile-papules-images: Dome-shaped to thread-like skin-coloured papules in one or several rows around the corona or sulcus of the glans; a normal anatomic variant, not infectious or premalignant, and more common in uncircumcised men. Distinguish from genital warts, molluscum and Fordyce spots. Histology: dilated thin-walled dermal vessels with star-shaped or multinucleate fibroblasts. Reassure; no treatment needed.
pemphigoid: Rare nodular variant of bullous pemphigoid: hyperkeratotic prurigo-like nodules plus blisters on extremities and trunk. Unlike nodular prurigo, it has blisters, linear IgG and C3 on DIF and BP180/BP230 antibodies. Proposed cause: rubbing and scratching inducing pemphigoid antibodies. Topical steroids alone are inadequate.
perianal-dermatoses: Perianal differential clues: erythrasma shows coral red Wood lamp fluorescence; perianal streptococcal dermatitis is a beefy red sharply demarcated ring in children; pinworm causes nocturnal itch. Biopsy for extramammary Paget disease and anal intraepithelial neoplasia (HPV 16/18, HIV). Perianal lichen sclerosus and lichen planus carry SCC risk. Avoid potent topical steroids except in lichen sclerosus and lichen planus.
perianal-streptococcal-dermatitis: Sharply demarcated perianal redness and itch in children (6 months to 10 years, male predominance 4:1) from group A beta-haemolytic strep; may have painful defecation, rectal pus/blood, vulvovaginitis or balanitis. Confirm by swab culture or rapid strep test; mimics are pinworms, flexural psoriasis, candidal intertrigo. Recurs in about 1/3, typically within 3 months.
perineal-pyramidal-protrusion: Smooth flesh-coloured or pink nodule in the midline anterior to the anus (perineal median raphe), over 90% girls, average age at diagnosis 14 months. Often associated with constipation and reported with lichen sclerosus (biopsy may exclude it). Differential: skin tag, wart, haemangioma, rectal prolapse, Crohn disease, child abuse. Tends to resolve on its own.
periocular-dermatitis: Localised periorificial dermatitis: small red scaly papules and pustules around the eyes, mainly women 16-45, often in people using topical corticosteroids (especially potent or fluorinated); also cosmetics, sunscreen, moisturisers. Stop all creams; taper any steroid, as it may flare on cessation. Topical options include metronidazole, erythromycin, azelaic acid; oral tetracyclines (macrolides if under 11).
periorificial-dermatitis-in-children: Grouped small erythematous papules, pustules or vesicles around the mouth, nose and eyes, sparing the narrow zone next to the vermilion border; no comedones, unlike acne. Rosacea-like; corticosteroid exposure (topical, oral or inhaled) in 58-72% of paediatric cases. Granulomatous variant: flesh-coloured papules in dark-skinned prepubertal children with non-caseating perifollicular granulomas.
peristomal-intestinal-metaplasia: Rare ileostomy or colostomy complication: intestinal mucosa and goblet cells within the peristomal epidermis, presenting as painful erosive plaques, ulceration or a granular eruption. Linked to chronic inflammation, effluent leakage and ill-fitting appliances. Biopsy the plaque border; adenomas and adenocarcinoma can develop, so monitor serially.
phace-syndrome: Large segmental facial infantile haemangioma (>5 cm for definite diagnosis) with Posterior fossa malformations, Arterial anomalies, Cardiac anomalies (coarctation) and Eye abnormalities; PHACES adds Sternal cleft or supraumbilical raphe. Girls affected 9 times more. Propranolol may cause hypotension if severe vessel anomalies are present.
photocontact-dermatitis: Light plus a photoreactive agent. Phototoxic: non-immunological, exaggerated sunburn or phytophotodermatitis (psoralens in limes, celery, parsley; painful linear streaks, hyperpigmentation). Photoallergic: delayed-type hypersensitivity, eczematous and itchy; sunscreen agents (benzophenone-3, octocrylene), fragrances, topical ketoprofen. Confirm with photopatch testing.
photosensitivity: Classify as primary (PLE, actinic prurigo, solar urticaria, chronic actinic dermatitis, hydroa vacciniforme), exogenous (phototoxic or photoallergic), photoexacerbated (lupus, dermatomyositis, Darier disease) or metabolic (porphyrias, pellagra). Clues: sharp cut-off at clothing and sparing of upper eyelids, under chin, behind ears and finger webs. Sunscreen alone does not protect in porphyria.
phrynoderma: Follicular hyperkeratosis from nutritional deficiency, commonly vitamin A (also vitamin E, B and essential fatty acids). Follicular papules with keratotic plugs begin on the back of the elbows and front of the knees; hands and feet spared, face rarely involved. Look for night blindness and Bitot spots; mimics keratosis pilaris and Darier disease; resolves with better nutrition.
piedra: Fungal hair infection with small stone-like nodules along the shaft: black piedra (Piedraia hortae) is firm, gritty and well attached; white piedra (Trichosporon spp.) is softer and easier to detach. Asymptomatic; negative hair pull test suggests a shaft problem. Culture is the gold standard; differential includes head lice, tinea capitis, trichorrhexis nodosa and trichomycosis axillaris.
pigmented-contact-cheilitis: Allergic or irritant reaction of the lips causing progressive dark purple-black discolouration, often starting as burning, itchy lip swelling. Reported causes: lipsticks, hair dye (PPD) on a moustache, and nickel in green tea. Diagnosed by patch testing with the patient's own products; avoid the culprit, and pigment may fade over 12 months but not always completely.
pik3ca-related-overgrowth-spectrum: Somatic mosaic gain-of-function PIK3CA variants (PI3K/AKT/mTOR hyperactivation) cause asymmetric overgrowth with vascular malformations, lipomatous tissue and epidermal naevi; includes Klippel-Trenaunay, CLOVES, MCM and CLAPO. Not inherited; present from birth or early childhood. Alpelisib (PI3Kalpha inhibitor) is FDA-approved for severe PROS; small increased Wilms tumour risk.
pilar-sheath-acanthoma: Uncommon benign follicular tumour: solitary papule up to 5 mm with a 1-2 mm central opening, no hair, keratinous material expressed on squeezing; face and head, often upper lip, in middle age. Histology distinguishes it from dilated pore of Winer and trichofolliculoma. Not associated with syndromes.
pilonidal-disease: Sinus tract in the sacrococcygeal cleft containing hair nests, with foreign body reaction on histology. Ages 20-40, 2-3 times more common in men; risks include coarse curly hair, obesity and prolonged sitting ('Jeep rider's disease'). Completes the follicular occlusion tetrad with hidradenitis suppurativa, acne conglobata and dissecting cellulitis.
pinworms: Enterobius vermicularis; perianal itch worse at night when females emerge to lay eggs. Confirm with the sticky tape test on the anal crease at night (eggs under the microscope). Spread by ingested eggs, with auto-infection from nail biting. Complications: UTI, perianal granuloma, vaginitis; treat the whole family at once (albendazole or mebendazole).
pityriasiform-seborrhoeide: Widespread, symmetrical light pink scaly variant of seborrhoeic dermatitis with poorly defined oval flaky patches, worst on scalp, ears, face, neck and trunk; thought to be hypersensitivity to Malassezia, so scrapings may be negative. Distinguish from psoriasis, pityriasis rosea (herald patch, fir-tree pattern, spares scalp/ears) and pityriasis versicolor. Emollients may aggravate.
pityriasis-amiantacea: Thick silvery or yellowish scale encircling hair shafts and binding down tufts of hair (like asbestos). A reaction pattern rather than a diagnosis; look for scalp psoriasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, atopic dermatitis, tinea capitis (also lice, lichen simplex). May cause impetiginisation and temporary or permanent alopecia.
plack-syndrome: Acronym: Peeling skin, Leukonychia, Acral punctate keratosis, Cheilitis, Knuckle pads. Extremely rare autosomal recessive generalised peeling skin syndrome from loss-of-function CAST (calpastatin) mutations, with calpain overactivity degrading (corneo)desmosomes. Painless peeling from infancy; confirm with CAST testing.
plant-dermatitis: Phytodermatitis is asymmetrical, linear or spattered. Mechanisms: irritant (mechanical or chemical), allergic type IV (poison ivy/rhus, primula, grevillea), phytophototoxic (furocoumarins in cow parsnip, lime peel oil; UVA-induced; burning pain) and contact urticaria (formic acid in nettles; latex). Airborne compositae allergy can cause eyelid dermatitis and chronic photosensitive dermatitis; true allergy is lifelong.
plasma-cell-balanitisvulvitis-images: Zoon balanitis: a single glistening orange-red plaque on the glans (several patches in plasma cell vulvitis, at the vestibule); biopsy shows numerous plasma cells, but this is non-specific. Cause unknown; many cases prove to be other diseases (infection, allergic contact dermatitis, psoriasis, lichen planus, penile/vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia). Circumcision is recommended for plasma cell balanitis and may cure.
plasma-cell-mucositis: Rare benign disorder sharing features with Zoon balanitis; bright red, glistening oral mucosa and gingiva, with 'strawberry' gingivae resembling granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Associated with khat chewing. Histology: dense subepithelial infiltrate of mature polyclonal plasma cells. Can cause airway strictures; none have evolved to plasma cell neoplasm. Plasma cell gingivitis follows cinnamon flavouring in toothpaste or gum.
plasmacytoma: Tumour of monoclonal plasma cells, usually in bone; extramedullary lesions are mostly head and neck (80-90%), with cutaneous involvement only 2-4% as red nodules or dome-shaped plaques that may ulcerate. Diagnosis requires excluding multiple myeloma; solitary bone plasmacytoma progresses to myeloma in 65-84% at 10 years. Cutaneous spread in known myeloma implies a poor prognosis.
pleomorphic-dermal-sarcoma: Dermal tumour on sun-damaged head and neck of elderly (median age 78), more in men and the immunosuppressed; solitary red or skin-coloured nodule/plaque, 1-7 cm, may ulcerate. Overlaps with atypical fibroxanthoma, separated histologically by subcutaneous, perineural or lymphovascular invasion or necrosis. UV-signature mutations (TP53, CDKN2A, NOTCH, TERT); metastasis usually to lungs.
podoconiosis: Ascending, usually bilateral lymphoedema of the feet and legs in people with long-term exposure to volcanic red clay soil at high altitude; genetically determined reaction to mineral particles, no infectious organism. Mossy changes, first-second toe web lichenification (Stemmer sign). Mimics: lymphatic filariasis (starts in the groin, usually unilateral) and leprosy. Skin grafting (Charles operation) is unsuccessful.
poikiloderma-of-civatte: Reddish-brown atrophic patches with telangiectasia on the sides of the neck and lateral cheeks of fair-skinned, postmenopausal women, sparing the shaded area under the chin. Histology: epidermal atrophy, pigmentary incontinence, telangiectasia and solar elastosis. Photosensitising fragrances may contribute. Differential: Riehl melanosis, dermatomyositis, lupus, Rothmund-Thomson.
poliosis: Localised patch of white hairs from lack of melanin or melanocytes in the hair bulbs; a clinical sign, not a diagnosis. Genetic: piebaldism, Waardenburg, tuberous sclerosis, NF1. Acquired: vitiligo, alopecia areata, halo naevus, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada, melanoma-associated leukoderma, drugs (imiquimod, bimatoprost, acitretin, chloroquine). May repigment in alopecia areata.
polycystic-ovary-syndrome: Diagnosis needs two of three: menstrual disturbance, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. Skin: hirsutism, persistent acne, androgenic alopecia, acanthosis nigricans, skin tags, hidradenitis suppurativa; insulin resistance is central. Spironolactone and isotretinoin must be avoided when pregnant or trying to conceive.
porokeratotic-eccrine-ostial-and-dermal-: Rare congenital keratinisation disorder, a type of epidermal naevus: linear small scaly papules on palm, fingers, sole or toes, which may extend to backs of hands and feet. Becomes more warty with time and nearly always persists despite treatment. Usually asymptomatic; keratolytics and retinoids only partly effective, laser, dermabrasion or excision for localised disease.
prader-willi-syndrome: Most common genetic cause of obesity; loss of paternally expressed genes on chromosome 15: paternal 15q11-q13 deletion (75%), maternal uniparental disomy (20%), imprinting defect (5%). Floppy, poorly feeding infant, then food-seeking obesity. Skin picking is the most typical cutaneous feature; piezogenic papules and erysipelas are common. Angelman syndrome is the distinct maternal-imprinting disorder on the same chromosome.
pressure-ulcer: Breakdown of skin over bony prominences from prolonged pressure (coccyx, heels, ankles, elbows; trochanters, ear helix). Staging: 1 = non-blanching erythema of intact skin; 2 = partial thickness; 3 = full thickness to fat; 4 = exposed muscle, tendon or bone, high risk of osteomyelitis. Stage 1 can be missed in darker skin; check warmth and firmness. Malignant transformation (Marjolin ulcer) is a complication.
pressure-urticaria: Chronic inducible urticaria with painful weals or angioedema 4-6 hours after pressure (standing, tight clothes, sitting on hard surfaces), lasting 8-72 hours; hands, feet, buttocks. Up to 60% also have chronic urticaria or dermographism. Biopsy: inflammatory infiltrate without vasculitis. Antihistamines rarely help; clobetasol may reduce inflammation. Mean duration 9 years.
pretibial-pruritic-papular-dermatitis: Itchy, smooth, flesh-coloured to erythematous papules on the shins of adult women, often coalescing into a cobblestone pattern; likely from chronic rubbing but distinct from lichen simplex chronicus and prurigo nodularis. Dermoscopy: dotted/globular vessels with a petaloid whitish scale collarette. Histology: papillary dermal fibrosis, stellate fibroblasts, eosinophils; weak CD30 may mimic lymphomatoid papulosis.
primary-cutaneous-anaplastic-large-cell-: Indolent CD30+ cutaneous T-cell lymphoma: rapidly growing solitary red-violaceous nodule of 2 cm or more that often ulcerates, in a systemically well patient (male 3:1, age 50-70). Sheets of large CD30+ cells in the dermis. Partial or total regression in 20-40%. Associated with lymphomatoid papulosis, which can be indistinguishable histologically; rule out systemic ALCL.
primary-cutaneous-cd30-positive-lymphopr: Indolent CD30+ T-cell neoplasms, second most common CTCL after mycosis fungoides: lymphomatoid papulosis (recurrent crops of papules that ulcerate, heal in 3-12 weeks with varioliform scars) and pcALCL (solitary rapidly growing ulcerating nodule, median age 60, systemically well). Looks malignant on histology; LyP is associated with other lymphomas in up to 20%.
protein-energy-malnutrition: Kwashiorkor (adequate calories, deficient protein): oedema, moon face, pot belly, 'flaky paint' skin starting at friction sites, sparse red-yellow hair with the 'hair flag sign'. Marasmus (protein and calorie deficiency): loose wrinkled skin, fat loss, triangular 'monkey' face. Skin signs worse in darker skin; zinc paste for skin; beware refeeding syndrome.
prurigo: Intensely itchy dome-shaped papules (primary lesions), unlike pruritus where there are none. Types: prurigo simplex, nodular prurigo (hard warty pigmented nodules, very resistant to treatment), prurigo pigmentosa (net-like pigmentation). Associations: atopy, iron deficiency, thyroid disease, HIV, renal failure, polycythaemia vera, lymphoma. Biopsy/DIF to exclude dermatitis herpetiformis; actinic prurigo is photosensitivity.
prurigo-of-pregnancy: Benign, non-specific pruritic papular eruption of the 2nd or 3rd trimester (up to 1 in 300 pregnancies): grouped, excoriated 0.5-1 cm papules on extensor limbs and sometimes trunk; pustules may occur but no vesicles. Histology non-specific, DIF negative; check liver function to exclude cholestasis of pregnancy. Resolves after delivery; no maternal or fetal risk.
pruritic-papular-eruption-of-hiv: Most common HIV-associated rash and often the presenting sign: intensely itchy firm papules on exposed extremities, sparing mucosae, palms, soles and web spaces, evolving to hyperpigmented macules. WHO stage 2; ~3x more common with CD4 <200. Biopsy: superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with eosinophils. Mimic: HIV eosinophilic folliculitis. Often resolves with HAART.
pruritus: Itch with no primary lesions, only excoriations and lichenification/prurigo from scratching. Systemic causes: uraemic (dialysis), cholestatic (worse at night, hands/feet), iron deficiency (with glossitis, angular cheilitis), polycythaemia vera (aquagenic), Graves disease, Hodgkin lymphoma, HIV, hepatitis C. Neuropathic: brachioradial, notalgia paraesthetica. Antihistamines help mainly in urticaria.
pseudopelade-of-brocq: Diagnosis of exclusion after lichen planopilaris and discoid lupus: smooth, soft, slightly depressed, non-scaly skin-coloured patches starting at the vertex in middle-aged women, described as "footprints in the snow". Histology: thin epidermis, sclerotic dermis with fibrotic streamers down to fat, no marked inflammation, absent sebaceous glands. No treatment stops it.
pseudoporphyria: Mimics PCT and variegate porphyria (fragile sun-exposed skin, tense blisters on hands and feet, milia, scarring) but porphyrin tests are normal. Phototoxic triggers: NSAIDs (naproxen), doxycycline, nalidixic acid, diuretics, retinoids, oral contraceptives, dialysis, sunbeds. Withdraw the agent.
psoriasis-of-the-palms-and-soles: Well-circumscribed red scaly plaques, or diffuse dry thickening of palms and soles with fissures, sharply bordered and symmetrical. More often associated with nail dystrophy and psoriatic arthritis than plaque psoriasis elsewhere. Do fungal scrapings (mimics tinea pedis, hand dermatitis). Lithium may flare it; TNF inhibitors may trigger palmoplantar pustulosis.
psoriatic-arthritis: A spondyloarthritis, seronegative (RF usually negative) with dactylitis, enthesitis, DIP involvement and nail disease (up to 90%). Radiology: pencil-in-cup deformity, ivory phalanx, whiskering. Patterns: asymmetric oligoarthritis (60%), arthritis mutilans (5%). Arthritis precedes skin disease in about 15%; risk higher with nail, scalp or flexural psoriasis.
pubic-lice: Phthirus pubis ('crabs'), spread by close and sexual contact; lives on pubic, perianal and axillary hair and can infest the eyelashes. Blood specks on underclothes, nits on hair shafts, itch from saliva. Insecticide (malathion, permethrin or pyrethrin) repeated at 7 days; eyelashes need forceps or petroleum jelly. Treat sexual partners and screen for other STIs.
punctate-type-palmoplantar-keratoderma: AD keratoderma appearing in late childhood or early adulthood with tiny hard bumps on the palms and soles. Three types: punctate (some are porokeratosis palmaris et plantaris disseminata), filiform (hard spikes; may lack family history) and marginal (bumps along the borders of the palms and soles). Persists for life.
purpura: Haemorrhage from small vessels: petechiae up to 2 mm, ecchymoses larger. Petechiae point to thrombocytopaenic purpura; coagulation defects give large ecchymoses without petechiae; vasculitis gives persistent, palpable purpura with an inflammatory component. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and early warfarin necrosis (relative protein C deficiency) cause purpura with necrosis. Senile purpura reflects fragile aged or sun-damaged skin.
pustular-psoriasis-of-pregnancy: Impetigo herpetiformis: generalised pustular psoriasis in pregnancy, usually third trimester, with annular erythematous plaques and sterile peripheral pustules starting in the folds; face, palms and soles spared. Constitutional symptoms (fever, malaise) are common; postulated triggers include hypocalcaemia and IL36RN mutation. Can recur earlier in the next pregnancy; risk of placental insufficiency and stillbirth.
pyoderma-faciale: Abrupt-onset painful nodules, pustules and sores on very red cheeks, chin or forehead of young adult women (also called rosacea fulminans); can develop in pregnancy and may scar. Unlike acne: no comedones, not oily, no males; unlike rosacea: no flushing or eye involvement. Cultures are negative. Oral antibiotics, isotretinoin or systemic steroids may help.
radiation-dermatitis: Sharply demarcated change confined to the irradiated field. Acute (within 90 days): erythema to moist desquamation to necrosis. Chronic (15 days to 10+ years): loss of follicular structures, dermal collagen increase, telangiectasia, fragile epidermis; secondary BCC. Radiation recall follows chemotherapy (methotrexate, etoposide). Risks: >55 Gy, cetuximab, connective tissue disease, ataxia telangiectasia, basal cell naevus syndrome.
ramsay-hunt-syndrome: VZV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion (CN VII): unilateral facial palsy plus painful vesicles in the ear canal or on the oropharynx/palate; CN VIII involvement gives hearing loss and vertigo. Zoster sine herpete (no blisters, ~10%) is confirmed by VZV PCR and must be distinguished from Bell palsy. Poorer prognosis than Bell palsy, especially if antivirals are not started within 72 hours.
raynaud-phenomenon: Episodic digital white, then blue, then red colour change with cold or emotion. Primary form has no associated condition; secondary form has a cause. Systemic sclerosis (CREST) is the connective tissue disease most likely to present with it; nailfold capillaroscopy helps. Drug causes: beta-blockers, ergotamine, bleomycin, clonidine.
reactive-arthropathy: Sterile asymmetric oligoarthritis of the lower limbs weeks after a GI (Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter) or GU (Chlamydia trachomatis) infection; HLA-B27 and HIV associated. Dactylitis, enthesitis; arthritis plus urethritis plus conjunctivitis was Reiter syndrome. Skin: keratoderma blenorrhagicum on soles, circinate balanitis, oral ulcers, nail changes.
reactive-infectious-mucocutaneous-erupti: Severe mucositis (oral, ocular, urogenital) with sparse or absent skin lesions, usually in children about a week after a respiratory infection; Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the commonest trigger (formerly MIRM). Lesions are vesiculobullous or atypical targetoid. Unlike SJS/TEN there is no extensive sheet-like detachment. Ocular and mucosal synechiae are the main sequelae.
red-ear-syndrome: Paroxysmal burning pain and redness of one or both ears, lasting up to 4 hours (typically 30-60 minutes). Primary form: children, often bilateral, migraine-associated, may be erythromelalgia; secondary form: adult women, usually unilateral, cervical spine (C3) or TMJ dysfunction, triggered by heat or touch. Mimics: relapsing polychondritis, chilblains, perichondritis. Usually refractory to treatment.
relapsing-polychondritis: Recurrent cartilage inflammation: auricular chondritis (up to 90%) with a red swollen pinna classically sparing the lobe, often bilateral (cellulitis is usually unilateral); nasal chondritis leads to saddle nose. Also airway collapse and aortic/mitral disease. McAdam criteria need 3 features. Can be a feature of VEXAS in middle-aged men; respiratory failure is a major cause of death.
remitting-seronegative-symmetrical-synov: Older man (70s-80s) with sudden pitting oedema of the distal extremities ('boxing glove' hands) unresponsive to diuretics, with tenosynovitis; RF and anti-CCP negative, no erosions. Associated with haematological and solid malignancy (up to 50% reported), so screen. Rapid response to prednisone 10-20 mg/day. Differential: PMR, hypothyroidism, RA.
reticular-erythematous-mucinosis: Net-like (reticular) erythematous papules on the mid-back or chest, mostly in middle-aged women; also called midline mucinosis. Biopsy: mucin between dermal collagen bundles. Sunlight may contribute; can resemble mucinosis of SLE. Usually responds to sun protection and antimalarials (hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine).
reticulohistiocytosis: Solitary reticulohistiocytoma: single yellowish-red lump in a healthy adult that resolves over months to years; excision is curative. Multiple lesions imply organ involvement (heart involvement may be fatal). Multicentric form: papulonodules, destructive arthritis, 'coral-beading' of nails; 20-30% have an underlying malignancy.
retiform-purpura: Non-blanching, branching or angulated purpura, often with necrosis or ulceration, from vessel wall damage or lumen occlusion. Inflammatory type (wide erythema, small necrotic centre) suggests infection or vasculitis; non-inflammatory (narrow rim, large necrotic centre) suggests occlusion. Clues: periumbilical = strongyloides; ear = levamisole; fatty abdomen or thighs = warfarin or heparin necrosis. Biopsy the peripheral purpuric rim.
rheumatic-fever: Follows group A streptococcal infection (usually pharyngitis) by weeks; diagnosed by Jones criteria. Migratory polyarthritis, carditis, Sydenham chorea. Erythema marginatum (about 10% of first attacks in children): fleeting non-itchy annular erythema on trunk and limbs, sparing face, palms and soles. Subcutaneous nodules (under 2%) over joints, usually with severe carditis. Prevent recurrence with continuous penicillin.
rhinophyma: Phymatous rosacea of the nose: thickened skin, enlarged sebaceous glands, pitted pores and telangiectasia, graded 1-3. Strong male predominance (M:F 5:1 to 30:1). Other sites: chin (gnathophyma), ears (otophyma), eyelids (blepharophyma), forehead (metophyma). BCC has been reported in it, but it is not considered a precursor for malignancy.
roseola: HHV-6B (possibly HHV-7) in children 6 months to 3 years: 3-5 days of high fever, then small rose-pink blanching spots on the trunk as fever subsides; non-itchy. Nagayama spots on soft palate and uvula. Febrile seizures in 5-15%. Also called exanthem subitum.
ross-syndrome: Triad of tonic (Adie) pupil, hyporeflexia/areflexia and segmental anhidrosis; abnormal sweating is mandatory for diagnosis. Patients usually present with compensatory segmental hyperhidrosis (often unilateral trunk, T5-T12); Minor starch-iodine test. Mimics: Harlequin (normal pupils and reflexes), Holmes-Adie (normal sweating), Horner (constricted pupil, normal reflexes). Risk of hyperthermia from anhidrosis.
rothmund-thomson-syndrome: Autosomal recessive RECQL4 (DNA helicase) mutations; also called poikiloderma congenitale. Photosensitivity in the first year, then poikiloderma (pigmentation, telangiectasia, atrophy) on cheeks, hands and buttocks by 3-5 years, with sparse hair and eyebrows, cataracts, absent/malformed radii and thumbs. Osteosarcoma is the second most common cancer; BCC, SCC and Bowen disease are common, so strict sun protection.
rubella: German measles: rash spreading from face to trunk and limbs lasting ~3 days, with tender retroauricular, occipital and posterior cervical nodes; Forchheimer sign (palatal petechiae). Arthritis in adult women. Part of TORCH; first-trimester infection gives congenital rubella syndrome: sensorineural deafness, cataract, PDA, blueberry muffin lesions.
rubinstein-taybi-syndrome: Broad thumbs and great toes, grimacing smile, beaked nose and developmental delay; CREBBP (55%) or EP300 (8%) mutations, ~99% de novo. Atraumatic keloids, typically on shoulders and chest from the second decade, are a key cutaneous feature; also hypertrichosis, supernumerary nipples, glabellar naevus simplex. Keloids respond poorly to treatment.
sapho-syndrome: Synovitis, Acne (conglobata or fulminans), Pustulosis (palmoplantar, like palmoplantar pustular psoriasis), Hyperostosis, Osteitis in any combination. Sternum and clavicles are classically involved; MRI shows marrow inflammation. Skin biopsy shows neutrophilic pseudoabscesses; bone biopsy shows sterile osteomyelitis. Hidradenitis suppurativa and dissecting cellulitis may also occur.
scalp-folliculitis: Small, very itchy pustules on the scalp, worst at the frontal hairline; linked to Cutibacterium acnes, Malassezia and Demodex (S. aureus in severe cases). Acne necrotica: blackened crusts leaving pox-like scars. Perifolliculitis capitis abscedens et suffodiens (dissecting cellulitis): nodules, cysts, scarring alopecia; associated with acne conglobata, HS, spondyloarthropathy; mostly black adult men.
scalp-psoriasis: Well-demarcated red plaques with silvery-white scale; about 80% of psoriasis patients have scalp involvement. Extension past the hairline onto the forehead, ears and neck is typical; heavy scale can form pityriasis amiantacea, and temporary alopecia may occur. Trichoscopy: red dots, hairpin vessels, red globular rings. Ddx seborrhoeic dermatitis (sebopsoriasis), tinea capitis, PRP.
scalp-tumours-and-cysts: Most scalp tumours (93-99%) are benign, and 40-50% of those are cysts; trichilemmal (pilar) cysts lack a central punctum and about 80% occur on the scalp. Among malignant lesions, BCC (about 41%) then SCC (about 17%) predominate; scalp tumours do worse than elsewhere (ulceration, recurrence, thicker melanomas). Angiosarcoma may present as painful, rapidly growing bruises.
schnitzler-syndrome: Rarely itchy chronic urticaria (wheals lasting 12 hours to 3 days) with intermittent fever, arthralgia/arthritis, bone pain and a monoclonal gammopathy, usually IgM. Biopsy is neutrophil-rich and may resemble urticarial vasculitis. About 15% progress to a lymphoproliferative disorder (Waldenstrom, B-cell lymphoma). Anakinra (IL-1 antagonist) controls symptoms but relapse follows stopping it.
scleroedema: Cutaneous mucinosis with symmetrical woody induration and peau d'orange of the neck, upper back and face; biopsy shows mucin between dermal collagen bundles. Type 1 follows Streptococcus pyogenes infection and resolves in 6 months to 2 years; type 2 is insidious with paraprotein or myeloma; type 3 (Buschke, diabeticorum) occurs in diabetics and is persistent. Not scleroderma.
scombroid-fish-poisoning: Histamine toxicity from decomposing dark-meat fish (tuna, mackerel, bonito): within an hour or two, flushing and a bright red, hot, itchy rash of face, neck, chest and upper back, urticaria-like but without wheals, with headache and GI symptoms. Not allergy and not infection; cooking does not reduce histamine. Responds to antihistamines; adrenaline, steroids and antibiotics not needed.
scrub-typhus: Orientia tsutsugamushi spread by trombiculid mite larvae (chiggers); fever, myalgia and headache with an inoculation eschar in most cases, plus lymphadenopathy and a truncal exanthem. Eschar mimics include anthrax and tularaemia. Responds to tetracyclines (doxycycline); untreated mortality may be as high as 60%.
sea-bathers-eruption: Itchy vesicles, papules, pustules and urticarial weals confined under the bathing suit hours after sea swimming, from nematocysts of thimble jellyfish (Linuche unguiculata) or sea anemone larvae. Worse with freshwater showers, rubbing and prolonged wear of the suit; later rash is likely immune-mediated. Differs from swimmer's itch, which affects exposed skin. Lasts 1-2 weeks, up to 2 months.
sebopsoriasis: Overlap of seborrhoeic dermatitis and psoriasis: greasy yellowish scale in seborrhoeic sites (scalp, nasolabial folds, eyebrows, retroauricular, sternum) but with deeper red, better-defined margins and thicker scale than seborrhoeic dermatitis, less silvery than psoriasis. Biopsy is intermediate; Malassezia on scraping is not diagnostic. Immunosuppression, HIV and Parkinson disease are linked to more severe disease.
segmental-pigmentation-disorder: Unilateral hypo- or hyperpigmented patches, mainly on the trunk, with a sharp anterior midline cut-off; seen from infancy, stable, no systemic or neurological associations (unlike hypomelanosis of Ito or other pigmentary mosaicism). Differential includes segmental vitiligo, tuberous sclerosis, Becker naevus and McCune-Albright syndrome. No treatment needed.
semen-contact-allergy: Rare allergic contact urticaria to seminal plasma, exclusively in women; over 40% symptomatic after first intercourse; strong atopy association. Localised (immediate vulvovaginal burning, swelling) and/or systemic (urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis; type I, IgE) reactions; prostate-specific antigen implicated. Condoms prevent symptoms. Prick test uses partner's seminal plasma. Not linked to infertility; desensitisation clears >95%.
senile-purpura: Bateman or actinic purpura: well-defined dark purple macules 1-4 cm on the extensor forearms and dorsal hands of sun-damaged older skin after minor trauma, resolving over 1-3 weeks without bruise colour changes and leaving brown haemosiderin staining. Recurrent. Corticosteroids and anticoagulants are risk factors. Histology: thin epidermis, abnormal elastic fibres, normal vessel walls. Coagulation studies are unremarkable.
septic-emboli: Infected clots lodge in small terminal vessels: painful, non-blanching red or purpuric spots (may contain pus) on the hands and feet. Osler nodes and Janeway lesions are classic when from endocarditis, particularly Staphylococcus aureus. Biopsy: clot occlusion with abundant neutrophils in deep dermal vessels. Always search for the source (blood cultures, cardiac ultrasound). Risk: prosthetic valves, injecting drug use.
serum-sickness-like-reaction: Fever, urticaria followed by bruise-like change, facial swelling and symmetric joint pain 1-3 weeks after a drug, classically cefaclor in young children. Unlike true serum sickness, no circulating immune complexes are found. More likely on a second or later course; penicillins and NSAIDs are also causes. Stop the drug; antihistamines and steroids have no proven benefit.
severe-cutaneous-adverse-reaction: Umbrella term for AGEP, DIHS/DRESS and SJS/TEN; latency differs. AGEP: 2-5 days, non-follicular sterile pustules in flexures, fever, neutrophilia. SJS/TEN: typically 7-10 days, atypical targets, mucosal involvement over 90%. DRESS: 2-6 weeks, liver involvement, eosinophilia, facial oedema. Overlaps occur; biopsy can help separate them.
sexually-acquired-human-papillomavirus: Low-risk types 6 and 11 cause anogenital warts, mucosal papillomas and juvenile-onset respiratory papillomatosis. Types 16 and 18 cause at least 70% of precancerous and cancerous anogenital disease; cervical cancer is the commonest HPV cancer. Cytology: koilocytes. Podophyllotoxin is not used in pregnancy; recurrence is common.
shiitake-flagellate-dermatitis: Itchy erythematous linear "whiplash" streaks (sometimes petechial), mostly on the trunk, about 24 hours (hours to 5 days) after eating raw or undercooked shiitake; toxic reaction to thermolabile lentinan, not from skin contact; about 2% of consumers; worse with sun; resolves in weeks. Other flagellate erythema: bleomycin, docetaxel, dermatomyositis, adult-onset Still disease.
shoe-contact-dermatitis: Symmetrical foot dermatitis with toe flexures and instep often spared; heel box allergens affect the heel and nickel buckles only adjacent skin. Key allergens: chromium in tanned leather (potassium dichromate), rubber accelerators, PTBP-formaldehyde resin adhesive (shoemakers). Patch test with pieces of the patient's own shoes plus a footwear series.
short-anagen-syndrome: Child whose scalp hair will not grow long ('never had a haircut') because anagen lasts only 1-2 years instead of 4-7. Hair shaft and density are normal and hairs are not fragile; the hair pull test is often normal, which separates it from loose anagen syndrome and telogen effluvium. Cause unknown; usually persists to adulthood, unlike loose anagen syndrome.
shrimp-nail: Curved nail plate with several ridges resembling the back of a shrimp, caused by repeated onychomadesis (matrix growth arrest); often the great toe, usually asymptomatic. Triggers: repeated microtrauma from poor shoes, infection (hand, foot and mouth), drugs, autoimmune disease, SJS/TEN, Kawasaki. Usually self-limited.
sister-mary-joseph-nodule-of-the-umbilic: Metastasis to the umbilicus, usually from advanced peritoneal adenocarcinoma, presenting as red papules or a nodule. Primaries mostly gastric, colonic or pancreatic, also ovarian or uterine; none found in about 15%. In a quarter the umbilical lesion is the first sign of cancer. Poor prognosis; most die within a year.
sjoegren-syndrome: Sicca (keratoconjunctivitis sicca, xerostomia), mainly older women; xerosis in 50%, small vessel or urticarial vasculitis up to 30%. Anti-Ro in 75% (neonatal lupus, congenital heart block) and anti-La in 50%. Lip biopsy: lymphocytic infiltrate; Schirmer under 5 mm in 5 min. Lymphoma (particularly MALT) lifetime risk 5-10%.
skin-metastasis: Firm, mobile, painless round or oval nodules, usually near the primary and late in known internal cancer. Patterns: carcinoma erysipeloides (sharp red patch from lymphatic blockage), en cuirasse (sclerodermoid), carcinoma telangiectoides, alopecia neoplastica (scalp, breast). Sister Mary Joseph nodule at the umbilicus signals extensive colorectal cancer. About 70% in women arise from breast.
smallpox: Variola virus, declared eradicated in 1980. Prodrome of high fever 2-4 days, then oral sores and a rash on face and limbs becoming firm, umbilicated pustules (4-6 mm) that crust and leave pitted scars. Variola major ~30% mortality. Mimics: chickenpox (trunk), zoster, impetigo, drug SCAR. Eczema vaccinatum occurs in atopic dermatitis.
sneddon-syndrome: Livedo racemosa (broken, branching net that does not fade with warming; buttocks and lower back first) plus recurrent TIAs/strokes, with livedo preceding strokes by over 10 years. Antiphospholipid antibodies in 50-80%; associated with SLE. Deep skin biopsy shows non-inflammatory thrombotic vasculopathy of small/medium arteries; yield rises with repeat biopsies. Progresses to cognitive decline and early dementia.
solar-comedo: Open or closed comedones on the face of older adults in actinically damaged skin, unrelated to acne vulgaris. With solar elastosis and larger pseudocysts it is Favre-Racouchot syndrome, around the eyes, temples and lateral neck; sun exposure plus heavy smoking. Cutis rhomboidalis nuchae may accompany it.
solar-elastosis: Yellow, thickened, furrowed skin from abnormal elastic tissue accumulation in chronic sun-damaged skin; can look like lemon skin (Milian citrine skin). Smoking also contributes, with elastic changes reaching deeper into the reticular dermis than UV damage. Mimics: pseudoxanthoma elasticum, Favre-Racouchot syndrome, Buschke-Ollendorff syndrome. Associated with melanoma, NMSC and actinic keratosis.
spa-pool-folliculitis: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (less often Aeromonas hydrophila) follicular papulopustules 8 hours to 5 days after hot tub or spa exposure, typically on swimwear-covered areas such as the buttocks. Hot hand-foot syndrome: tender nodules on palms and soles, especially in children. Gram stain shows Gram-negative rods; usually self-resolves within 14 days.
spider-bite: Widow spiders (Latrodectus: black widow, katipo, red-back) have neurotoxic venom: two fang marks, then cramping chest and abdominal pain, sweating, hypertension; systemic features aid diagnosis more than the skin. Loxosceles (recluse, violin) have cytotoxic venom: painless bite, pain at 2-8 h, 'bull's eye' lesion, necrotic ulcer healing over months with scar. Cellulitis and necrotising fasciitis are falsely blamed on spider bites.
spider-telangiectasis: Central red papule (feeding arteriole) with radiating fine vessels, on the face, neck and upper chest. Compressing the central arteriole (glass slide or dermatoscope) makes the radial legs disappear, and they refill rapidly on release. Multiple lesions occur with pregnancy, combined oral contraceptive, liver disease (cirrhosis) and thyrotoxicosis; oestrogen-induced lesions often resolve within 6 months. Not the same as blue spider veins.
spindle-cell-melanoma: Rare histologic variant (>90% spindle cells), often an amelanotic nodule on trunk, head or neck that is not suspected clinically and is mistaken for other spindle cell tumours. S100, SOX10, HMB-45 and Melan-A positive; cytokeratin negative. Leiomyosarcoma is SMA positive, DFSP CD34 positive. About 30% carry BRAF mutations; desmoplastic melanoma is a related variant.
spitzoid-melanoma: Malignant melanoma that mimics Spitz naevus histologically; enlarging papule or nodule, amelanotic or pigmented, usually round and uniform so ABCDE fails. Versus Spitz naevus: asymmetric, poorly circumscribed, no maturation at depth, deep atypical mitoses, may be necrotic. Equivocal lesions are called STUMP. Adult prognosis resembles other melanomas of the same thickness.
spondyloarthropathy: Five seronegative disorders: ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic, reactive and enteropathic arthritis, and undifferentiated; HLA-B27 in about 95% of ankylosing spondylitis. Inflammatory back pain before age 45, sacroiliitis, enthesitis, dactylitis, uveitis. Skin clues: psoriasis and nail pitting; erythema nodosum and pyoderma gangrenosum (enteropathic); keratoderma blennorrhagicum and circinate balanitis (reactive).
sporotrichoid-lymphocutaneous-infection: Nodular lymphangitis: firm inflamed nodules, which may ulcerate, start distally on an upper limb and appear proximally in a roughly linear pattern. Most commonly sporotrichosis (Sporothrix schenckii); also Nocardia, atypical mycobacteria, Leishmania. Cutaneous sarcoidosis and in-transit melanoma metastases can mimic it. Identify the organism before starting treatment.
spotted-fever: Rickettsial spotted fevers: fever, severe headache and myalgia, then a rash at 3-6 days starting on the limbs and spreading to trunk, palms and soles. Rocky Mountain spotted fever (R. rickettsii) is the severe one with petechial/purpuric rash, necrosis and mortality up to 30%. African tick typhus often has multiple eschars; rickettsialpox (R. akari, mite) has a sparse papulovesicular rash. Tetracyclines are effective.
squamous-cell-papilloma: HPV-6 and -11 benign papilloma; oral lesion is a solitary soft pedunculated mass with finger-like projections (pink raspberry-like or white cauliflower-like if keratinised) on the tongue, cheeks or lips, ages 30-50. Not associated with malignancy. Nasal and throat papillomas are multiple, recurrent and can cause asphyxiation.
staphylococcal-skin-infection: S aureus is carried in the nostrils and flexures by 15-40% of healthy people and invades via broken skin. Causes folliculitis, furuncles/carbuncles, impetigo, ecthyma and folliculitis decalvans; toxin disease includes scalded skin syndrome (children under 5, or adults with kidney failure) and toxic shock (TSST-1 or enterotoxin B superantigens). Risk factors include severe atopic dermatitis, Job and Wiskott-Aldrich syndromes; MRSA is increasing.
steatocystoma-multiplex: Numerous oily, yellow-fluid-filled cysts appearing at puberty, mostly on the chest; autosomal dominant, familial cases linked to keratin 17 (K17) mutations, which also cause one form of pachyonychia congenita. Histology: thin-walled dermal cyst with sebaceous glands in the wall and lanugo hair in the lumen. Mimics: acne conglobata, milia, epidermoid cysts.
steroid-acne: Acne-like eruption, mainly on the chest, with high circulating corticosteroids (Cushing disease, systemic steroids; anabolic steroids cause severe acne). Lesions are more uniform than in usual acne. Often it is Malassezia folliculitis: itchy, same-sized papules and pustules on chest and back without comedones. Distinct from steroid rosacea, which follows topical steroids.
steroid-rosacea: Rosacea-like mid-face eruption from potent topical steroids or their withdrawal: erythema, papules, pustules, burning heat and itch, later telangiectasia. Rebound flare when the steroid is stopped; slow withdrawal advised. Variant of (or the same as) periorificial dermatitis; can be confused with tinea faciei or tinea incognito. Distinct from steroid acne (oral steroids).
stomatitis: Inflammation of the oral mucosa; most commonly due to xerostomia, viral or Candida infection, trauma, tobacco, chemotherapy (including methotrexate) or radiation. Also consider immunobullous disease, erosive lichen planus, Behcet disease, SJS/TEN and nutritional deficiency. Folic acid can reduce methotrexate-induced stomatitis. Burning mouth syndrome is soreness despite a normal appearance.
stretch-marks-striae: Dermal tearing from stretch: red-purple striae rubrae perpendicular to skin tension fade to white striae albae. Pregnancy, adolescence, obesity, corticosteroids, Cushing syndrome, Marfan; steroid/Cushing striae are wider and may involve the face. Rubrae histology: elastolysis, reduced fibrillin microfibrils. Mimic: linear focal elastosis (increased elastic fibres).
stucco-keratosis: Benign stuck-on 1-4 mm white-grey flat keratotic papules on the lower legs, ankles and dorsal feet of older men; scale can be flicked off, leaving a dry non-bleeding surface, but it reforms in days. Histology: church-spire hyperkeratosis and papillomatosis without horn cysts or dysplasia. Not premalignant; possible HPV association.
subcorneal-pustular-dermatosis: Sneddon-Wilkinson disease: crops of soft pustules on the trunk and flexures, often within a red patch, mainly women over 40, otherwise well. Associated with IgA monoclonal gammopathy, multiple myeloma and pyoderma gangrenosum, so check protein electrophoresis. Close to generalised pustular psoriasis and AGEP. Dapsone often works; systemic steroids ineffective and may precipitate a flare.
subcutaneous-fat-necrosis-of-the-newborn: Rare, self-limiting panniculitis: firm red to purple nodules or plaques on the back, buttocks, cheeks, arms and thighs in the first weeks of life, in term and postterm infants. Risks include perinatal hypoxia, therapeutic hypothermia and maternal diabetes. Histology: lobular panniculitis with histiocytes, giant cells and needle-shaped clefts. Check calcium periodically for months because of hypercalcaemia. Compare with sclerema neonatorum.
subepidermal-calcified-nodule: Winer nodular calcinosis: a solitary (80%), firm, chalky yellow-white nodule on the head and neck (cheek, ear, eyelid), usually in children, with normal serum calcium, phosphate and PTH. Dermoscopy: yellow-white clods with linear vessels. Histology: calcified globules with giant cells. Mimics pilomatricoma and molluscum; excision cures.
subungual-exostosis: Benign bone outgrowth under the nail, most often the medial great toe; a firm nodule lifts the nail (onycholysis) and is often painful. Half of cases occur by age 20; women more affected. X-ray confirms bony origin. Mimics subungual wart, pyogenic granuloma, glomus tumour and amelanotic melanoma. Treated by surgical removal with curettage of the bone.
sunscreen-allergy: Many sunscreen allergies are due to inactive ingredients (fragrance, preservatives) rather than the UV filter. Photocontact pattern spares upper eyelids, under the chin and behind the ears; photopatch testing shows chemical absorbers are a common cause of photoallergic dermatitis. Metal oxide sunscreens (titanium dioxide, zinc oxide) have not been reported to cause allergic contact dermatitis.
