superficial-thrombophlebitis: Inflammation of a superficial vein from a clot: tender red cord, vein may feel hard or knobbly, usually the leg. Risks: varicose veins, IV sites, pregnancy, oral contraceptive or HRT, factor V Leiden, Buerger disease, polyarteritis nodosa, underlying cancer. Usually settles in 2-6 weeks; DVT is the complication if the clot reaches the superficial-deep junction. Septic thrombophlebitis needs urgent venous excision.
supernumerary-nipple: Failure of mammary ridge regression along the milk line from axilla to groin (about 5% lie outside it); present at birth and mimics a melanocytic naevus. Nipple-only type is commonest; glandular tissue can enlarge at puberty and lactate. Familial cases autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance; Ruvalcaba-Myhre, Hay-Wells syndromes.
swimmers-itch: Cercarial dermatitis ('duck itch'): allergic reaction to schistosome cercariae from aquatic snails (bird parasites) penetrating human skin. Itchy papules within hours, limited to skin exposed to water; swimwear-covered skin is spared (unlike sea bather's eruption). Needs repeated exposure to sensitise; resolves in 1-3 weeks. Differential: seaweed dermatitis, insect bites.
symmetrical-drug-related-intertriginous-: Formerly baboon syndrome: sharply demarcated, symmetric erythema of the buttocks and/or V-shaped inguinal erythema plus at least one other flexure, with no systemic symptoms. Type IV reaction to a systemic drug; amoxicillin and other beta-lactams cause about 50%. Mimics: AGEP, DRESS, flexural psoriasis. Benign, but recurs on re-exposure.
systemic-amyloidosis: Skin is significantly involved only in AL type (plasma cell dyscrasia, e.g. myeloma) and may be the clue: purpura and haemorrhagic blisters on the eyelids after minor trauma or coughing, waxy papules in flexures, macroglossia, nail dystrophy, alopecia. Congo red shows apple-green birefringence. AA amyloid (e.g. pustular psoriasis, Muckle-Wells) has no skin signs.
talaromycosis: Talaromyces marneffei (formerly Penicillium marneffei), a dimorphic fungus from bamboo rats and soil in Southeast Asia, southern China and India; AIDS-defining infection, also seen with anti-interferon gamma autoantibodies. Skin lesions in 70% of HIV cases: umbilicated necrotic papules on the head and upper chest (mimics molluscum, histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis). Culture is gold standard; yeasts in macrophages on PAS/GMS.
telangiectasia: Visible small linear red vessels (blue ones are venulectasia). Inherited causes: hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, ataxia-telangiectasia, Rothmund-Thomson, Bloom, Kindler syndromes. Acquired: rosacea, pregnancy, liver disease, Cushing, systemic sclerosis (CRST, mats), lupus, dermatomyositis, mastocytosis, CTCL. Also radiation, erythema ab igne, BCC, topical or systemic steroids, calcium channel blockers.
temporal-triangular-alopecia: Non-scarring triangular or spear-shaped patch on the frontotemporal scalp, usually unilateral, noticed in childhood (2-9 years) and unchanged for life. Dermoscopy: vellus hairs throughout with terminal hairs at the edge; no exclamation mark hairs, yellow or black dots (alopecia areata) and no streamers (male pattern). Histology: normal follicle number, mainly vellus type. No regrowth; treatment is generally not required.
textile-contact-dermatitis: Delayed reaction usually to formaldehyde finishing resins, dyes (PPD, azo/anthraquinone disperse dyes) and other additives rather than the fibre itself; affects friction/sweat sites (antecubital and popliteal fossae, axillae, groin, buttocks). Metal jean studs are a common cause of nickel dermatitis. More common in women; clothing is not labeled, so cause is hard to pin down.
thermal-burn: Superficial partial-thickness burns are painful, red, moist and blistered with hair intact; deep partial may be painless and dry with hair usually gone; full-thickness is painless, pearly white or charred and leathery. Depth is often underestimated initially; extent by Rule of Nines. Early cellulitis is Streptococcus pyogenes; invasive eschar infection is Pseudomonas and other gram-negatives.
thromboangiitis-obliterans: Buerger disease: thrombosis of small and medium arteries (less often veins) of hands and feet, almost exclusively in smokers (also long-term cannabis). Painful purple/blue digits, early loss of pulses, gangrene. Histology: intraluminal thrombus with microabscesses; internal elastic lamina classically spared (unlike other vasculitis). Arteriogram: corkscrew collaterals.
tick-bite-induced-red-meat-allergy: IgE to the carbohydrate galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose (alpha-gal) after a tick bite. Reaction to beef, pork or lamb is delayed 3-8 hours, unlike minutes in other food allergy; urticaria, angioedema, GI upset, rarely anaphylaxis. Poultry lacks alpha-gal. Also reactive: gelatine, cetuximab, pig-derived valves. Diagnose with alpha-gal IgE; skin prick may be falsely negative.
tinea-barbae: Dermatophyte infection of the beard and moustache in adult men, usually zoophilic: T. verrucosum from cattle or T. mentagrophytes var. equinum from horses (farmers). Very inflamed with pustules and crusting around hairs (kerion) that pull out easily, yet not excessively itchy or painful. Id reaction can follow starting treatment. Usually needs an oral antifungal.
tinea-faciei: Dermatophyte infection of the face excluding the beard; asymmetric, often unilateral annular scaly patches, aggravated by sun, often misdiagnosed as atopic or seborrhoeic dermatitis, rosacea, perioral dermatitis, cutaneous lupus or PMLE, especially after steroids (tinea incognito). Sources: T. rubrum from feet/nails, M. canis from pets, T. verrucosum from cattle. Confirm by microscopy and culture or PCR.
tinea-manuum: Dermatophyte infection of the hand; chronic form is a dry, peeling, hyperkeratotic palm with white scale in the skin markings, usually one hand with both feet involved ("one hand, two-foot syndrome"), from an anthropophilic fungus such as T. rubrum. Zoophilic or geophilic fungi give an inflammatory ringworm-like rash. Unilateral involvement distinguishes it from hand dermatitis; confirm with scrapings.
tinea-nigra: Brown-black, slightly scaly, asymptomatic patch on a palm or sole, unilateral or asymmetric, from the brown mould Hortaea werneckii (tropical regions, hyperhidrosis). Mimics melanoma and naevus; dermoscopy helps, and scrapings from the edge show septate pigmented hyphae. Black colonies on culture within a week; clears with a topical antifungal for 2-4 weeks.
topical-corticosteroid-withdrawal: Rebound after stopping prolonged moderate/high-potency topical steroids (facial use, atopy): burning red exudative skin from 48 hours to over 3 months later, may spread to untreated areas. Red sleeve sign (limb erythema sparing palms/soles), headlight sign (face sparing nose and perioral skin), 'elephant wrinkles' on extensors. Histology non-specific; erythematoedematous and papulopustular subtypes.
toxic-erythema-of-the-newborn: Benign, affects up to half of full-term newborns (less in premature infants); onset in the first days. Erythematous macules, papules and pustules wax and wane, individual lesions rarely last over a day, palms and soles usually spared, infant well. Histology: eosinophils, with subcorneal pustules packed with eosinophils. Mimics: transient neonatal pustular melanosis, infantile acropustulosis, miliaria, infections.
trachyonychia: Rough 'sandpaper' nails with diffuse longitudinal ridging and brittleness; twenty-nail dystrophy when all 20 are affected. Peak age 3-12 years. Opaque type is more severe and common; shiny type has small geometric pits. Associated with alopecia areata, lichen planus, psoriasis, atopic dermatitis. Spongiosis typical on histology; often resolves over years.
transient-lingual-papillitis: Painful red or white bump on one or a few fungiform papillae near the tongue tip, lasting 1-2 days and recurring ('lie bumps'); no illness or lymphadenopathy. Eruptive (familial) form in children has fever, lymphadenopathy and household spread. U-shaped variant is the commonest oral change in COVID-19.
trichilemmoma: Benign tumour of the hair follicle outer root sheath; skin-coloured, wart-like papules on the central face, ears or neck. Histology needed to separate from trichoepithelioma, trichofolliculoma and BCC. Multiple facial lesions: examine for Cowden disease. Can arise within a sebaceous naevus.
trichomycosis-axillaris: Bacterial, not fungal (Corynebacterium, Serratia marcescens): 1-2 mm yellow (commonest), red or black concretions encircling axillary hairs, with malodour and discoloured sweat. Wood lamp shows pale-yellow fluorescence. Corynebacterial triad: erythrasma, trichomycosis axillaris and pitted keratolysis. May resemble pubic lice; shaving or clipping the hair is the fastest way to clear it.
trichophagia: Hair eating, occurring in about 30% of patients with trichotillomania and mostly seen in children and adolescents. The usual presentation is a trichobezoar (abdominal pain, vomiting, weight loss, halitosis, palpable mass, anaemia), extending into the bowel as Rapunzel syndrome. Complications include obstruction, perforation and intussusception; abdominal CT is diagnostic in about 97%.
trichophyton-mentagrophytes-genotype-vii: Anthropophilic dermatophyte spread by skin-to-skin or sexual contact, mostly in MSM (the 'Thai variant'). Painful, pruritic, highly inflammatory annular scaly plaques or pustules on the genitals, groin, buttocks, face or beard, with kerion-like lesions and hair loss; mimics bacterial folliculitis, herpes simplex and mpox. DNA sequencing confirms genotype. Avoid topical steroids; oral terbinafine or itraconazole.
trichostasis-spinulosa: Multiple (5-60) entrapped vellus hairs in a dilated, hyperkeratotic follicle, giving black comedo-like dots on the nose and face that are mistaken for acne. Dermoscopy: tiny pigmented hairs from one pore; KOH shows a vellus hair bundle in a keratinous sheath. Mimics: comedonal acne, keratosis pilaris, Favre-Racouchot, phrynoderma.
trigeminal-trophic-syndrome: Crescent-shaped ulcer of the ala nasi after trigeminal nerve damage (eg, trigeminal rhizotomy or alcohol injection of the Gasserian ganglion); numbness or paraesthesia provokes picking. Nasal tip is spared (different nerve supply); scarring may draw the lip up into a sneer. Differs from dermatitis artefacta by an identifiable neurological abnormality. No characteristic biopsy; exclude infection, lupus, GPA, sarcoid, BCC/SCC.
tripe-palms: Rare paraneoplastic sign: thickened, velvety, yellowish palms with accentuated dermatoglyphics resembling stomach lining; about 90% have internal malignancy (gastric, lung most often). Coexists with malignant acanthosis nigricans in ~7 of 10; biopsy is non-specific. Work up for cancer if none known.
tuberculids: Hypersensitivity reaction to TB elsewhere; organisms are not isolated from the lesions, and Mantoux/IGRA is positive. Erythema induratum (Bazin), the commonest: tender blue-red nodules on the backs of the legs in young to middle-aged women, with granulomatous lobular panniculitis and neutrophilic vasculitis. Others: papulonecrotic (varioliform scars), lichen scrofulosorum (follicular papules). Resolve with anti-TB therapy.
turner-syndrome: Single functional X (45,X in ~50%); 45,X/46,XX mosaicism has a better prognosis. Triad: infertility, failure of puberty, short stature. Skin: neonatal lymphoedema of hands/feet/neck (80%), neck webbing after cystic hygroma, over-curved nails, low posterior hairline, many melanocytic and halo naevi without increased melanoma risk. More alopecia areata, vitiligo, psoriasis and thyroid autoimmunity. Diagnosed by karyotype.
typhus: Typhus group rickettsioses: epidemic louse-borne (R. prowazekii; overcrowding, refugee camps; untreated mortality 20-50%; Brill-Zinsser recurrence months to years later) and murine (R. typhi; fleas, milder). Fever, headache, myalgia, then a maculopapular rash sparing face, palms and soles; no eschar, unlike scrub typhus. Tetracyclines (doxycycline) are effective.
uraemic-pruritus: CKD-associated itch affecting about one-third of dialysis patients (more with haemodialysis than CAPD); not seen when uraemia is from acute renal failure. Mostly the back, worse at night, with heat and stress; relieved by cool temperatures and activity. Some develop acquired reactive perforating collagenosis. Oral antihistamines and systemic steroids are generally not effective; transplant usually resolves it.
urticaria-an-overview: Individual wheals resolve within 24 hours; chronic if >6 weeks. About half of chronic spontaneous cases have functional IgG autoantibodies to IgE or FcεRIα; associated with thyroid disease, SLE, coeliac disease. Vessel-wall damage on biopsy means urticarial vasculitis. Angioedema without wheals: consider ACE inhibitor or C1 esterase deficiency.
urticaria-in-children: Acute urticaria is far more common than chronic in children, and about 40% of acute cases have angioedema. Viral infection triggers about 40%; about 50% have no trigger. Food allergy usually on or after first exposure (egg, milk, soy, peanut, wheat). Mimics: insect bites, contact dermatitis, erythema multiforme, urticarial vasculitis (wheals >24 h, leave bruising).
urticarial-vasculitis: Urticaria-like wheals that persist >24 hours in a fixed location, are burning or painful rather than itchy, and heal with ecchymoses or hyperpigmentation. Biopsy: neutrophilic leukocytoclastic vasculitis early, lymphocytic later. Hypocomplementaemic form has more systemic disease (angioedema, abdominal and joint pain) and is linked to SLE.
varicose-veins: Engorged, tortuous veins (>3 mm = CEAP C2) of the lower legs, a manifestation of venous insufficiency; diagnosed clinically, with duplex ultrasound to define truncal reflux. Risks: obesity, pregnancy, prolonged standing, family history (both identical twins affected in 75%). Complications: bleeding, thrombophlebitis, stasis dermatitis, lipodermatosclerosis, venous ulcer.
venous-insufficiency: Chronic venous hypertension from incompetent valves, previous DVT or failed calf muscle pump. Ankle pitting oedema worse at day's end, haemosiderin rusty-red pigmentation, varicosities, and corona phlebectatica paraplantaris (malleolar flare), a sign of severe stasis. Complications: venous eczema, lipodermatosclerosis, atrophie blanche, stasis ulcer. Duplex ultrasound shows reflux.
vexas-syndrome: Adult-onset, almost exclusively male autoinflammatory disease from a somatic UBA1 mutation (p.Met41) on the X chromosome. Skin: Sweet-like neutrophilic dermatosis, nose/ear chondritis sparing airways and ribs, vasculitis. Macrocytic anaemia with normal B12/folate; marrow shows vacuolated erythroid and myeloid precursors; MDS, myeloma or MGUS may coexist. Treatment-resistant; only high-dose steroids help consistently; poor prognosis.
vogt-koyanagi-harada-syndrome: Bilateral granulomatous panuveitis with neurological signs (meningism, tinnitus, hearing loss) and skin signs, from CD4+ T-cell autoimmunity against melanocytes. Vitiligo, poliosis and alopecia areata (~30% of patients) appear in the chronic convalescent stage with a 'sunset glow' fundus. More common in pigmented races and women (2:1). Sympathetic ophthalmia can mimic it almost identically.
vulval-intraepithelial-neoplasia-images: Two types. Usual type (uVIN/HSIL): HPV 16/18/33, smoking, immunosuppression; younger, often multifocal; p16 positive; warty cancers; vaccine reduces risk. Differentiated (dVIN): HPV-independent, arises in lichen sclerosus or erosive lichen planus, older women, basal dysplasia, p53 positive, up to 85% progress to SCC untreated. Biopsy hyperkeratotic areas unresponsive to potent steroids.
waardenburg-syndrome: Neurocristopathy: sensorineural deafness plus pigmentary change (white forelock/poliosis, heterochromia iridis, leukoderma). Type 1 (most common, PAX3) has dystopia canthorum; type 2 has normal inner canthi; type 3 (Klein) adds limb anomalies; type 4 (Shah) adds Hirschsprung disease. Mostly autosomal dominant; EDN3/EDNRB usually recessive. Causes 2-5% of congenital deafness.
wells-syndrome: Recurrent itchy or burning erythematous plaques resembling cellulitis/erysipelas on a limb that do not respond to antibiotics. Histology: dermal oedema with eosinophils and no vasculitis, then flame figures (not pathognomonic; also in bullous pemphigoid, arthropod bites, EGPA), later granulomatous. Eosinophilia in about 50%. Rapid response to oral steroids but relapses as dose is reduced.
wet-gangrene: Gangrene from necrotising bacterial infection (dry gangrene is ischaemic); initially mimics cellulitis. Red flags: haemorrhagic bullae, ecchymosis preceding necrosis, crepitus, cutaneous anaesthesia, pain out of proportion. Causes: polymicrobial (diabetics), group A strep, Vibrio vulnificus (oysters), Clostridium perfringens gas gangrene. Surgical exploration is the gold standard for necrotising fasciitis.
whipple-disease: Tropheryma whipplei, an intracellular gram-positive rod accumulating in duodenal macrophages (PAS-positive; also PCR, EM, immunohistochemistry). Classic tetrad: arthralgia, weight loss, malabsorptive diarrhoea, abdominal pain; skin signs are very rare (malnutrition-related pigmentation, purpura, ichthyosis, or eczema/psoriasis/erythema nodosum-like). Treatment can trigger Jarisch-Herxheimer or IRIS.
white-sponge-naevus: Autosomal dominant, bilateral white spongy folded mucosal plaques (buccal mucosa most common) that cannot be scraped off; keratin 4 or 13 mutation. Biopsy shows large clear epidermal cells. No skin, nail or hair change (unlike pachyonychia congenita, Darier disease, dyskeratosis congenita). Misdiagnosed as candidiasis (peelable) or lichen planus; no oral cancer reported.
wilson-disease: Autosomal recessive ATP7B mutation (chromosome 13) with copper deposition in liver, then brain; hepatolenticular degeneration. Kayser-Fleischer rings, low serum ceruloplasmin (normal in 5-10%), liver copper over 250 mcg/g dry weight. Liver disease usually first (cirrhosis in the first decade), neurological signs in 2nd-3rd decade. Skin: hypermelanotic pigmentation, jaundice, spider telangiectases, palmar erythema. Haemolytic anaemia can occur.
winter-itch: Pruritus hiemalis: itch without a primary rash in cold weather, mainly older people with dry skin; legs (thighs, behind knees, calves, ankles), sparing hands, feet, face and scalp. Sudden onset, worse at night and on undressing, aggravated by wool; not influenced by bathing frequency or water temperature. Clears in summer; emollients are the mainstay.
wiskott-aldrich-syndrome: X-linked (WASP gene): microthrombocytopenia with small platelets, eczema indistinguishable from atopic eczema (80%), and immunodeficiency with recurrent infections (molluscum, HSV, Pneumocystis). Low IgM and IgG, normal-to-high IgA and IgE. Autoimmunity (haemolytic anaemia, vasculitis), leukaemia and B-cell lymphoma risk. Live vaccines (BCG, MMR) contraindicated; avoid NSAIDs; stem cell transplant is curative.
x-linked-agammaglobulinaemia: BTK mutation: boys with no mature B cells or plasma cells and severely low immunoglobulins; infections start at 6-18 months as maternal antibody wanes. Recurrent sinopulmonary infections (pneumococcus, streptococcus, staphylococcus), giardia diarrhoea, skin infections; small tonsils and lymph nodes. Avoid live vaccines (MMR, polio, rotavirus, varicella); lifelong immunoglobulin replacement.
xylazine-induced-skin-ulcers: Veterinary alpha-2 agonist ('Tranq') mixed with fentanyl; profound vasoconstriction causes ischaemic necrosis. Well-demarcated, painful, malodorous ulcers with black eschars, mainly over extensor surfaces of the extremities, sometimes at sites distant from injection. Short half-life makes toxicology unreliable; respiratory depression may not respond to naloxone. Mimics: pyoderma gangrenosum, ecthyma gangrenosum, dermatitis artefacta.
zika-virus: Flavivirus spread by Aedes aegypti (also sexually and vertically); only ~1 in 5 symptomatic. Milder than dengue: itchy morbilliform or scarlatiniform rash starting on the face, conjunctivitis, palatal petechiae. Complications: Guillain-Barre syndrome; congenital microcephaly with intracranial calcifications. Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs; serology cross-reacts with dengue.
zygomycosis: Mucorales (Rhizopus, Mucor, Lichtheimia) cause mucormycosis, mainly in diabetes (leading predisposing cause), haematological malignancy and iron overload: necrotic eschar with induration; biopsy shows broad non-septate vasculotropic hyphae, and culture is negative in up to 50%. Rhinocerebral red flags: palatal black ulcer, proptosis, cranial nerve palsy. Entomophthorales give painless firm subcutaneous swelling in healthy hosts.
